#3035. Today, Voyager 1 Becomes the First Spacecraft a Full Light-Day From Home

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Voyager 1 has been flying at about 38,000 mph since 1980. This morning, that steady pace carries it a full light-day from home.

NASA’s Voyager 1 left Earth on Sept. 5, 1977, carrying a camera, a set of science instruments and a gold-plated record of sounds and images from home. Forty-nine years later, it’s reaching a distance no spacecraft has attained before: one light-day, or roughly 16.1 billion miles, from Earth. At that range, light needs a full 24 hours to make the trip between Earth and the probe.

At 5:16:07 a.m. ET on Wednesday, Nov. 18, Voyager 1 became the first human-made object to reach that light-day milestone. From that point on, a radio signal between the spacecraft and NASA’s Deep Space Network takes more than a day to travel in either direction.

NASA puts the journey at 49 years, two months and 11 days, counting from Voyager 1’s launch in September 1977. The probe still sends data home, though at a rate slower than dial-up, and NASA plans a live discussion with the Voyager team on Thursday to mark the occasion.

It’s quite an accomplishment for a spacecraft built in the mid-1970s. One light-day is the distance that light travels in a single day at the speed of light, which is approximately 186,282 miles per second. That translates to 25.9 billion kilometers or about 16.1 billion miles in a single day. At an average human walking speed of 3 mph, it would take a human 612,015 years to travel that distance on foot.

Fortunately, Voyager 1 has been traveling a bit faster. It currently zips through the cosmos at a steady 37,763 mph, a speed it achieved in 1980 after a gravity-assisted Saturn flyby. It has been flying at that speed ever since.

The milestone comes 14 years after Voyager 1 crossed the heliopause, the point where the sun’s heliosphere ends, and entered interstellar space. It’s also 28 years after the spacecraft passed Pioneer 10 to become the human-made object that has traveled the farthest into space.

NASA marked the milestone with a global Shine Bright for Voyager’s Light-Day event on Tuesday evening. Just after sunset, the agency wanted people to head outside and point their smartphone or tablet lights skyward to spark a planet-wide wave of light as Earth rotates, much like fans doing the wave at a stadium.

The space agency also made a website for the occasion. The website is simple. It flashes Voyager’s VGR call sign in Morse code. If you want to try it, click the link, hit begin, and then point your phone or tablet screen at the sky. The website does all the work for you.

NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory will follow up on Thursday at noon ET with a moderated discussion on the milestone, featuring status updates on both Voyager probes and a live Q&A with reporters and audience members.

The historic milestone isn’t without its drama. Voyager 1 has been in space for nearly half a century, and in that time, the Jet Propulsion Laboratory has done everything it can to extend the spacecraft’s life. That includes troubleshooting issues, performing maintenance, and shutting down various systems to save power and extend the spacecraft’s lifespan.

Several of those efforts took place in 2026. The team running Voyager 1 spent weeks shutting down three devices and powering on three low-power alternatives to reduce overall power usage. This initiative, which was internally called the Big Bang, was also performed on Voyager 2. The transition was completed in early September, giving Voyager 1 more time with its dwindling power supply while also keeping it warm enough to continue operating in the frigid conditions of interstellar space.

It was a tricky maneuver that required the team to simultaneously turn multiple instruments on and off. The difficulty of the maneuver was amplified by the fact that it took almost a full day for a signal to reach Voyager and another full day for Voyager to send a signal back, with hours of downtime while the spacecraft performed the operations.

All of this took place several months after Voyager 1 experienced a sudden drop in power, which necessitated shutting off one of its three instruments still in operation. Voyager 1 now has only two operational instruments.

Making it a whole light-day away from Earth is likely going to be Voyager 1’s final milestone while it still has enough power to communicate with Earth. Voyager 1 is powered by three radioisotope thermoelectric generators. They are essentially nuclear-powered batteries that generate energy by converting the steady heat from decaying plutonium-238.

When Voyager 1 first launched, its radioisotope thermoelectric generators produced about 470 watts of power. But plutonium-238 doesn’t last forever, and after 50 years in space, those generators now produce about 215 watts of power, with an average loss of about 4 watts per year. Most of that power is used to keep Voyager 1 up and running, which is why NASA has shut down eight of the 10 instruments that Voyager had when it launched.

At its current rate of usage and decay, Voyager 1 is expected to shut down its final science instrument in the 2030s and will eventually lose communication with Earth in 2036 due to insufficient power to send back a radio signal.

The same fate is expected for Voyager 2, Voyager 1’s twin, which has also spent half a century in space. While it is labeled the sequel, Voyager 2 actually launched 16 days before Voyager 1, and the two have spent nearly identical amounts of time traversing the cosmos. Thanks to its slower speed and trajectory, it likely won’t reach the one light-day distance until after its instruments shut down.

Voyager 1 will lose all of its power before it hits its next milestone, which is the beginning of the Oort Cloud, a vast, icy shell of comets at the edge of our solar system. It’ll take about 300 years for Voyager 1 to make it there.

Thanks to the near-perfect vacuum of outer space, Voyager 1 will continue to fly at its current speed even after it shuts down entirely. So it’ll still hit that milestone; it just won’t be able to phone home to tell us about it.

#3033. Which Laptops Last the Longest? Check Out the Laptops I’ve Tested With the Best Battery Life

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

As part of our video series Holiday Office Hours From the Labs, I share laptop recommendations and explain why battery life surged in 2026.

I can almost guarantee that your next laptop will run longer on battery power than whatever you’re currently using. We’ve seen a huge leap in laptop battery life in recent years, to the point where getting 20 or more hours on a single charge isn’t uncommon. This year alone, the average battery life of the laptops we’ve tested at CNET has increased by more than five hours. And it’s nearly doubled since the start of the decade.

With many of today’s laptops, you can leave the charger at home for days at a time. The longest-lasting laptop I tested this year lasted more than 34 hours!

This increase in battery life is one of the biggest stories in laptops this year. In the laptop episode of our video series Holiday Office Hours From the Labs, I explain what’s behind this surge in battery life and highlight some of the laptops that lasted the longest in testing.

Plus, my colleagues Kyle Kucharski from ZDNET and Joe Osborne from PCMag share their own holiday laptop picks. Kyle looks at Apple’s entry-level MacBook Neo and its imitators, and Joe breaks down what to look for in a budget gaming laptop.

Unlike raw performance, where the more you spend, the more you get, lengthy battery life can be found just as easily in a budget laptop as in an expensive, high-end powerhouse. And, in fact, less powerful components and lower screen resolutions can give cheaper laptops an edge in battery life.

The biggest factor behind longer battery life in laptops is the advancement in mobile processors. They’ve become much more power efficient, and in the case of Apple’s and Qualcomm’s chips, they’re based on an architecture other than the traditional x86 instruction set that’s been at the heart of Intel processors since the dawn of the PC era.

Apple’s run of battery-life winners started when it shifted from Intel processors to its own M-series chips. Apple’s M-series processors are based on the Arm architecture, a power-efficient chip architecture found in phones and tablets. Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X-series processors are also Arm-based, and they can be found in the two longest-running laptops we’ve tested: the HP OmniBook 3 16 and OmniBook 5 14. The OmniBook 3 16’s record-setting battery performance earned it a CNET Lab Award for longest battery life.

Intel has made huge strides in processor efficiency with its last two generations of chips: the Core Ultra 200 series developed under the name Lunar Lake, and the Core Ultra 300 series, also known as Panther Lake. Last year, the Lenovo Yoga 9i 2-in-1 Aura Edition became the first Intel laptop to last longer than a day, running for 25 hours, 45 minutes in testing. It’s still the longest-running Intel laptop we’ve tested, but the MSI Prestige 14 Flip AI Plus with Intel’s next-gen Core Ultra X7 358H processor came close with a time of 25 hours, 18 minutes.

Read more: Laptops With the Best Battery Life

Whether Arm or x86, there are two more reasons behind greater processor efficiency and longer laptop battery life. For one, the size of a processor shrinks with every generation. The smaller a processor is and the more tightly packed its components are, the less power is required to flip its tinier transistors on and off. For another, today’s mobile processors feature more flexible designs with a mix of performance and efficiency cores. A processor engages its higher-performance cores only when needed, using the efficiency cores for as many general, everyday tasks as possible, so your laptop stays cool and quiet and runs longer.

For more, you can read my Labs exclusive on the huge increase in laptop battery life this year and check out the video above for my holiday laptop picks and those from my colleagues.

#3032. With Democrats to Control Congress, Is It Better to Buy Bitcoin or an Index Fund?

Investors tend to have a number of misconceptions about what happens when Congress changes political hands.

By Alex Carchidi – Nov 18, 2026 at 7:45AM EST

Control of Congress just changed poltical hands in a big way, and, much as with all major changes, it's no surprise that it's making some investors a bit uneasy. Many holders of Bitcoin (BTC -1.68%) openly worry that the new Democratic majority will have a grudge against crypto due to the Trump administration's embrace of it. At the same time, index fund owners, even for the funds tracking the entire market like the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO +0.13%), are concerned about high valuations, persistent inflation, and artificial intelligence (AI), and those worries are amplified by widespread (and overstated) impressions that Democratic congresses tend to be bad for asset prices.

So, in light of the congressional switchover and the many uncertainties in the market right now, does it make more sense to buy Bitcoin, or an index fund?

First, let's establish some basic facts. A party gaining control of both houses of Congress is not something that's strongly associated with the market tanking or flying afterward.

From 1955 to 2023, the S&P 500 (^GSPC +0.06%) delivered a total return of 8.6% annually in years when a Republican president was balanced by a Democratic Congress (and one of those years, during the 2008 financial crisis, skews those results to the downside significantly). Patience and consistency were still the most important traits that investors needed to have to build their portfolios during those periods.

For Bitcoin, the last time Democrats held control of both congressional chambers, through all of 2021 and 2022, it fell 48%. But don't read too much into that; during the same time, the crypto industry was being rocked by the spectacular collapse of the FTX exchange, and Bitcoin was in one of its bear markets after a strong upward trend in the prior years.

Still, Senator Elizabeth Warren, a loud critic of the cryptocurrency industry, is expected to chair the Senate Banking Committee when the new Congress is seated in 2027. She's also one of the senators that detractors traditionally single out as being noxious to stock and crypto prices. A closer inspection reveals that Warren's recent crypto scrutiny has focused on allegedly corrupt practices of some crypto businesses, like those associated with the Trump family and the Trump administration. Similarly, Warren has been in politics for a long time, and the stock market has still on average increased annually during her tenure.

So, it's my assessment that many of the politics-related concerns about Bitcoin and the U.S. stock market are heavily overstated despite being modestly grounded in reality.

Politics aside, there are other reasons that investors propose for being a bit squeamish about buying either Bitcoin or an index fund.

The lofty valuation of the market is a big and real concern. One valuation metric, the Shiller cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings (CAPE) ratio, divides the S&P 500's price by its average inflation-adjusted earnings during the prior decade, and it was near 40 on Nov. 17, whereas its long-run mean is 17.5. High valuations tend to predict lower future returns until either earnings catch up or share prices go down; Vanguard's forecast as of Sept. 30 is for  U.S. stocks to return 4.8% to 6.8% per year during the next decade, suggesting a lower-than-average annual return.

Bitcoin is having somewhat of the opposite problem. With its price at $63,360 as of Nov. 17, it's almost 50% below its peak set in October 2025. Its price now is just a bit higher than it was five years ago. That can make it hard to stomach making a purchase.

If you must pick between buying Bitcoin and shares of an index fund, pick the index fund.

An index fund tracking the S&P 500 holds shares of roughly 500 large companies, so its value rests on corporate profits even if valuations shrink. Furthermore, a committee at index provider S&P Dow Jones Indices periodically swaps out companies that no longer meet its criteria, and companies whose market value is growing carry more weight in the index. In contrast, Bitcoin has no cash flow, so its price depends on new buyers willing to pay the market price, and it's obviously harder to attract them when its price isn't climbing steadily.

Of course, most people needn't choose only one of these assets. Anyone buying Bitcoin should already own plenty of index fund shares, and Bitcoin is also something that should be a limited part of most diversified portfolios already.

#3031. Have $1,000? This Beaten-Down Biotech Has 4 Phase 3 Obesity Trials Underway.

Even a small share of the massive market for weight loss drugs could lead to a significant increase in this company's share price.

By Lee Samaha – Nov 18, 2026 at 8:00AM EST

10 stocks we like better than Viking Therapeutics ›

Phase 3 trials are always interesting because of their proximity to approval and ultimate commercialization of drugs, and particularly so when it involves one with a huge total addressable market (TAM) such as obesity. In addition, the drug in question here, Viking Therapeutics' VK2735, is in a class that already includes one blockbuster drug: Eli Lilly's (LLY -0.89%) tirzepatide (Zepbound for obesity and Mounjaro for obesity with type 2 diabetes), which is approved. All these developments make Viking Therapeutics an attractive stock for investors. Here's why.

The four phase 3 trials comprise two ongoing 78-week trials of VK2735 in subcutaneous form (obesity and obesity with type 2 diabetes; results due in 2027) and two recently started 68-week trials in oral form (results more likely in 2028) for the same indications.

The trials are part of management's strategy to potentially offer VK2735 across a range of dosing options, including a dual formulation option in which initial weight loss from subcutaneous dosing could be followed by maintenance dosing with a more convenient oral form.

Investors have high hopes for the glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1) and glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) receptor agonist, on the back of the success of Eli Lilly's GLP-1/GIP agonist, tirzepatide, and the phase 2 data from the VK2735 trials, which indicate it could achieve a steeper rate of weight loss than tirzepatide. I use cautionary language, as any comparison between two independent trials (let alone a phase 2 and a phase 3) should be accompanied by qualifications.

That said, VK2735 has demonstrated an impressive ability to produce rapid weight loss, as confirmed in a recent small 33-week maintenance study, in which an initial 21-week subcutaneous dose was followed by a subcutaneous maintenance dose over 12 weeks. An exploratory cohort in this trial reported 21.7% weight loss after 33 weeks.

The success of this maintenance trial, the first part of a two-part trial, encouraged management to raise a net $547.8 million in a well-received stock offering at $35 and convertible senior notes.

As good as the maintenance trial was, investors should note the second part of the trial (ongoing) is arguably more important, as it involves an initial 21-week subcutaneous dose followed by oral dosing over 12 weeks. The point is that phase 2 of oral VK2735 had questionable tolerability (a 20% discontinuation rate due to adverse events in the treated group), and Viking will have to demonstrate better tolerability in the maintenance trial and the phase 3 oral trials.

I previously outlined the math showing how a $10,000 investment in Viking Therapeutics could grow to $47,800 in 2030; it follows that a $1,000 investment could grow to $4,780.

That's the bullish case scenario, but investors always need to consider the risk that the phase 3 trials will fail to meet their primary endpoints or could deliver efficacy or tolerability data that negatively impacts the commercial appeal of the drug, not least because it's a highly competitive market with Eli Lilly, Novo Nordisk, and others developing rival drugs.

The strongest case for the stock isn't that VK2735 will become a blockbuster drug, but rather that even if it captures only a relatively small share of the market, it will be enough to drive a significant increase in the share price of the $3.5 billion market-cap company.

It could do so provided its phase 3 trials deliver on the weight loss generated in the phase 2 trials and, ideally, some improved tolerability data in the maintenance study, which is due to report results next year. Investors will need to be patient, as the oral trial results (crucial to the dual formulation strategy) aren't likely to be available until 2028. The long-term potential is obvious, and Viking Therapeutics could always be acquired by a larger company seeking a late-stage obesity drug candidate.

#3030. Ray Dalio says Bessent move is sign that a debt crisis is getting closer; recommends gold and bitcoin

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's debt buyback announcement this week fits into a broader pattern that can signal a forthcoming crisis, according to billionaire investor Ray Dalio.

The Bridgewater Associates founder said Bessent's plan to increase government debt purchases may portend trouble for the U.S. economy. Coupled with the Japanese government reducing its U.S. bond market exposure and surging long-dated American bond yields, Dalio said investors may want to prepare their portfolios for increased risk by owning cryptocurrencies and gold.

"I am confident that the government's financial condition is at an inflection point," Dalio wrote in a LinkedIn post published Friday. "If this is not dealt with now, the debts will build up to levels where they can't be managed without great trauma."

Dalio noted that the Treasury Department has "only limited capacity" to buy back bonds. Bessent told CNBC on Thursday that his team was going to "make a market" and that the purchases would likely top $4 billion.

The U.S. is spending about 40% more than it's bringing in, resulting in the burgeoning budget deficit, Dalio said. The U.S. budget deficit topped $432 billion in July, but Bessent told CNBC that it's likely peaked under President Donald Trump's administration.

Bessent said in the interview that a team was looking at ways to shrink spending by hundreds of billions of dollars. But Dalio said there is "very little ability" to do so given that it is either committed or considered essential.

After years of overspending, Dalio said total debt now dwarfs what the U.S. brings in each year. If the U.S. government was a business, Dalio said debt service payments would come in at roughly $11 trillion — about 200% of annual revenue.

Dalio, 77, warned the cost of repaying principal and servicing the debt will only grow over time.

To solve this, Dalio said the U.S. needs to carefully employ a three-part strategy to get the budget deficit down to 3% of gross domestic product.

First, Dalio said the U.S. government needs to reduce its spending. Second, he said tax revenue needs to be raised. Finally, the New York native and Harvard Business School alumni said lower interest rates were needed.

"All three need to happen concurrently so as to prevent any one from being too large," Dalio said. "If any one is too large, the adjustment will be traumatic."

Dalio cautioned against ramming through these adjustments by "force." For instance, "it would be very bad if the Federal Reserve unnaturally forced interest rates down," he said.

Dalio said it's important to to take steps now, while the economy is healthy. An economy in recession requires increased government spending, he said.

Dalio said the exact timing of a debt crisis can be swayed by variables ranging from military conflict to political change. On its current trajectory, the U.S. could enter such a crisis in as early as one year or as late as five. "My guess, which I suppose will be a bad one, is that it will come in three years, give or take two, if the course we're on is not changed."

To prepare, Dalio recommended investors are underweight debt assets, such as bonds.

As much as 10% to 15% of a portfolio could land in gold, as well as "a bit" of bitcoin, the hedge fund founder said.

Dalio's post came at the tail end of a volatile week for U.S. financial markets. Rising long-term Treasury yields have pressured stocks, leading the S&P 500 to snap a a three-week-long advance.

#3029. Nvidia Is in Turmoil, But Earnings Are Still Rocketing Higher. Is the Stock a Buy?

Jensen Huang resigned last week following allegations of affairs.

By Adria Cimino – Nov 18, 2026 at 8:05AM EST

Nvidia (NVDA -0.46%) just continued to do something that it's done quarter after quarter in recent years: The tech powerhouse reported earnings that beat analysts' estimates and spoke of soaring demand for its high-powered artificial intelligence (AI) chips. So Nvidia has once again demonstrated that the potential slowdown some investors feared hasn't materialized.

That's fantastic news, but this comes at a time of turmoil for Nvidia. Jensen Huang, who founded the company and led its successes for more than 30 years, stepped down last week. This followed allegations of affairs, including one with a person U.S. intelligence says is a Chinese spy. Nvidia's board named longtime finance chief Colette Kress as interim CEO while a search for a permanent leader takes place.

Against this backdrop of uncertainty yet tremendous earnings growth, is the stock a buy? Let's find out.

So, first, a quick summary of the Nvidia story over the past few years. The company got in early on AI, designing its chips to suit this area well before others. This gave Nvidia a head start from a technology perspective and the time to build valuable relationships with customers. All of this resulted in earnings soaring once the AI boom gathered momentum -- and Nvidia's stock price followed as investors were eager to bet on this high-potential space.

Jensen Huang took center stage through it all due to his leading role in Nvidia's successes and his significant presence in the AI community. He was viewed as a driving force at the company and within the industry as a whole. So his departure clearly introduced an element of uncertainty.

That said, the technology built under Huang's leadership and the plan set out for the coming years haven't disappeared. Nvidia has a solid foundation, as we can see through the fiscal 2027 third-quarter earnings numbers. Revenue soared 103% to $115 billion, beating analysts' estimates of about $109 billion, and net income of more than $65 billion surpassed estimates by about $5 billion.

The period was an important one for Nvidia as it rolled out its most advanced platform yet, Vera Rubin, and the ongoing solid demand for this system bodes well for the quarters to come. In this, its first quarter, Rubin generated almost $20 billion in revenue, for Nvidia's fastest product ramp ever, Kress said during the earnings call.

Nvidia's compute continues to be fully used across customers, a testament to demand and the popularity of the company's chips. And based on data center readiness, the durability of demand, and customer access to capital, Nvidia raised its outlook for growth in the coming full year to 75% from its earlier estimate of 70%.

All of this is reassuring for investors who might have worried about a potential flagging of demand.

Meanwhile, Nvidia shares look dirt cheap, trading at a little over 16x forward earnings estimates.

Still, it's important to remember that Huang's absence, as well as uncertainty about who will be the next leader at Nvidia, could weigh on the stock in the weeks to come. Sentiment, rather than earnings figures and market position, may guide the stock price. Huang also must testify before Congress following allegations of his relationship with a possible spy. Any information gathered could lead to more government scrutiny concerning Nvidia or even greater regulation.

Of course, that is one possibility. Considering the stock already dropped 35% from early last month through Nov. 17, it might be ripe for a rebound. Investors could jump to get in on this opportunity, pushing the stock higher over the next few weeks.

That said, until Nvidia names a permanent CEO and that person lays out a clear roadmap for the future, a certain amount of risk remains. Should you buy? If you're a cautious investor, you might prefer to wait on the sidelines for now, but if you don't mind a bit of risk, the positive points I mentioned above may outweigh the negatives, and now might be a great moment to pick up a few Nvidia shares.

#3028. Intel vs. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing: Which Tech Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

Intel is betting big on external foundry customers, while Taiwan Semiconductor's margins sit above 50%. Which chipmaker deserves your capital heading into the next cycle?

By Erin Kennedy – Updated Nov 18, 2026 at 8:08AM EST

The chip industry is undergoing a massive shift as artificial intelligence and local manufacturing take center stage. Choosing between Intel (INTC -0.40%) and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM +0.76%) requires weighing a turnaround story against a market leader.

Intel focuses on designing its own processors while opening its factories to external customers. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing serves as a pure-play foundry, producing high-end chips for nearly every major player among semiconductor stocks. Both companies are central to the global tech supply chain but offer very different risk and reward profiles.

Intel designs and manufactures a wide range of processors, accelerators, and software solutions for the modern computing world. Under its latest strategy, the company is combining its internal chip design with a massive expansion of its foundry services to manufacture chips for other businesses. Its customer base is diverse, including distributors, original equipment manufacturers, and cloud service providers across sectors like healthcare, finance, and telecommunications.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 26, 2026, revenue reached approximately $59.9 billion, representing revenue growth of nearly 12.1% compared to the previous period. However, the company faced significant headwinds, reporting a net loss of roughly $12 billion during this time frame. This result highlights the high costs associated with its ongoing efforts to regain a leading position in the semiconductor market.

As of Intel's December 2025 balance sheet, the company carries a debt-to-equity ratio of nearly 0.4, which compares total debt to shareholder equity. The current ratio is approximately 2, indicating the ability to cover short-term financial obligations with assets that can be converted to cash within a year. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 27, 2025, free cash flow was approximately negative $4.9 billion. Note that stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 25.1% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation, since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing operates as a pure-play foundry, focusing exclusively on manufacturing semiconductors designed by its customers. It serves the most demanding segments of the market, including smartphones and high-performance artificial intelligence applications, from its base in Taiwan and facilities worldwide. By acting as a manufacturer for others, the company avoids competing directly with its clients while maintaining a critical role in the global tech supply chain.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached nearly $150.2 billion, an increase of approximately 36.1%. This growth translated into net income of close to $76.8 billion, resulting in a robust net margin of roughly 51.1%. These figures demonstrate the strong demand for the advanced manufacturing nodes that the company provides to its diverse customer base.

As of TSM's December 2025 balance sheet, the current ratio was roughly 2.5, reflecting a healthy cushion for meeting short-term liabilities. The company maintains a conservative debt-to-equity ratio of nearly 0.2, showing that its total debt is low relative to its equity. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was approximately $30.1 billion, providing substantial capital to reinvest in the next generation of chip technology.

Intel faces intense competition from companies like NVIDIA (NVDA -0.46%) and AMD (AMD +2.09%), as well as hyperscalers who are increasingly designing their own custom silicon. The company is also navigating legal challenges, including shareholder lawsuits filed in November 2026 alleging concealment of manufacturing and inventory issues. High capital intensity and the operational risks of its turnaround strategy remain significant hurdles as it builds out new leading-edge factories while relying on sole-source suppliers like ASML (ASML +0.48%) for critical tools.

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing is exposed to risks associated with the high concentration of its manufacturing facilities in a single geographic region. This concentration creates sensitivity to geopolitical tensions and potential supply chain disruptions that could impact its global operations. Additionally, the company must continually invest billions in new technology nodes to stay ahead of rivals, which entails significant capital risk if demand for high-end chips from major customers like Apple (AAPL +0.85%) or NVIDIA fluctuates.

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing looks cheaper on a forward P/E basis, while Intel has a lower P/S ratio based on sales over the past 12 months.

Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

A large part of the reason Intel reported that $12 billion loss is because it's in the midst of a turnaround. It's pivoting toward providing chip manufacturing services for third parties. In order to do so, the chipmaker is having to shell out a lot of money to build fabrication plants. Intel even suspended its dividend a few years ago in pursuit of this new strategy. That spending will likely continue, as turning around a ship of Intel's size is neither a fast nor an easy endeavor.

Now, let's see how each stock has performed over the past 10 years:

Intel's stock is miles behind Taiwan Semiconductor's, and worse yet, it hasn't even kept pace with the S&P 500 (^GSPC +0.06%), trailing it by over 180 percentage points.

Taiwan Semiconductor dominates the foundry market and maintains a strong net margin despite operating in a capital-intensive business. It also pays a modest dividend.

I think there are too many unknowns tied to Intel's strategic transformation. Taiwan Semiconductor looks like a better buy for 2027 and beyond.

#3024. Prediction: This Cryptocurrency Will Outperform Bitcoin in 2027

Solana has a track record of significantly outperforming Bitcoin during bull market cycles.

By Dominic Basulto – Nov 18, 2026 at 8:10AM EST

Given that Bitcoin (BTC -1.68%) typically leads the crypto market higher or lower, it's no surprise that it gets the most attention from crypto investors. Bitcoin is a reliable barometer of how the crypto market is doing at any point in time.

But here's the thing: Altcoins typically have higher highs than Bitcoin, as well as lower lows. For that reason, they tend to outperform Bitcoin significantly during crypto bull market cycles.

If you're expecting the crypto market to rally next year, it will be altcoins dazzling investors with their performance. The one altcoin that I'm focused on right now is Solana (SOL +0.86%), and here's why.

Ever since its launch back in 2020, Solana has been touted as a potential Ethereum (ETH -1.82%) killer, due to its faster speeds, lower costs, and superior scalability. In 2023, Cathie Wood of Ark Invest specifically pointed to Solana as a potential disruptive force in the crypto market. After years of waiting, 2027 could be the year that Solana finally puts it all together.

For one, Solana is rapidly outgrowing its reputation as simply a place to buy, sell, and speculate in meme coins. It's moving into institutional-grade finance, and is picking up some big-name backers along the way. That's raising Solana's profile in the world of decentralized finance (DeFi).

Take tokenized equities, for example. Solana recently partnered with the Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation (DTCC) to bring tokenized equities to the Solana blockchain. Heading into 2027, Solana is already one of the top blockchain networks for trading tokenized equities, or crypto that represents the ownership of stocks or other assets.

The same story is being repeated in other key niches of the blockchain and crypto world. That includes stablecoins, where Solana is now rapidly challenging the market-leading role of Ethereum.

When big-name corporations want to launch new stablecoins, they now turn to Solana. Case in point: Solana partnered with Western Union (WU -0.66%) in May on a new stablecoin launch.

Admittedly, the data set on market performance is limited, given that Solana has only been trading since 2020. But the numbers certainly hint at the type of outperformance Solana is capable of delivering over short periods of time (12 months or less).

In 2021, for example, Solana skyrocketed by 11,166% while Bitcoin cruised to a gain of 60%. In 2023, Solana soared by 920%, while Bitcoin rose by 155%.

On the flip side, Solana definitely has lower lows than Bitcoin. In 2022, for example, Solana collapsed by 94%, while Bitcoin lost 64% of its value. That helps to explain why Solana is down 45% this year, while Bitcoin is only down 28%.

If you're counting on a crypto rebound in 2027, then it will be altcoins leading the way, not Bitcoin. And the one altcoin that I'm expecting to be at the front of the pack is Solana.

#3023. Your AI's Confidence Score Won't Catch Products You Don't Carry

Srijith Ravikumar is a Principal Engineer at Amazon building AI search and recommendation systems. Published at ACM CIKM and IP&M.

In 2024, a Canadian tribunal ordered Air Canada to compensate a customer who had relied on its website chatbot’s advice about bereavement fares, and it rejected the airline’s argument that the chatbot was responsible for its own actions. Retailers face a version of that exposure: AI recommendations for products the store doesn’t carry. A tempting way to decide when to trust those suggestions is a score the model reports about itself.

Ask a recommendation model how confident it is, set a threshold and drop everything below it. That guardrail is easy to build and easy to report upward. In my tests, it barely worked. Across 48 test settings, filtering on stated confidence cut the share of out-of-catalog suggestions by a median of 0.02 percentage points, and in 18 of them, the filtered list came out slightly worse.

My study measured how often suggestions miss the catalog, not what a miss costs. The likely costs are easy to name. A customer taps a suggestion, finds nothing to buy and trusts the feature a little less. A slot that could have sold something goes to an item that can’t. An assistant that names products the store lacks invites complaints. Treat those as hypotheses to check against your own numbers.

This year I tested four widely used large language models from four different developers. Each suggested 10 items from a user’s history, working from memory with no access to the catalog, on three public datasets covering movies, local businesses and retail toys. I checked every suggestion against the catalog it was meant to come from, using a matching method validated against about 200 human judgments, and counted anything not in that catalog as a miss, whether or not it exists elsewhere.

The out-of-catalog rate depended heavily on the catalog. Across the four models and three catalogs, it ran from 0.6% to 61%. Every model stayed under 3% on movies and reached roughly half or more on toys, with identical instructions. A rate measured in one domain tells you little about another, and a vendor demo is one domain.

Confidence barely moved. Each model’s stated confidence on toys stayed within about four points of its confidence on movies, while its out-of-catalog rate rose twentyfold or more. Researchers have already shown that models stating their own confidence tend to be overconfident, a bias you could at least correct for. Here the bias wasn’t stable. Across the 12 model-and-catalog combinations, the models were underconfident in seven and overconfident in five: All four were underconfident on movies, and all four were overconfident on toys. A correction tuned on one catalog would point the wrong way on the next.

One explanation fits the data, though the data don’t prove it. Asked how confident it is, a model seems to rate how good it thinks the suggestion is. It can’t check whether the item sits in your catalog from memory.

The filter I used is split conformal abstention, which uses conformal prediction, a standard statistical technique, to drop the least-confident suggestions while guaranteeing that a set share of the good ones survive. Its best result across the 48 settings was a cut of under two percentage points. The method largely kept the good items, as designed. Its guarantee says nothing about removing bad ones.

I tested only the confidence a model states in words. Token probabilities, agreement across repeated samples and constrained generation are different signals I didn’t test, and they may do better. If your model only picks among candidates retrieved from your catalog, the failure changes shape: The risk becomes a poor pick among real items, and this study doesn’t speak to that.

Within that scope, these are the questions I’d bring to a product review, an AI governance meeting or a decision to fund the next phase.

Is every suggestion checked against the live catalog before a customer sees it? It removes items you can’t sell, though it won’t fix relevance.

How was the out-of-catalog number measured? If items are matched by title, the matching rule can move the answer more than the model does. On identical model outputs, plausible off-the-shelf matching rules disagreed on the toy catalog’s out-of-catalog rate by more than a factor of 10. Ask for a check against a couple of hundred hand-labeled cases, with the remaining error reported next to the number. Having the model return product IDs avoids the problem.

Is a promising fix being tested as an experiment? On the business catalog only, I told two models to recommend from a fixed catalog that I didn’t show them and asked how sure they were that each title was in it. Out-of-catalog suggestions fell from 12.9% to 1.5% for one model and from 14.4% to 8.9% for the other. Each cut is at least three times the filter’s best result. The paper reports the figures and compares the first cut directly against that result. That prompt changed the instruction and the confidence question at once, and it covers two models in one catalog. Before a rollout, ask for a test that changes one prompt element at a time, runs on a held-out sample of the live catalog and reports both the out-of-catalog rate and whether the suggestions stayed relevant.

Was it measured on your own catalog, including the long tail of products customers rarely look for? A benchmark from someone else’s data, or a pilot on your bestsellers, says little about those.

Keep the confidence score for sorting results or deciding where a person looks first. The governance question is a different one: What share of our AI suggestions aren’t in our live catalog, measured across the long tail? The confidence score can’t answer it.​

#3022. History Says AGNC's Dividend Can Survive a Stock Market Crash -- but Not Always at Full Size

AGNC has a long history of paying dividends, but that history is actually a fairly volatile one.

By Reuben Gregg Brewer – Nov 18, 2026 at 8:15AM EST

10 stocks we like better than AGNC Investment Corp. ›

AGNC Investment (AGNC +0.10%) is a well-respected mortgage real estate investment trust (REIT). That, however, does not mean it is a good option for every investor. That's important to keep in mind for dividend investors, noting the stock's massive 17% dividend yield. History makes it very clear that the dividend can be volatile, as highlighted by a dividend cut during the 2020 bear market. But there's more to this story than that one dividend cut. Here's what you need to know.

AGNC Investment is a REIT, a special corporate structure designed to pass income on to shareholders. As long as a REIT distributes at least 90% of its taxable income to shareholders, it avoids corporate-level taxation. Shareholders have to treat REIT dividends like regular income. (If you hold a REIT in a Roth IRA, however, you can avoid paying taxes on the dividends.) Basically, AGNC will likely always pay a substantive dividend because its corporate structure is designed to do just that.

That said, AGNC isn't a property-owning REIT, which is a fairly easy-to-understand business model. It is a mortgage REIT, which means it buys mortgages that have been pooled into bond-like securities. The company's value is essentially the value of its mortgage security portfolio. It earns the difference between its cost of capital and the interest its portfolio generates. There are two important facts here.

First, the value of its mortgage securities will change as interest rates rise and fall. The relationship is inverse: rising rates lead to a decline in value, and vice versa. This is important right now because rates are rising and AGNC's portfolio value is declining. Meanwhile, rising rates increase the company's cost of capital and can squeeze its profits. That said, falling interest rates aren't great either. While costs decline and the value of existing mortgage securities rises in that situation, new mortgage securities come with lower yields. There are a lot of moving parts, which makes AGNC and other mREITs most appropriate for more active investors.

This discussion hasn't even looked at what can happen during a bear market. Dislocations like that can cause unexpected outcomes. For example, during the 2020 bear market that accompanied the coronavirus pandemic, interest rates fell, the value of AGNC's portfolio declined, and it cut its dividend.

At the time, AGNC tied the cut directly to the decline in the value of its mortgage security portfolio. It also noted that the cut would allow it to invest for the future. However, the dividend has remained static since that cut. Meanwhile, the cash the mREIT generated in the third quarter of 2026 to pay its dividend was $0.37 per share compared to a dividend of $0.36 per share. That's not a lot of wiggle room. And it is facing the impact of rising rates on its portfolio, with its value falling nearly 17% in the quarter. To make matters worse, Wall Street is broadly concerned about the risk of another bear market. It isn't unreasonable to be worried about a possible dividend cut.

As the chart above highlights, however, the dividend has a much longer history of volatility. Note, too, that the stock price has tended to follow the dividend higher and lower. Given AGNC's corporate structure, you are likely to continue collecting dividends through both good and bad markets. But its history makes it pretty clear that the dividend simply can't be counted on if you hope to use it to pay your living expenses in retirement.

Conservative dividend investors generally look for companies that pay consistent dividends, with a preference for dividends that grow steadily over time. That's just not what AGNC has to offer. That doesn't mean it is a bad investment. It simply isn't a good fit for most income-focused investors given its history of dividend volatility. In fact, AGNC Investment makes the most sense if you reinvest dividends and focus on total return. Indeed, for many investors, this mREIT is a diversification tool rather than an income tool.

Each fall, our investing team spends the latter half of the year hands-on testing a wide range of brokers, from legacy firms like Charles Schwab and Fidelity to newer, mobile-first firms like Public and M1.

This year, we opened or tested more than 15 brokerage accounts, funded them and placed real trades. We sent each broker a detailed questionnaire covering more than 65 data points and then verified, categorized and scored their responses using our proprietary scoring system. And finally, though our team is spread across the U.S., we met in person to compare the experience of using each platform.

While our updated reviews and final star ratings are still in the works, here is a preview of five things that really stood out to us this season — and two things we’re feeling a bit wary of.

Setting up buy and sell orders can be a pain point for some investors, especially beginners. Until recently, every platform required you to type in the ticker symbol, choose between dollars and shares, punch in the numbers and choose your order type. This creates opportunities for mistakes.

In recent months, AI has stepped in to help. Many platforms have launched agents that you can ask to set up trades for you using natural language. Beginners aren’t the only people who benefit; some trading agents can also set up automated strategies based on prompts, thereby saving advanced traders a lot of time and effort monitoring the markets.

Public’s “Agents” feature, which started rolling out in March and became available to all users in August, has become a trailblazer in agentic trading. It can place trades for you, set up recurring trades to automate a strategy (Managing Editor Chris Davis experimented with a “buy the open, sell the close” strategy for a while), and even sweep uninvested cash into one of Public’s high-yield cash management account options.

Robinhood also waded into the agentic trading space in early 2025 with the launch of its Cortex assistant, whose early iterations could place individual trades for you. In September of this year, the broker began rolling out Robinhood Agents, a more sophisticated natural-language interface that can build automated strategies based on a prompt, similar to Public’s Agents.

Interactive Brokers also offers a simple AI agent (IBot) that can set up trades for you, as does Cash App (Moneybot), but these are limited to one-time actions and cannot automate more complex strategies. Still, they can simplify the trading experience for beginners. That might be especially valuable to Cash App users, given the platform’s “My First Brokerage” ethos.

» Curious about trading with a text prompt? Compare brokers with AI trading tools

There’s been another profound shift in the past year that involves AI: agents that can actually help you manage your brokerage account. So far, some of the newer, mobile-first platforms seem to have an edge over the long-established financial behemoths. It’s also a mind-bending gray area: If an AI is giving you portfolio advice, who’s accountable for the advice it gives? Can you trust it? And how is it any different from a robo-advisor?

In our reviews this year, we looked into these questions. But here's a quick look at how one platform in particular is approaching this new frontier.

From my testing over the years, I was already a huge fan of M1’s portfolio-building system, and now that it's integrated an AI advisor into the app (to be specific, M1 bills it as an SEC-registered AI fiduciary investment advisor legally required to act in your best interest), M1 has created what I truly think is a one-of-a-kind product and service. I checked the forms M1 is required to submit to the SEC, and the company declares outright that the AI advisor looks at your entire financial situation and gives actionable recommendations. In my experience with the app, those recommendations are based on your balances, the knowledge you provide and the ongoing conversations you have. There’s a lot to discuss here, which we’ll cover in our full M1 review, but suffice it to say, this is very impressive.

Most brokers don’t charge many fees these days. Trading, inactivity and account fees have slowly but surely disappeared, making investing more affordable over the years. But there is one fee you still have to pay: an expense ratio.

Most of the time, brokers have little control over expense ratios, since they’re set by fund managers. The only way a broker could offer an index fund without an expense ratio is if it was big enough to eat the cost.

This is exactly what Fidelity did back in 2018, when they introduced their “ZERO” funds. These funds have no expense ratios and no minimums, meaning they’re totally free for investors.

Fidelity remained the only broker to offer this kind of fund until 2025, when E*TRADE introduced a very similar lineup of no-expense-ratio index funds. The suite of funds from both brokers is fairly broad — think large-cap, total market, international — which makes them especially attractive to beginners building a portfolio from scratch.

Now, you may be wondering why these brokers decided to stray from the industry standard and offer products that don’t make them money. The idea is that the free funds will get you in the door — since you can only buy them if you have an account with that particular broker — and you’ll spend money on some other product they offer.

But does that make free index funds any less great? No. I still think it’s a big step toward making investing more accessible for everyone, and I’m excited to see which brokers might add a similar offering in the future.

» Take a closer look: Compare Fidelity's and E*TRADE's free index funds

I'm a big believer in putting every dollar to work, but that goal can sometimes fall through the cracks. Idle cash sitting uninvested in your brokerage account is a common oversight. It can easily pile up if you forget to reinvest sale proceeds or dividends (something I do more often than I’d like to admit). Or maybe you leave it parked for too long in your brokerage’s default account while waiting on a good investment opportunity.

Thankfully, most brokerages offer some form of interest on that uninvested money. Some put the idle funds in a money market fund, which can offer yields that mirror market rates. Others “sweep” your unused cash into partner banks to take advantage of FDIC insurance.

In today’s environment, people with money in savings vehicles like high-yield savings accounts or new CDs are well-positioned to take advantage of high rates. What sets some brokerages apart is whether they operate similarly. That is, do they raise rates in response to larger economic circumstances? And if so, how quickly?

Robinhood and Public are two firms on our radar that are offering competitive rates in response to hikes, ranging from 3.6% to 3.75% as of this writing. Robinhood requires a premium subscription to unlock those higher rates, while Public’s already high base rate of 3.3% applies to all users and can be boosted to 3.75% with a Reserve membership. For investors who keep a lot of cash in their account, the extra fee can be worth it.

Interest rates, of course, shouldn’t be the main reason you pick one broker over another. Costs, the types of securities available and platform usability are better starting points. But when a company meets those expectations and also offers a compelling interest rate on your uninvested money, it’s worth taking a closer look.

» See which brokers pay the most on idle cash: Best brokerages for high interest rates

Direct indexing is a strategy in which you replicate an existing stock index (like the S&P 500, for example) but customize it how you like. The most popular reason people choose direct indexing is for tax optimization — but it’s not the only one.

Direct indexing can also be used to avoid overexposure to a specific company. For instance, if you work at Apple and get company stock, you probably don’t need even more exposure to Apple through the S&P 500. Direct indexing lets you replace that one stock with a similar company instead.

And then there’s the reason direct indexing appealed to me: it lets you avoid buying into companies you just don’t support. I’m sure we all invest in companies we don’t necessarily mesh with morally, but direct indexing can help you avoid that.

The strategy used to be available only to people with an advisor managing their investment account, and they had to have millions to get started. More recently, these minimums have dropped. And now, it’s not just for people with financial advisors — online brokers offer the strategy, too.

While some brokers still have steep minimums of $100,000 or so, others let you get started with less. Fidelity, in true Fidelity fashion, started offering direct indexing to clients a few years ago through a managed portfolio that has a minimum investment requirement of only $5,000.

I was pleased to see Public launch direct indexing with a minimum of only $1,000 a year ago. However, we should note that with a low investment amount, you can only track a portion of an index.

But even with those limitations, I think it’s great that these companies are putting out the message that there shouldn’t be a huge barrier to entry to customize your portfolio. As direct indexing continues to gain popularity, we’ll be watching whether more brokers start offering it, as advancements in AI undoubtedly make it easier to do so.

It’s hard to ignore the rise of prediction markets in the mainstream. These days, it takes just a few clicks to bet on who might win the Super Bowl or take home a Grammy. These markets, which operate on contracts with binary outcomes, are easy to access and use everyday language, making them all the more tempting to try — and now they are beginning to appear on many broker platforms and apps.

We’d like to be clear on this one: Our editors have no intention of telling you how to spend your extra discretionary money. If you have a solid financial foundation and have allocated a few bucks to bet on some event contracts, that’s all good. But as editors who view investing apps as vehicles for legitimate wealth-building strategies, we draw the line at these products being marketed alongside other investments, such as stocks, ETFs and mutual funds.

In fact, this year we’ve actually decided to dock points in our annual reviews and ratings from brokerages that offer unrestricted access to event and sports-style prediction markets. In our view, these products aren’t conducive to long-term investing, and they’re speculative without enough oversight — a troublesome combination. You can read more about our stance and why we’re taking it here.

I’d venture to say that since the dawn of social media, people have been talking about investing online. And nowadays, the online investing community is huge. The r/investing subreddit has more than 3.5 million followers, and even on a video-forward platform like TikTok, #investing has 4.1 million posts under it.

But is where people go to talk about investing online changing?

The first broker I saw incorporate a social media–style element into its platforms was etoro. When you scroll down on the app's “home” tab, you’re met with what looks like an X feed. And the CopyTrader feature lets you copy another person’s portfolio, with that section of the app highlighting “trending investors,” “market outperformers,” and more.

This wasn’t a huge surprise to me coming from a niche broker with presumably a large user base of active traders. What surprised me was when Robinhood added a social media-style section to its app, testing a beta version in March and expanding it to all U.S. users in October.

Robinhood Social is, again, much like an X feed but for showing people which stocks you’re buying or selling. When I created an account to see what it was all about, the app encouraged me to share my “stats” on my profile (my one-day and one-year profit and loss, and my profit rate). “Trading stats build trust and transparency on Social,” the app said.

You could argue that other, even bigger brokers promote social trading. Fidelity, for example, has a “customer orders” section that shows how many Fidelity users are buying and selling certain stocks (though, I’ll say, they don’t promote this feature and it’s buried in the app).

The huge difference, in my opinion, is that Fidelity leaves it up to you to research these stocks. There’s no feed or comment section. On etoro and Robinhood, people can say whatever they want about why they bought or sold a certain security — whether truthful or not — or worse, why you should or shouldn’t invest in something.

To me, the whole concept of social trading feels like the antithesis of long-term investing. It’s a trend that I hope we don’t see becoming more popular among big-name brokers.

Disclosure: Neither the authors nor the editor owned any of the aforementioned investments at the time of publication.

#3020. Your AI Roadmap Is Really A Planning Problem

Monisha Somji | Senior Digital Transformation & AI Executive.

Walk into almost any large enterprise today, and you will find AI everywhere: copilots in the inbox, pilots in every function, a steering committee or two. Yet the financial results rarely match the activity.

In my experience, the pattern is consistent. The demo works, the pilot succeeds and the initiative stalls anyway because nobody owns the step between a working prototype and a changed way of working.

The data agrees. McKinsey’s latest global survey found that 88% of organizations now use AI in at least one business function, but only 39% report any enterprise-level EBIT impact, and just 6% qualify as “high performers.” Gartner predicts that “over 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027, due to escalating costs, unclear business value or inadequate risk controls.”

The usual explanation is that the technology is not ready or that employees need more training. Having led digital transformation and product programs across technology, retail and mobility, I see a different culprit: the planning and funding machinery wrapped around the model.

Across industries, leaders often avoid saying out loud that this is a leadership problem, not a technology problem. Pilots are popular because they are politically safe. They let every executive show AI progress without consolidating a team, giving up a budget or killing a sponsored project. Redesigning a workflow forces decisions about who owns it, who loses control of it and what stops.

Those decisions are hard because incentives point the other way. Leaders are rewarded for launching initiatives, not retiring them. Budgets belong to functions, not workflows, so no one gains by consolidating. Risk teams are measured on avoiding incidents, so they review late and cautiously. Everyone behaves rationally inside a system that quietly rewards the wrong thing.

Most large organizations still run on annual budgets, quarterly planning and intake queues designed for software that ships a few times a year. AI capabilities shift in months. A use case approved in one cycle can reach production two cycles later on a model already a generation behind.

That is why McKinsey’s research keeps landing in the same place. Of the 25 organizational attributes it tested against EBIT impact, workflow redesign had the strongest effect. The companies capturing value are not adding a tool to an old process. They are rebuilding the process.​

Every function runs its own AI queue, with its own vendors and its own definition of success. It is common to find three teams funding near-identical summarization tools from three vendors, each unaware of the others, until a budget review puts the requests side by side.

A pilot gets a budget and a deadline. When the money ends, the initiative ends, whether or not it worked. Pilots routinely hit their targets and still die because the funding line closes the same quarter the results arrive and no one owns the workflow they were meant to change.

Consolidate the front door. Create one intake and prioritization path for AI work, shared by product, technology and the business. One view of demand makes it possible to sequence work, reuse components and kill duplicates early.​

The next phase of enterprise AI will not be won by whoever licenses the most capable model, because those models will be available to everyone. It will be won by organizations that decide quickly, fund the right workflows, govern as they build and change how work actually gets done.

#3019. Corning vs. Vertiv: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

Corning and Vertiv both ride the AI data center boom, but one carries far heavier customer concentration risk while the other trades at a lower forward multiple.

By Brendan Coffey – Updated Nov 18, 2026 at 8:20AM EST

As artificial intelligence drives a massive expansion in data center capacity, investors are weighing the long term potential of Corning Inc. and Vertiv Holdings Inc. (VRT +1.90%). Both companies are essential to modern digital infrastructure, but they serve different parts of the technology stack. Choosing between them involves deciding which stock is a better buy for the next several years.

Corning provides the physical glass and fiber optic cables that move data, while Vertiv supplies the power and cooling systems that keep servers running. Both companies benefit from the same high-level trends, yet their financial profiles and risk factors vary significantly. This comparison evaluates their current performance and valuation to help you determine which fits your investment strategy.

Corning operates in the materials science space, but it is often classified alongside industrial stocks because of its manufacturing breadth. The company serves a concentrated customer base, with Apple Inc. (AAPL +0.85%) being a primary partner for durable cover glass used in mobile devices. Its optical communications segment is currently seeing high demand as telecommunications carriers and hyperscale data center operators upgrade their networks for artificial intelligence. Because a small number of customers account for a high percentage of sales, this customer concentration adds a layer of risk to the business.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached about $17.7 billion, representing revenue growth of approximately 18.8%. Net income for this period was around $2.1 billion, a significant increase compared to the prior year. This growth is largely supported by the company's ability to innovate in optical physics, providing specialized fiber solutions that allow data centers to pack more connections into smaller spaces.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, its current ratio stands at approximately 1.6x. The current ratio measures a company's ability to pay short-term debts with its current assets, with a figure above 1.0 generally suggesting healthy liquidity. The debt-to-equity ratio, which measures total debt relative to shareholders' equity, is nearly 0.9x. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was approximately $1.4 billion, providing capital for research and development.

Vertiv focuses on critical digital infrastructure, specifically power management and thermal cooling solutions. Its major customers include hyperscale and cloud providers such as Microsoft Corp. (MSFT -0.12%) and Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN +2.16%), as well as enterprise clients like Walmart Inc. (WMT -0.40%). As artificial intelligence chips generate more heat, the demand for Vertiv's liquid cooling systems has accelerated. The company also maintains strategic partnerships to ensure its own supply of semiconductors for power management units.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached around $13.1 billion, showing robust revenue growth of about 35.3%. Net income during this time was approximately $2.1 billion, reflecting a net margin of roughly 16%. This significant growth in sales and profitability highlights the intense demand for physical infrastructure as new data centers are built globally to support cloud computing.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 0.8x. Vertiv's current ratio is nearly 1.5x, indicating a solid buffer between its liquid assets and short-term liabilities. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was about $1.9 billion. This strong cash generation allows the company to reinvest in manufacturing capacity to keep up with its growing order backlog.

Corning faces risks related to its high customer concentration, as losing a major electronics or telecom partner could significantly impact sales. The company is also vulnerable to supply chain disruptions and inflationary pricing for specialized raw materials. Because much of its manufacturing occurs in the Asia Pacific region, it is exposed to geopolitical tensions and potential trade restrictions. Protecting its intellectual property is also a constant challenge, as any loss of proprietary glass technology could erode its competitive advantage.

Vertiv is susceptible to shifts in data center spending, as any slowdown in cloud investment by large-scale providers could lead to decreased demand. The company competes with large industrial players like Eaton Corp. (ETN +0.67%) and Schneider Electric (SBGSF -0.80%), which can lead to pricing pressure. Vertiv also carries significant indebtedness, and its credit agreements contain restrictive covenants that could limit its operating flexibility. Managing operational costs and supply chain logistics remains critical, particularly when passing on inflationary costs to large, powerful customers.

Vertiv currently trades at a lower multiple of future earnings estimates, while Corning appears more attractive when viewed in terms of market value relative to total sales.

Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.

Vertiv has been a specialist in computer cooling systems since World War Two, and it also offers complementary products for mission-critical technological infrastructure, such as uninterruptible power supplies. The AI-driven data center boom presents a long-term opportunity for Vertiv, especially for its liquid cooling systems. Liquid cooling is better for quickly removing heat from high-powered chipsets. Vertiv believes one-third of the total addressable market for data center cooling will eventually use liquid solutions (technically, some air-cooling and heat-dissipation systems will always be needed to work in tandem with liquid systems).

For 2026, Vertiv revenue should rise 44% to $14.7 billion, with net income shooting up about 90% to $2.5 billion as AI data center demand powers the business. Those figures are much stronger than anticipated just a few months ago. For 2027, analyst consensus calls for Vertiv revenue to jump about a third, with net income up more than 40% to $4.6 billion.

Recently struck deals with Meta Platforms (META -0.04%), Nvidia Corp. (NVDA -0.46%), and Amazon's AWS division have led Corning management to believe it can execute on its so-called Springboard program to jump annual sales to $20 billion this year, $30 billion in 2028, and $40 billion in 2030. Each of the deals is in Corning's core area of expertise: fiber optics and connectivity. These are for AI data centers and new manufacturing plants being planned in the U.S. Much of the new capacity Corning needs to fulfill these deals will come from its own U.S. expansion, reducing its tariff and general geopolitical risk. In its fiscal 2026 third quarter, sales grew 19%, and net income rose about 60% to $660 million. Wall Street consensus sees net income rising 53% to $2.44 billion.

One of the keys to Corning's growth is sharing its development plans with major customers well in advance, allowing it and its partners to tweak plans and development as needed to better meet future needs. The addition of new AI customers also helps reduce its risk of overreliance on Apple, which makes the iPhone glass, among other products.

So which is the better buy for 2027? Corning's continual improvement of its fiber-optic and connectivity products has led to impressive growth, with much more on the way. Vertiv, too, is executing well on its position, meeting an essential data center construction need. Still, while Corning comes at a premium, its plans to more than double sales by decade's end seem to offer great promise for long-term investors.

#3018. Top Wall Street analysts believe in the growth potential of these 3 stocks

Geopolitical uncertainty in the Middle East and soaring bond yields weighed on global markets this past week. And investors are closely assessing the valuations of artificial intelligence stocks amid concerns about the sustainability of high spending on AI infrastructure.

Despite those continued challenges, top Wall Street analysts are bullish on the prospects of several stocks due to their long-run growth potential and exposure to lucrative business lines, including AI.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Cybersecurity company CrowdStrike Holdings (CRWD) is this week's first stock pick. The company is scheduled to announce fiscal second-quarter results on August 26.

Ahead of Q2 FY27 earnings, Truist analyst Junaid Siddiqui reiterated a buy rating on CrowdStrike stock and raised his price target to $245 from $187.50. Following CrowdStrike's impressive fiscal first-quarter performance and guidance raise, Siddiqui expects another strong quarter.

The 5-star analyst's optimism is backed by continued strength in Falcon Flex adoption and encouraging large deal activity. Siddiqui also cited continued momentum across emerging products. With the FY27 outlook assuming persistent strength in CrowdStrike's net new annual recurring revenue (ARR), Siddiqui is more focused on the longevity of key growth catalysts such as Falcon Flex adoption, platform consolidation and AI-led demand.

The analyst highlighted that talks with partners were encouraging, with pipeline generation and momentum in large deals remaining healthy in the fiscal second quarter despite tough, year-over-year comparisons.

"We continue to view CrowdStrike as one of the primary beneficiaries of platform consolidation, though we expect investors to remain focused on competitive dynamics and whether current growth levels represent a new baseline or a period of demand acceleration," the analyst said.

Siddiqui ranks No. 226 among more than 12,400 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 80% of the time, delivering an average return of about 40%. See CrowdStrike Financials on TipRanks.

Shares of personal computer maker Dell Technologies (DELL) have rallied 251% this year, driven by strong demand for AI servers. Recently, Evercore analyst Amit Daryanani reiterated a buy rating on DELL and raised his price target to $550 from $500.

The 5-star analyst contends that while Dell's AI compute segment is getting investors' attention, the company's Storage business is underappreciated and well-positioned to drive revenue and profit acceleration. Daryanani expects the storage business to see higher demand once enterprises start to bring workload back on-premises.

The analyst highlighted that Dell's Storage business, estimated to account for only 10% of FY27 revenue, is one of the factors that could help improve profit margins, given its higher profitability compared to AI servers. Daryanani estimates that the Storage business's operating margin is currently in the low-20% range, while margins for the AI server and traditional server businesses are in the mid-single-digit and mid-teens range, respectively.

Overall, Daryanani views the Storage business as an important catalyst for three reasons: Dell has one of the broadest storage portfolios in the industry; Storage has a significantly higher margin profile than AI servers; and the shift toward proprietary, software-defined storage and AI-focused platforms.

"We think DELL's storage business is becoming increasingly strategic as AI infrastructure deployments move beyond GPU procurement and toward full stack + AI-ready architectures," said Daryanani.

Daryanani ranks No. 19 among more than 12,400 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 71% of the time, delivering an average return of 38.70%. See Dell Technologies Statistics on TipRanks.

SanDisk (SNDK) is benefiting from AI-driven demand for its memory and storage products. Following the company's 2026 Investor Day event, J.P. Morgan analyst Harlan Sur resumed research coverage of SNDK with a buy rating (it was earlier, "Not Rated") and a price target of $2,250.

The 5-star analyst believes SanDisk is well-positioned to capitalize on a structural inflection reached in NAND demand, driven by strong growth in AI inference. Sur's bullishness is based on three key factors.

First, Sur believes that SanDisk's New Business Model (NBM) framework (or long-term agreements) has enhanced its margin profile and reduced cyclicality. SNDK's eight signed NBMs represent a total contract value of $94 billion and a gross margin of about 80%, even at the floor pricing.

Second, Sur highlighted the growing NAND market and expects the total addressable market to surge from about $70 billion in calendar year 2025 to over $300 billion in 2026 and about $500 billion in 2027. Importantly, the analyst noted that data centers are the largest driver of NAND growth, as hyperscalers increasingly deploy flash for AI inference workloads.

Finally, Sur is optimistic on SanDisk due to its technology dominance. The company's BiCS10 technology is sampling ahead of schedule and has 65% more bits per wafer than BiCS8, the analyst said. Also, Sur expects SanDisk's High Bandwidth Flash to become a differentiated memory platform for AI inference.

"Layered on top, mgmt's commitment to returning 100% of excess cash flow to shareholders should drive an aggressive share count reduction trajectory that further amplifies EPS growth on a per-share basis," said Sur.

Sur ranks No. 15 among more than 12,400 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 71% of the time, delivering an average return of 43.20%. See SanDisk Ownership Structure on TipRanks.
