#3017. Preparing For Changing ABA CPT Codes In 2027

Juan Pablo Montoya is Founder and CEO of Solum Health, which automates insurance verification and prior authorization with AI.

When a code set changes, the first thing practice owners ask me is which codes are new. I understand why, but it’s the wrong place to start. A new code can’t really hurt you because your billing system has never seen it and will say so. Deleted codes are also noisy since the claim usually bounces within days.

What hurts is a code that keeps its number and changes what it means. That claim goes out clean, and you find out weeks later from a denial or an auditor’s question nobody on the team can answer.​

On January 1, 2027, applied behavior analysis gets that kind of change. Speech therapy gets a big dose of the other kind.​

The ABA Coding Coalition’s crosswalk spells out the ABA CPT code changes: six new codes, revised descriptors for 97151 through 97158 and two Category III codes deleted. The change that matters is 97155. Under the 2019 descriptors, it covered protocol modification by the behavior analyst, with or without directing a technician, so it was where the analyst’s own hands-on treatment got billed. Beginning in January, it will mean the analyst directing a technician, and the analyst’s direct treatment will get its own code (97173).​

In speech, 92507 is deleted on January 1. ASHA described 10 replacements across five clinical categories, each built as a base code for the first 30 minutes plus an add-on for every additional 15 minutes. The group code, 92508, is revised into a stand-alone code. Outside Medicare, each payer decides when to add the new codes to its fee schedule.​

This is a data problem before it’s a billing problem. If your system treats a CPT code as a plain label, “97155” in July and “97155” in January are the same string, and nothing downstream knows they describe different work. A code is really a definition with a start date. An authorization approved under last year’s definition doesn’t carry over to this year’s on its own.​

The timing makes it worse. Most ABA authorizations I see run six months, so almost anything approved since midsummer will still be open in January. Those approvals funded 97155 hours that belong to two different codes from January 1, and unless the payer says otherwise in writing, the authorization won’t tell you how to split them.

The claim to worry about is the one that pays. If an analyst keeps billing hands-on treatment as 97155 out of habit, it matches the old authorization and goes through, and it stays wrong until someone reads it against the 2027 definition. The speech authorizations I see are usually written as a number of 92507 visits, which in January becomes a count of visits for a code that no longer exists.​

Don’t expect payer reporting to flag any of this for you. The largest Medicaid-managed care insurers denied 14% of standard prior authorization requests in 2025, and the published figures can’t show which services those were. If the cutover produces a run of mismatches, you’ll see it in your own data or not at all.​

This should be a single query: every authorization ending after December 31 that references 97151 through 97158, 0362T, 0373T, 92507 or 92508. If it turns into a week of opening PDFs and reading notes fields, that’s your real finding.​

Your code table needs start and end dates, so a December session is read against the 2026 definition and a January session against the 2027 one. Keep last year’s descriptors instead of overwriting them because sooner or later, someone will ask you to justify a 2026 claim. Load the crosswalk as reference data that your claim logic actually reads.​

HIPAA-covered payers must accept code sets valid on the date of service, but each one decides when it will cover, price and authorize the new codes. For a stretch, one payer may have 97173 loaded and priced while another hasn’t, so your system needs to know which payers have moved. Ask each one, in writing, how it will treat authorizations that cross January 1.​

Splitting an authorization between technician direction and the analyst’s own treatment is a clinical call. Your behavior analysts have to make it, and the payer has to amend the authorization to match, ideally before the first January session.

While you’re asking, consider whether you also need the new code for non-face-to-face analyst work, 97180, which no 2026 authorization could have listed. For speech teams, the equivalent job is turning approved visits into base and add-on units.​

Set up a weekly view of rejections, denials and authorization mismatches on every new and revised code, and keep it running through February. Put paid 97155 claims in that view, too. Nobody reviews claims that paid, which is exactly where the habitual billing errors will sit.​

Most of January’s coding problems will announce themselves with a rejection. The expensive one won’t; it’ll be a familiar number on an authorization you approved months ago now describing different work. I’d treat the cutover as a data migration rather than a coding update, and I’d start that inventory now while payers still have time to process amendments.​

#3016. Why S&P 500 ETF Investors Don't Have to Worry (Much) About Nvidia Stock Plunging

CEO scandals drive home the value of diversification.

One of the biggest stories on Wall Street this week is the resignation of Jensen Huang, former CEO of Nvidia (NVDA -0.46%), caused by a shocking scandal involving extramarital affairs and a romantic relationship with a possible Chinese spy. Many investors are worried that Huang's departure could lead to weaker performance for his company, negative spillover effects for the entire semiconductor industry, or even a broader downturn in the artificial intelligence (AI) industry.

It's important to keep in mind that the stock market is much bigger than one company and one CEO. And Jensen Huang's departure is just one factor affecting Nvidia's stock price, which was already in significant decline before the scandal broke. As of Nov. 13, Nvidia shares have dropped by about 7% over the past week, by 13.5% in 2026, and by nearly 33% since reaching a record high on Oct. 6. Since Nov. 13, the stock has been turbulent, with a slight bounce in pre-market trading on Nov. 18 following its latest earnings release.

But if you own S&P 500 index (^GSPC +0.06%) exchange-traded funds (ETFs), there's no reason to panic about Nvidia's scandal and a possible further sell-off in the stock. Let's look at a few reasons why.

Jensen Huang. Image source: Getty Images.

If you own individual shares of Nvidia, and the stock makes up a significant percentage of your portfolio, you might want to think carefully about whether you're still bullish on the company's future without Jensen Huang. Even though Huang resigned, the Nvidia scandal might not be over yet. There are significant risks and uncertainties facing Nvidia, regardless of who the CEO is.

As of this writing, Huang and Nvidia have not been accused of criminal wrongdoing. But Huang and the company are likely to face further investigations. And more news about the scandal keeps coming out. Jensen Huang was romantically involved with a Chinese businesswoman who was also an alleged Chinese spy. And according to reporting from The Information, this alleged spy might have used her relationship with Huang to gain access to billions of dollars' worth of cutting-edge Nvidia semiconductors, which she then helped provide to companies in China.

But the U.S. government doesn't want Nvidia's best chips going to China, for national security reasons. Nvidia's chips have been subject to targeted export controls since 2022. Again, this is hypothetical -- no one has accused Jensen Huang or other Nvidia employees of violating export controls or other U.S. laws. The company has said that it has no reason to believe that Nvidia corporate secrets or U.S. national security were compromised and has denied any knowledge of Nvidia chips being smuggled into China.

But what happens if more bad news comes out, or an investigation finds that the company violated export control laws or SEC regulations? What if the U.S. tightens its export controls on advanced semiconductors, making it harder for Nvidia to sell its chips worldwide? That could be more bad news for Nvidia stock going forward.

This is a lot of complexity and uncertainty, and it might be more than Nvidia shareholders want to accept. Even after a solid earnings report, the stock could have further to fall.

Nvidia is one of the largest stocks in the S&P 500. As of Sept. 30, it was the largest holding in the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO +0.13%), making up about 8.4% of the fund's assets. As of Nov. 12, after its recent sell-off, Nvidia has fallen to second place in the S&P 500 index, making up about 6.15% of the index.

What if Nvidia stock falls further from here? Let's say the stock goes into another 10% decline by the end of 2026. That's bad news for individual shareholders. But if you own Nvidia through an S&P 500 ETF, that one stock makes up only about 6.15% of the fund's portfolio. If that one stock drops by 10%, the fund's value would only drop by about 0.62%.

In this example, even if Nvidia declines by another 20% from its Nov. 12 share price, an S&P 500 ETF's Nvidia holdings would only decline by about 1.24%. And that doesn't mean the ETF would automatically go down along with Nvidia. Nvidia is only one stock; the other 499 companies in the S&P 500 index might go up. Just because one stock goes down doesn't mean all the stocks or sectors will follow.

Other semiconductor stocks or AI stocks might go up even if Nvidia goes down. Investors might shift money into other companies that they believe will be more competitive in the future if Nvidia struggles to recover. The S&P 500 is constantly sorting and rebalancing itself as some companies gain or lose market cap.

The S&P 500 is not guaranteed to go up or be a "safe" investment. The entire stock market can still go down by 10%, 20%, or more in any given year. But the S&P 500 tends to be steadier than any individual stock, and the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF has delivered annualized returns of about 12% over the past five years.

The Nvidia scandal shows the value of diversification. It's easy to be confident about individual stocks when the economy is booming, and everything is going well. But when crisis hits, prominent CEOs resign in disgrace, and companies are suddenly thrust into uncertainty and face allegations of serious misconduct, that's when putting too many eggs in one stock's basket can hurt investors.

#3015. 5 Student Loan Scams to Avoid in 2026

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Student loan scams use pressure tactics and make false promises. Here’s what to watch out for.

Student loan scams can be costly, but they usually leave clues. Scammers will often try to hook victims with tempting claims of “act now or miss out” and “we promise to get you student aid."

The communication might seem realistic, but unexpected fees, unknown contacts and big promises are usually red flags. The age-old adage is true: if an offer sounds too good to be true, it probably is.

Here’s a breakdown of common student loan scams and what to do about them.

» MORE: How to spot student loan repayment scams

The scam: A fraudulent private company offers to manage your student loans and help you get them relieved or even fully forgiven. These services can cost more than $1,000, and there’s no guarantee that you’ll actually get the help you’re looking for.

How to avoid it: You can manage your federal student loans for free. According to the U.S. Department of Education, you never have to pay for help with your federal student loans[1]U.S. Department of Education. Avoiding Student Aid Scams. View all sources . You can work with your loan servicer to adjust your payment plan, consolidate loans and apply for loan forgiveness at no cost to you.

If you’re being promised immediate student loan forgiveness, are asked for personal identification information like your FAFSA login credentials or asked to authorize a power of attorney, proceed with caution — it’s likely a scam.

» MORE: How to get help with student loans

The scam: A company charges you an upfront fee to combine multiple student loans into one new loan to reduce your monthly payment. The company may be illegitimate and is likely to pocket the fee without actually consolidating your loans.

How to avoid it: You can consolidate federal student loans for free. There is no fee to consolidate your loans through the Department of Education at studentaid.gov. If you’re looking to reduce your monthly payment through consolidation, start by contacting your loan servicer. And if you get unsolicited communication from a company promising federal student loan consolidation, it's probably a scam.

The scam: Scammers use transitions in federal loan programs to take advantage of borrowers. For example, the Education Department was set to resume wage garnishments after a long pause, but in January 2026 announced a temporary delay implement repayment reforms.

When federal decisions go back and forth like this, it creates a gray area for scammers to make wage garnishment threats. For borrowers who may not know if wage garnishment restarted, it can be hard to know what to do. This goes for other federal changes, too; any uncertainty can be an opportunity for bad actors to take advantage of the confusion.

How to avoid it: If your wages are truly being garnished, the communication will come from the federal government and not a private company. Likewise, if a company offers to stop your wage garnishment for a fee, you’re probably getting scammed.

The scam: Criminals impersonate a real person and apply to colleges in their name. Then, they can collect financial aid, take out loans and use their college admission to net discounts on goods and services. This is known as a “ghost student” scam.

How to avoid it: Follow the steps on identitytheft.gov to report fraud and get a recovery plan. There are a few safeguards you can put in place to prevent this form of identity theft, such as setting up a credit freeze and monitoring your FSA ID activity.

How it works: You might receive a call from someone claiming to be from your school’s financial aid office saying you have unpaid tuition. The caller may threaten that you cannot start your classes until your tuition bill is paid in full. Scammers can be creative and convincing, even going so far as to replicate a school’s phone number to display on your caller ID.

How to avoid it: The Federal Trade Commission warns that schools will not call and pressure you to pay tuition[2]Federal Trade Commission. Got a call about unpaid college tuition? It could be a scam. Accessed Nov 16, 2026. View all sources . Rather than trust the caller, use your school's secure student portal to check your account balance. Know for certain what you owe and to whom before sending money. You can also call your financial aid office to confirm the legitimacy of a phone number that has called you requesting tuition funds.

Realizing you’ve been scammed is stressful, and it’s natural to feel overwhelmed or embarrassed. But acting quickly can make a real difference. The sooner you report what happened, the better your chances of limiting the financial damage and getting your accounts back on track. Here’s what to do:

If you’ve already paid a scammer, report the problem to the bank that issued the payment. If you paid with a credit card, for instance, contact the company and tell them what happened. They may be able to freeze your account or reverse the transaction.

Reach out to your federal student loan servicer as well and report what happened. They can check to make sure no changes have been made to your account and, in the case that changes did occur, they can help you get your loan back on track.

File complaints with the Education Department, the Federal Trade Commission and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. Filing complaints with these agencies helps hold scammers accountable, can result in enforcement action or business shutdowns, and in some cases may help you recover lost funds.

#3014. The Most Important Number In Nvidia's Earnings Report Was 75%

Nvidia’s next-year forecast says more about its post-Huang confidence than any quarterly beat.

By Patrick Sanders – Nov 18, 2026 at 8:28AM EST

Nvidia (NVDA -0.46%) had plenty to prove when it reported its fiscal third-quarter earnings after the market closed Nov. 17. It was the company's first earnings report since Jensen Huang's sudden departure. Investors wanted to know whether the artificial intelligence chipmaker could maintain its momentum without its longtime CEO.

The numbers were outstanding. But I think the most important figure in Nvidia's earnings report wasn't its revenue, earnings, or even its guidance for the current quarter.

That's how much Nvidia now expects its revenue to grow in fiscal 2028, up from its previous forecast of 70%. And that increase tells us something important about the company's confidence in its ability to keep delivering AI processors to customers – even without Huang running the show.

For the third quarter of fiscal 2027 (ending Oct. 25, 2026), Nvidia reported revenue of $115.84 billion, up 103% from a year ago, and topping analysts' expectations of $109.10 billion. Its data center business generated $107.6 billion in revenue, up 110% year over year, as demand for AI computing infrastructure continued to grow.

"Our momentum is real," interim CEO Colette Kress said. "Nvidia is an exceptional technology leader, powered by the relentless innovation of our people. Vera Rubin is off to an explosive start, our roadmap is on track, and our ambition has never been greater."

Nvidia also projected fourth-quarter revenue of approximately $130 billion, ahead of the $125.1 billion consensus estimate compiled by LSEG. While that number stands out, it's also important to know that Nvidia's fiscal fourth quarter includes an additional week of revenue. Melius Research estimates that accounts for approximately $9 billion to $10 billion of the roughly $14 billion sequential increase in Nvidia's guidance.

That's why I'm paying more attention to what Nvidia expects to happen next year.

The increase in Nvidia's fiscal 2028 growth forecast is what really got my attention. In August, Nvidia projected 70% revenue growth for its 2028 fiscal year, and acknowledged that its ability to supply enough processors would limit how quickly it could expand.

Now the company is bumping that projection up to 75% growth.

During the company's earnings call with analysts, Kress said that Nvidia evaluated both customer demand and the additional supply it expects to make available. The company believes it can deliver that growth despite ongoing supply constraints and new U.S. export restrictions.

Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress. Image source: Nvidia.

Nvidia's ability to grow depends on more than designing powerful chips. It needs manufacturing capacity, advanced memory, packaging, networking components, and customers with enough data center capacity to put its systems to work.

And just as importantly, Nvidia needs to keep those relationships going even in the post-Huang era. Huang was forced to resign Nov. 12 after the board began investigating allegations that he had a relationship with a Chinese businesswoman who U.S. intelligence officials believe is a Chinese spy. Other extramarital relationships with Nvidia employees also came to light.

There are some, including President Donald Trump and people at Nvidia, who suggest that Huang be reinstated. And Huang issued a lengthy statement on the social media platform X saying he would return if asked.

But Nvidia closed that door on Tuesday, stating that Huang would not be reinstated and citing his "personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms."

Huang's departure created legitimate questions about Nvidia's leadership and its relationships with customers and suppliers. Those concerns won't disappear after one earnings report. But the company's higher fiscal 2028 forecast suggests its manufacturing partnerships, customer relationships, and product roadmap remain intact.

I think the increased forecast is more significant than a quarterly earnings beat. While its first earnings report without Huang suggests the business can continue delivering exceptional results, a revenue growth rate of 75% in the next fiscal year shows Nvidia is hardly running out of momentum.

#3013. The 5% Redesigned The Work First; The 60% Got Nothing Back

Manu Khetan is Founder and CEO of Rolling Arrays, a LinkedIn ‘Top Voice’ Influencer and Creator of the R7 Framework.

​The most common thing a CEO says to me about AI this year is some version of the same sentence: We invested, and we cannot find the return.

In 2025, BCG put a number on that feeling. It surveyed 1,250 senior executives across 68 countries and nine industries. About 60% of companies reported no material value at all from AI, despite substantial investment. Around 35% are scaling. About 5% are getting value at scale. Note what is being counted: companies, not pilots.

Most boards read that and blame the models. BCG’s own reading points somewhere else. The firms getting value, it says, “go well beyond automation and incremental productivity improvements to reshape current workflows and invent new ones.”

They redesigned the work first, and brought the agent to the redesigned work.

BCG describes what the winners do. What the 60% did is my own reading, from 17 years inside enterprise workforces and from every AI budget I have watched up close, and I want it labeled as mine rather than as something the survey says. In those rooms, the pattern is consistent. They bought agents and left the work exactly as it was.

The ones who got something back did the unglamorous thing first. They took a process apart, decided which tasks should stay human, redesigned what was left and only then went shopping.

The public cases show the same order of operations. Octopus Energy has AI answering customer emails at a workload of around 250 people, with satisfaction higher than on the human-handled queue, 80 against 65. JPMorgan’s COIN took roughly 360,000 hours a year of document review off the desk, and that was nearly a decade ago.

IKEA is the one I keep coming back to. AI-powered chatbot “Billie” absorbed about 47% of inbound customer inquiries, over 3 million conversations. Billie’s savings over two years came to around 13 million euros. Then they retrained roughly 8,500 call-center workers into remote interior-design advisors, and that remote channel sold about 1.3 billion euros in the 2022 financial year.

Those two figures measure different things, a year of sales against two years of savings, so they are not a ratio. But nobody builds a billion-euro channel by shopping for agents.

Every AI budget I see falls into one of four patterns.

Redesigners are the 5%. They cut the work, not the people, and the people who stayed moved into work worth more than what left. IKEA is the archetype.

Reversers automated the moments their customers needed a human, paid for it in quality and corrected course. Klarna did this in public, which took some courage.

Experimenters are most of the 60%. Pilots everywhere, nothing at scale, a conclusion that AI is overhyped. Their skepticism is accurate about their own deployments and wrong about the frontier.

Installers take the output, and the humans simply exit. Output up, humans out. It is proof of power, not of governance, and I will come back to what it costs in Part 5.​

We run a 400-person business across six countries, and we are adopting AI as we speak, so I am doing this while also advising on it. The order was harder to follow than to describe.

Our delivery work runs through 18 roles, three ladders of six, from associate to director, and like every professional services firm, we allocated it by asking who could do it. That habit was the first thing in the way because real people sat in those roles, and we couldn’t cut them into tasks.

What unlocked it was stopping looking at the roles and starting to look at the client’s work. In a services firm, the work is defined the day the contract is signed. It lives in the scope. Read task by task, asking what kind of work each is—physical, cognitive or relational—and who should own it: execution, judgment or trust; it could be cut without anyone’s job title in the room. Cognitive execution became a candidate for agents. What stayed human became the new roles.

Mindset is the second thing in the way. The instinct is still to ask who fills the integration consultant slot, not what the work is. Hiring is where we are weakest. The new roles concentrate judgment, client relationship and accountability and need less of the configuration depth we used to interview for. The job descriptions changed faster than the interviews did. What helped more than I expected is a framework to teach, not a slogan to repeat. A grid people can apply to their own tasks gets you arguments, then adoption, slowly.

I am not going to tell you that puts us in the 5%. That is a result, and you don’t get to announce a result on the day you decide to go after it. Don’t buy an agent before you know where the work lives, and don’t hand it whatever it can take and leave the rest to roles designed for humans. Cut the work, not the people.

Whether AI is good enough is not the question, or rather, it is a question with no general answer. It gets asked task by task and only about today.

The question that separates the four patterns is different. Ask which of them you are funding. Then ask the harder version. Take the last AI investment your board approved and find the work that changed shape because of it. Not the tool that got installed. The work. If a process looks exactly as it did before, only faster in one spot, you have bought a tool and kept a workflow, and the 60% is where that lands.

And it points to a sharper money question: If the winners were not buying salary savings, what exactly should the agent dollar buy, especially if agents keep getting more expensive rather than cheaper? That is Part 4.​​​

#3012. Survey: Gen Z Loves a Winter Challenge, but Money Goals Often Fizzle

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Gen Zers are apt to try cold-weather challenges like “winter arc.” But they’re also the generation most likely to say they generally quit challenges before finishing and set the same money goal more than once due to not sticking with it.

It’s not technically winter yet, but depending on where you live, it may feel like it. For many of us, this is a time of hibernation, but for others, it’s prime time for a glow-up.

“Winter arc” is a popular social media challenge through which people aim to improve themselves before the new year. It typically runs from October through December, but can be started any time during the cold months. The aim is to jump-start the “new year, new me” season before the ball even drops.

Whether they call it a winter arc or not, plenty of Americans are working on self-improvement as the chill sets in. According to a new NerdWallet survey, conducted online by The Harris Poll, 75% of Americans say they’re working on their physical health, and 69% say the same about their finances.

Popular as it is, winter arc isn’t the only cold-weather challenge out there. The survey found that half of Americans (50%) say they’ve tried some sort of winter improvement challenge. And no one likes a challenge like Gen Z: Nearly three-quarters of Gen Zers (74%) have tried a winter challenge, compared with 64% of millennials, 42% of Gen Xers and 29% of baby boomers.

Note: The survey defines Gen Zers as those 18-29; millennials, ages 30-45; Gen Xers, ages 46-61 and baby boomers, ages 62-80.

But there’s a difference between starting a challenge and successfully completing one. Gen Zers reign supreme as those most likely to hop on a winter challenge. But they’re also the most likely to say they generally quit challenges before finishing, buy products they saw on social media in an effort to stick with the challenges and set the same financial goal more than once.

Gen Zers are more likely than any other generation to say they:

Have tried a winter financial challenge other than no-spend January (21%, vs. 11% of millennials, 5% of Gen Xers and 2% of baby boomers).

Generally quit challenges before they finish them (59%, vs. 42% of millennials, 36% of Gen Xers and 22% of baby boomers).

Expect to spend more on at least one discretionary expense this winter than they would during another season (90%, vs. 83% of millennials, 61% of Gen Xers and 48% of baby boomers).

Put off dealing with money until after the holidays (60%, vs. 47% of millennials, 35% of Gen Xers and 15% of baby boomers).

Aren’t currently working on improving their finances, but want to make it a priority (15%, vs. 8% of millennials and 6% each of Gen Xers and baby boomers).

“Embracing the winter arc trend can be a great way to find motivation to make progress on a goal over the slower winter months,” says Kimberly Palmer, personal finance expert at NerdWallet. “Pick a winter challenge that aligns with a longer-term goal for the coming year.”

Winter challenges popular with Gen Z include diet- or fitness-related challenges (29%) and self-improvement challenges, like winter arc or 75 Hard, a mental toughness challenge that runs for 75 days and includes two workouts every day, a strict diet and daily nonfiction reading (25%).

While winter arcs typically focus on physical, mental and intellectual self-improvement, Gen Z is game to try a financial challenge as well: One long-standing financial challenge — no-spend January — is more popular among younger Americans (22% of Gen Zers and 20% of millennials) than their older counterparts (12% of Gen Xers and 6% of baby boomers). As for other types of financial challenges, Gen Z is more likely than any other generation to have tried at least one: 21% compared with 11% of millennials, 5% of Gen X and 2% of baby boomers.

Of course, it’s one thing to try a challenge, during wintertime or otherwise. It’s another thing entirely to follow through and complete it. That’s the hard part for many Gen Zers.

When taking on a self-improvement challenge, the beginning tends to be easiest. You’re motivated and excited to reach goals and better yourself. But as time goes on, it’s easy to slip back into old habits or for the shine of a brand-new challenge to dim. And Gen Zers report that they are most likely to quit early.

According to the survey, nearly 3 in 5 Gen Zers (59%) say they generally quit challenges before they finish them. That compares with 42% of millennials, 36% of Gen Xers and 22% of baby boomers.

Along with challenges in general, money goals can be difficult to follow through with, especially for younger Americans. Around two-thirds of Gen Zers (64%) say it’s been hard to stick to financial goals they’ve set in the past, compared with 52% of Gen Xers and 34% of baby boomers. Gen Zers are more likely than any other generation to say they’ve set the same financial goal more than once because they didn’t stick with it — 33%, compared with 20% of millennials, 15% of Gen Xers and 7% of baby boomers.

This isn’t for lack of desire, though. Seven in 10 Gen Zers (70%) say they’re working on improving their finances. All generations show high levels of effort here: 76% each of millennials and Gen Xers say the same, along with 59% of baby boomers.

So why is it so hard to stick with money goals? One possibility is that it’s difficult to see meaningful progress on finances, particularly when you’re young. According to the survey, 65% of Gen Zers say it’s harder to see progress on financial goals than on physical goals.

This makes perfect sense for this age group — for those light on money but rich in youthfulness, desired physical changes may show up faster than financial progress. On top of that, the current job market is tough for younger Americans. Recent college grads now have a higher unemployment rate than workers in general. Even if you’re still on the job hunt, your 20s are a great time to start taking steps, however small, toward building future wealth.» MORE: I’m 25. Here’s How I Got Started Investing

“To increase your chances of success, try coordinating winter arc plans with a friend or giving yourself smaller goals along the way,” Palmer says. “Leaning on the support or coaching from a loved one can make it easier to keep going, as can celebrating incremental progress.”

Self-improvement is a noble pursuit. But as with most things in life, it’s easy to lose sight of the ultimate goal in favor of buying things to help you reach it.

“It’s easy to feel like a quick purchase can help us meet our goals, and sometimes a product can be a useful tool, but the reality is that true winter arc progress comes from putting in the hard work. There’s no option for ‘purchasing’ it instead,” Palmer says.

According to the survey, more than a quarter of Gen Zers (26%) say they’ve bought a product they saw on social media to help with a personal goal or challenge. This is more than any other generation: 17% of millennials, 11% of Gen Xers and 7% of baby boomers say they’ve made social media buys for self-betterment.

Some self-improvement purchases may be billed on a monthly basis. More than 1 in 5 Gen Zers (23%) say they're still paying for a subscription or membership they signed up for during a past goal or challenge. This is also true for 17% of millennials, 9% of Gen Xers and 2% of baby boomers.

These challenge purchases may pile onto already higher winter expenses. A majority of Gen Zers (90%) say they expect to spend more on at least one discretionary expense this winter than they would during another season, more than any other generation. Top expenses include food delivery (38%), entertainment at home (35%) and indoor family entertainment (30%). A quarter of Gen Zers (25%) expect to spend more on fitness or wellness apps this winter compared to other seasons.

Some may be spending more to make themselves feel better during the cold, gray months. Nearly 1 in 5 Gen Zers (18%) say they tend to combat winter blues by spending money, compared with 10% of Gen Xers and 3% of baby boomers.

The holiday season is an expensive time of year for many of us, and it’s easy to sweep finances under the rug until the new year. According to the survey, 3 in 5 Gen Zers (60%) say they generally put off dealing with money until after the holidays. This is more than any other generation: 47% of millennials, 35% of Gen Xers and 15% of baby boomers say the same.

Even for those taking on financial challenges before the new year hits, it’s easy for the resulting “savings” to disappear. Nearly three-quarters of Gen Zers (74%) say money they save by cutting back in one area usually just gets spent somewhere else instead of staying “saved.” This is also true for 68% of millennials, 63% of Gen Xers and 45% of baby boomers.

For some, the holidays are just one thing competing for their money. Over half of Gen Zers (52%) say they’d rather spend money on how they look now than save it for their future financial security. This compares with 26% of Gen Xers and 13% of baby boomers.

We don’t begrudge anyone for their desire to look and feel their best this upcoming season. But that doesn’t have to mean you can’t level up your money at the same time.

More than 2 in 5 Gen Zers (43%) say they’re putting consistent work into improving their finances, and 27% are putting some work into this, but not consistently. Moreover, 15% of Gen Zers aren’t working on improving their finances but want to make them a priority. No matter your age, here are some ideas for a financial glow-up before the spring thaw.

Start small if you tend to quit. Nearly 2 in 5 Americans (38%) say they generally quit challenges before finishing them. Early-challenge motivation can make it easy to overcommit. If you often take on challenges impulsively then peter out a few weeks later, try starting small. For example, maybe no-spend January is a stretch, but you can still save by intentionally creating two no-spend days a week.

Move money the day you save it. Over 3 in 5 Americans (61%) say money they save by cutting back in one area usually gets spent somewhere else. If you’re cutting back, transfer the difference to savings that same day, so it can’t leak out elsewhere.

Make money progress measurable. Half of Americans (50%) say it’s harder to see progress on financial goals than physical goals. There’s a saying that what gets measured, gets managed. Choose one number to track. This might be down payment savings, debt payoff progress or an investment milestone. It may not move much month to month, but you’d be surprised at the difference a year can make, even without a ton of money each month to dedicate toward your goal.

Begin before January. More than a third of Americans (37%) say they put off dealing with money until after the holidays. Facing your finances during the often busy and expensive final months of the year can be daunting, but don’t put your head in the sand until after the holiday credit card balances come due. Put a cap on your winter spending before the new year to avoid going overboard during the tempting sales this time of year.

“If you’re trying to choose a winter arc, pick one that’s realistic but also a stretch goal, so it’s satisfying to accomplish while not being completely out of reach,” Palmer suggests. “Chances are you’ll be glad with what you got done over the colder months when springtime hits.”

#3011. This Magnificent Vanguard ETF Could Turn $500 per Month Into $1 Million in Under 30 Years

Investors can build life-changing wealth in the stock market with a combination of patience and consistency.

By Anthony Di Pizio – Nov 18, 2026 at 8:29AM EST

10 stocks we like better than Vanguard Morningstar Growth ETF ›

The Vanguard Morningstar Growth ETF (VUG +0.58%) is an exchange-traded fund (ETF) that exclusively invests in America's most valuable growth stocks. These stocks are known for delivering high capital returns, separating them from value stocks, which typically generate comparatively modest gains, supplemented by dividend income.

Here's how the Vanguard ETF could turn a consistent investment of $500 per month into $1 million in under 30 years.

The Vanguard Morningstar Growth ETF holds 135 stocks from 11 different economic sectors. However, a whopping 72.1% of its assets are parked in technology companies alone, which is fitting given their tendency to generate faster revenue and earnings growth than companies in other sectors. High exposure to tech is a key reason why the ETF tends to outperform the S&P 500 (^GSPC +0.06%) index over time.

The Vanguard ETF is also top-heavy because its 10 largest holdings alone represent 66.1% of the value of its entire portfolio.

Data source: Vanguard. Portfolio weightings are accurate as of Oct. 31, 2026, and are subject to change.

Following a recent decline in Nvidia stock sparked by the departure of founder Jensen Huang, Apple is now the world's most valuable company once again. The company continues to expand its Apple Intelligence suite of AI features and applications, bringing new capabilities to the iPhone, iPad, and Mac lineup of computers. With over 2.5 billion active devices globally, Apple could soon be the largest distributor of AI software to consumers.

While the future of Nvidia's leadership team remains uncertain, there is still an unprecedented amount of demand for the company's data center chips, which do most of the heavy lifting in AI workloads. Nvidia has already revealed some of its product pipeline through to 2030, with the Feynman AI semiconductor architecture slated to replace the latest Rubin architecture from 2028. As a result, the data center business is likely to grow nicely no matter who leads the company.

While Apple could dominate consumer AI, Microsoft, Alphabet, and Amazon are battling for market share in the enterprise AI space. They have each enhanced their legacy product platforms with AI, and their respective cloud computing platforms provide businesses with all of the tools they need to leverage this revolutionary technology themselves.

These AI powerhouses have led the Vanguard ETF higher over the last few years. However, it does hold a number of stocks from outside the tech sector, including payment giants Visa and Mastercard, retail behemoth Costco Wholesale, industrial powerhouse Boeing, and even Starbucks.

The Vanguard Morningstar Growth ETF has delivered a compound annual return of 11.8% since it was established in 2004, but it has delivered an even faster annual return of 24.6% over the last three years specifically, thanks to the AI boom.

Here's how long it could take the ETF to turn a monthly investment of $500 into $1 million, based on three different average annual returns.

It's unrealistic to expect any ETF to deliver an annual return of over 20% indefinitely, because the law of large numbers eventually becomes a headwind. For example, if Apple's market cap grew by 20% annually for the next 20 years, it would become a $198 trillion company, making it more valuable than the output of the entire global economy, which was $118 trillion in 2025.

But even if the Vanguard ETF's annual return reverts back to its long-term average of 11.8%, it could still turn $500 per month into $1 million in under 30 years.

With that said, I think above-average returns are likely for the foreseeable future. Although the AI boom is facing some headwinds, this technology is laying the foundation for the industries of the future, from robotics to autonomous vehicles to quantum computing. Given the Vanguard ETF's concentrated exposure to the technology sector, it's likely to hold the companies driving those potential revolutions.

However, that can be a double-edged sword at times, because a concentrated portfolio will also experience higher volatility than a diversified portfolio. This is something investors should keep in mind when buying the Vanguard Morningstar Growth ETF.

#3009. Applied Materials vs. Marvell Technology: Which Tech Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

Two chipmakers, two very different bets: one sells the tools that build the chips, the other designs the networking silicon that moves data between them.

By Erin Kennedy – Updated Nov 18, 2026 at 8:38AM EST

10 stocks we like better than Applied Materials ›

As the race for dominance in artificial intelligence intensifies, choosing the right infrastructure provider is critical. Should you invest in equipment giant Applied Materials (AMAT +0.32%) or connectivity specialist Marvell Technology (MRVL -1.30%)?

Applied Materials supplies the tools that actually build the chips, making it a foundational player in the semiconductor ecosystem. Marvell designs the custom chips and networking components that move data between servers. Comparing these two reveals different ways to play the ongoing shift toward high-performance computing and massive data center expansion.

Applied Materials sells materials engineering solutions used to produce nearly every new chip and advanced display in the world. It serves a concentrated customer base of logic, foundry, and memory manufacturers, including giants like Intel (INTC -0.30%) and Micron Technology (MU -0.63%). Two specific customers accounted for approximately 19% and 15% of net revenue, respectively. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business.

In the 12 months ended Oct. 25, 2026, revenue reached nearly $34.4 billion. This represented growth of roughly 21.4% compared to the prior period, driven by strong demand for advanced chipmaking equipment. Net income totaled approximately $10.1 billion, showcasing the profitability possible at this scale.

As of Applied Materials' October 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 0.3. This ratio measures total debt against shareholder equity, with lower numbers typically suggesting less financial leverage. The current ratio, which compares short-term assets to short-term liabilities, is roughly 2.3. For those following semiconductor stocks, strong cash flow is vital for R&D. In the fiscal year ended Oct. 25, 2026, free cash flow was nearly $6.2 billion.

Marvell Technology operates as a fabless supplier, meaning it designs high-end semiconductor solutions but outsources the actual manufacturing. The company focuses on data center core networks and the network edge, serving original equipment manufacturers and cloud service providers. For its most recent annual reporting period, two customers each accounted for 10% or more of net revenue, and the 10 largest customers collectively accounted for 82% of net revenue. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business.

In the 12 months ended Aug. 1, 2026, revenue reached nearly $9.5 billion. This figure reflects growth of close to 30.6% over the previous 12 months as the company expanded its footprint in AI infrastructure. Net income for the same period was approximately $2.6 billion, marking a significant turnaround from previous years.

As of its January 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is roughly 0.3. Its current ratio is approximately 2, indicating a solid ability to meet short-term obligations. In the fiscal year ended Jan. 31, 2026, free cash flow was close to $1.4 billion. Note that stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 33.8% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation, since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

Applied Materials faces significant geographic concentration, with a heavy reliance on customers in China. This exposure makes the company sensitive to trade policies and export restrictions. It also manages legal risks involving export controls, including a $252 million settlement reached in February 2026 for export violations involving Semiconductor Manufacturing International. Furthermore, its reliance on complex global supply chains creates vulnerability to regional disruptions or inventory obsolescence.

Marvell Technology has high customer concentration. Its 10 largest clients account for nearly 82% of revenue, and it often competes with rivals like Broadcom(AVGO +2.33%). The company is also navigating a massive $115 billion pending acquisition of Lumentum Holdings (LITE -1.67%). This deal introduces risks related to shareholder dilution and the complex process of integrating two large organizations. Additionally, Marvell's dependency on third-party foundries in the Pacific Rim creates supply chain risks if regional political conflicts arise.

Applied Materials currently appears to be the more conservative value choice, while Marvell Technology commands a higher premium given its faster growth profile.

Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

The forward P/E compares the stock price to future earnings estimates, helping you see how much you are paying for every dollar of projected profit. The P/S ratio measures the market price relative to sales over the past 12 months.

Marvell and Applied Materials are riding the current tech boom, with both stocks hitting all-time highs earlier this year. They've since pulled back a considerable amount, but they're still handily outpacing the S&P 500 (^GSPC +0.06%) by massive margins:

There's not a ton of daylight between the two stocks' recent returns. And as for business performance, Applied Materials has a slightly higher net margin, while Marvell is posting stronger revenue growth.

I lean toward Applied Materials in this matchup. Marvell's revenue growth is impressive, but its pending acquisition of Lumentum introduces a fair amount of risk. There's the possibility of dilution, but there's also the potential that the combined company doesn't create the cost-savings and synergies management had hoped for. That could lead to significant writedowns, which would almost certainly impact the stock negatively.

Applied Materials just seems to have less risk, which makes it my pick for 2027 and beyond.

TL;DR: Mortgage rates continue to climb under pressure from inflation.

Mortgage rates keep rising as markets anticipate a near-certain Fed rate hike next month.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage rose to 7.34% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is seven basis points higher than yesterday and 34 basis points higher than a week ago. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.)

Here are the average APRs we're seeing today, as well as movement over the past month for context:

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

On Friday, the Bureau of Labor Statistics released the Producer Price Index for October, which tracks the change in prices that U.S. producers are able to get for their products. This is one way to measure inflation on the market end, rather than the consumer end.

The results were mixed. While prices didn’t rise quite as high as economists anticipated month-over-month (0.3% vs. 0.4%), year-over-year price growth did reach 6.5% — the largest increase in four years. This points to even higher costs for consumers coming in the near future.

Investors are convinced that the Federal Reserve will raise overnight borrowing rates again in December to pull inflation down. And higher overnight borrowing rates — called the federal funds rate, which is what banks pay to fund products like mortgages — usually lead to higher mortgage rates.

» MORE: How the Federal Reserve affects mortgage rates

Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

With rates where they are right now, you may want to start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.84% or higher.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

» Time to refi? Compare refinance rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

» Is now a good time to buy? See NerdWallet’s analysis

If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

🤓 Nerdy Reminder: Rates can change daily, and even hourly. If you’re happy with the deal you have, it’s okay to commit.

#3006. The 'debasement trade' returns after Bessent bond maneuver. Crypto and gold are back in style

The debasement trade is gaining new traction on Wall Street as concern over the size and cost of the budget deficit mounts.

The conventional wisdom behind the trade is that perceived hard assets, like cryptocurrencies and precious metals, gain as investors try to hedge against a weaker U.S. dollar and Treasury debt in the face of ballooning government spending. Those fears reached a fever pitch last week before, and after, the Treasury Department's unusual step of increasing debt buybacks under Secretary Scott Bessent.

"The size of the Treasury purchases announced so far by Bessent are trivial in comparison to the size of the overall market, but the [signaling] effect was very powerful," said Stephen Coltman, head of macro at 21Shares, a crypto-focused creator of exchange-traded funds.

Gold touched three-month highs Monday, building on last week's advance of more than 5%. The yellow metal has climbed for five straight weeks and in August is on track for its biggest monthly rise since 1999.

Bitcoin added 2% Monday, to the highest since May. Last week, the digital currency soared 22%, its biggest three-day rally since 2023. Overnight Tuesday, the crypto touched $80,000.

The U.S. dollar index, which tracks the dollar against six other leading currencies, hit three-month lows last week and recorded its third down week in the last four. The index was little changed on Monday as investors expressed little appetite to bid up the greenback.

The Treasury Department said last week that it would double the maximum size of its bond buyback, to at least $4 billion from $2 billion. Two senior Treasury officials told CNBC Monday that the department could use its General Account to help fund the plans.

Last week's announcement followed news that the monthly U.S. budget deficit in July reached a five-year high and came at the same time as total federal government debt topped $40 trillion. Bessent told CNBC last week that he wields a "big toolkit" to calm the government bond market amid concerns about the government's financial health.

Long-dated U.S. Treasury yields surged last week, at one point sending the 30-year yield to almost a 20-year high of 5.34%, up from 4.82% in late June. Yields dipped and then rebounded in the wake of the Treasury buyback move, a signal that bond investors believed Bessent's moves were inadequate.

"Markets are saying something," the billionaire philanthropist and former energy trader John Arnold said in a Friday post on X. The weaker dollar, lower Treasury prices and strengthening hard assets, are "all part of the debasement trade," he wrote.

The Treasury's moves could aid the bond market, but also translate into outsized pain for the dollar, according to Nohshad Shah, Citadel Securities' head of fixed income sales for Europe, the Middle East and Africa.

The stakes are high for monetary policymakers, as a weaker greenback can ease financial conditions, Shah said. U.S. inflation — above the Federal Reserve's 2% target for five years — could worsen.

The Fed might need to hike interest rates in response, Shah said. Fed funds futures reflect about a 56% chance the central bank raises borrowing costs at its October meeting, up more than seven percentage points from a week ago, according to CME's FedWatch tool.

"The bond market's message is straightforward: fiscal or monetary policy should be tighter," Shah said in a Monday note. "Households may ultimately pay for policymakers' unwillingness to fix the roof whilst the sun is shining."

Coltman at 21Shares said the appetite for alternative stores of value also stems from mounting geopolitical tension. The U.S. on Monday rolled out a global sanctions program focused on segregating Iran from the global economy, days after slapping 50% tariffs on billions of dollars in Canadian exports.

Still, assets that would benefit from a debasement trade have recently received votes of confidence on Wall Street.

Deutsche Bank analyst Michael Hsueh said in a Monday note that gold could surpass his target price of $4,800 an ounce. Already, that level suggests the precious metal only need to rise another 3% or so from where it closed on Friday. "We see the Treasury policy change as underlining the gold constructive view," Hsueh said.

Billionaire investor Ray Dalio recommended investors remain overweight gold and bitcoin ahead of what he warned could become a debt crisis in the U.S. as a result of unchecked government spending. Gold could account for as much as 15% of a model portfolio, the Bridgewater Associates founder said.

"The government's financial condition is at an inflection point," Dalio wrote on LinkedIn Friday. "If this is not dealt with now, the debts will build up to levels where they can't be managed without great trauma."

Others are less sure, devaluing the notion of a debasement trade.

It's probably too early to endorse the idea unless it's clear that the Fed will go along with the Treasury Department, said Alexander Lis, investing chief at Social Discovery Ventures.

#3005. The 3 Best AI Stocks to Buy Now (Yes, Nvidia Is One of Them)

Nvidia may be going through a tumultuous period, but the business is still strong.

By Keithen Drury – Nov 18, 2026 at 8:44AM EST

The artificial intelligence sector of the stock market isn't the most popular place to invest right now. There are questions surrounding how the AI build-out will be allowed to proceed, with Democrats sweeping the U.S. midterm elections. This could put a pause on some data centers, affecting companies that provide the components. Still, many projects are underway, and many builds will likely be allowed to continue as-is, with newer facilities coming under greater scrutiny.

While AI investment sentiment is currently negative, I think there are plenty of great investment opportunities right now. They include Nvidia (NVDA -0.46%), Broadcom (AVGO +2.33%), and Micron (MU -0.63%). While Nvidia is in a bit of a mess with its CEO resigning last week, I think the stock has cratered to the point where it makes sense to buy shares. The other two are also genius buys and make for timely investments, with the market not being bullish on the AI outlook.

First, let's look at Nvidia. CEO Jensen Huang resigned due to relationships with staff and a potential Chinese spy. This is a huge loss for Nvidia because Huang co-founded the company and built it into what it is today. At the same time, Nvidia's products are so impressive and have such a dominant market share that they practically sell themselves. This means business will likely go on as usual at Nvidia, and investors should use the global sell-off as a buying opportunity for the stock.

After the sell-off, Nvidia trades at a dirt cheap price of 10.5 times next year's earnings estimates.

NVDA PE Ratio (Forward 1y) data by YCharts

That's a huge discount, and considering the S&P 500 (^GSPC +0.06%) trades for about 20 times forward earnings, I can see Nvidia having an impressive rebound in 2027.

While Nvidia is a timely buy, it still has some troubles. So, investors should also look to other stocks.

Broadcom has been taking market share from Nvidia for a while. Instead of making a broad-purpose GPU like Nvidia, it's partnering directly with AI hyperscalers to develop custom AI chips that are tailored to their workloads. This has major cost advantages, as running workloads on these chips is far cheaper than on GPUs. However, they cannot be used in every situation, so there will always be a large place for Nvidia GPUs.

Next year, Broadcom expects its AI semiconductor revenue to double, and double again in 2028. That's huge growth and will also outperform Nvidia over that time frame. As a result, I think it's a top option to buy in addition to or instead of Nvidia.

Micron is a key supplier to both Broadcom and Nvidia, as it makes memory chips for computing devices. The memory chip industry has seen practically all of its production capacity consumed by the AI build-out, causing chip prices to soar. This has led to a record-setting year for Micron, but it could get even better.

During Micron's latest earnings report, its management team noted that market conditions will be worse in 2027 and 2028 than they were in 2026. When Micron says "worse," it means worse for its clients, not for itself. The company will do well because high demand for memory chips has driven up prices, translating into pure profit for Micron.

Historically, Micron has been a cyclical stock, which is why the market isn't valuing it at its full potential.

The market is valuing Micron's stock as if its business will evaporate tomorrow; we know that won't happen for several more years, given the strength of the AI build-out. This mismatch is your investment opportunity, and I think Micron is a top stock to buy now.

10 stocks we like better than Space Exploration Technologies ›

#2997. Airbnb vs. Shopify: Which Consumer Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

Airbnb's cash generation is substantial, but Shopify's growth rate and valuation gap raise a tougher question about what a dollar of future earnings is worth.

By Jake Lerch – Updated Nov 18, 2026 at 8:45AM EST

Will the future of growth be driven by global travel experiences or the expansion of independent digital commerce? Deciding between Airbnb (ABNB -0.04%)and Shopify (SHOP -0.21%)involves choosing between two very different platform leaders.

Airbnb connects millions of travelers with unique stays, while Shopify provides the software backbone for modern retail. Both companies benefit from powerful network effects, where more users or merchants make the platform more valuable for everyone involved.

Airbnb operates as a massive marketplace for lodging and experiences, connecting more than 5 million hosts with guests in roughly 220 countries. In its latest annual report, the company highlights its reliance on Amazon (AMZN +2.16%) for platform hosting and its use of third-party providers for community support. As the platform evolves, it is exploring the use of AI in travel to enhance its search capabilities and host support.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached nearly $13.9 billion. This represents a revenue growth of approximately 16.7% compared to the prior twelve-month period. During the same time frame, the company reported net income of nearly $3.2 billion.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the current ratio, which measures a company's ability to cover its short-term debts with liquid assets, reached roughly 1.4x. The debt-to-equity ratio, which measures total debt relative to shareholders' equity, is approximately 0.3x. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was close to $4.6 billion, though note that stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 34.3% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation.

Shopify serves as the central operating system for millions of merchants across 175 countries, providing tools for both online and in-store sales. The company supports everyone from small entrepreneurs to large enterprise brands, relying on partners like PayPal and Stripe for payment processing. This ecosystem approach allows it to scale without owning inventory, creating a software-centric business model with high recurring potential.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached close to $14.2 billion. This reflects a revenue growth of roughly 32.5% over the preceding period. Shopify also reported a net income of approximately $2.1 billion for these twelve months.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the current ratio is approximately 6.0x, indicating a strong ability to meet short-term obligations. The debt-to-equity ratio is roughly 0.0x, indicating a very low level of debt relative to equity. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was nearly $2.0 billion, and stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 22.1% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation.

Airbnb faces significant regulatory hurdles, such as the restrictions on short-term rentals in New York City, which could be adopted by other global cities. The company also competes intensely with major travel platforms like Booking Holdings (BKNG +0.09%), Expedia Group (EXPE +2.69%), and Trip.com Group (TCOM -1.02%), as well as search engines like Alphabet. Furthermore, an ongoing IRS tax audit involving a $1.3 billion claim adds a layer of financial uncertainty to the company's long-term outlook.

Airbnb appears to be the more conservatively valued stock, carrying both a lower Forward P/E and a lower P/S ratio compared to Shopify. The Forward P/E compares the stock price to future earnings estimates, while the P/S ratio is the market cap divided by sales over the past twelve months.

Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.

When comparing Airbnb and Shopify, investors should consider a few key factors. Let's have a look at them and see what that tells us about each stock.

Firstly, we should consider revenue growth. Here, Shopify can claim an advantage. Over the last three years, the company has averaged year-over-year revenue growth of 28.7%. What's more, in recent quarters, that growth has accelerated, with Shopify delivering 31.6% revenue growth in its most recent quarter. Airbnb's three-year average is 13.5%; its growth has also accelerated, with the company reporting 17.7% revenue growth in its most recent quarter.

Another factor to consider is each company's profitability. Both companies have been consistently profitable in recent years. However, Airbnb can claim an edge in the category. Its operating margin is 22.6%, while Shopify's is 18.1%.

Finally, there's valuation. Since both companies are delivering consistent profits, let's use price-to-earnings (P/E) to compare their valuations. Airbnb stock trades at a P/E multiple of 34x, while Shopify trades at around 87x. That makes Airbnb stock significantly more affordable.

To sum up, investors may want to consider both of these consumer stocks, given their impressive growth rates and profits. However, in this particular head-to-head comparison, Airbnb has the overall edge, in my view. The company's profitability, combined with its more reasonable valuation, complements its revenue growth, which exceeds 15%, making it my choice in this battle of consumer stocks.

#2994. Eliminate Before You Automate: The Agentic AI Step Missing From 2027 Plans

Murthy Malapaka builds enterprise intelligence for peak business performance, from autonomous IT operations to every workflow and data layer

As 2027 planning gets underway, most technology budgets I see include a line for agentic AI. Far fewer include a line for finding out which work should exist at all.

That gap is expensive. An agent placed on top of an unnecessary workflow does not remove the waste. It runs the waste faster, at scale, with a token bill and a new layer of oversight attached. The organization then reports automation gains on work that never needed doing.

I saw this with every customer we onboarded to our AI-native operations platform. Each arrived with plans to automate runbook tasks, password resets and routine end-user requests. When we ran historical intelligence on their ticket data, a large share of that work should never have been a ticket. Password resets belonged in self-service identity management. Runbook triggers belonged in existing monitoring and orchestration tools. Many end-user requests disappeared once their root causes were fixed. Those were one-time configuration changes, not candidates for an agent.

The better sequence is simple to state and hard to practice: Eliminate first, then decide what is left for AI.

Most enterprises are sitting on years of tickets, logs, alerts, change records and telemetry. This data is usually treated as an operational exhaust: kept for compliance, searched during incidents, then forgotten.

Read as a whole, it is a map of how work actually flows. It shows which requests recur every week, which alerts get closed without action, which approvals never get rejected and which handoffs exist only because two systems do not talk to each other.

No interviews or consulting workshops can match that record. It captures what people do, not what process documents say they do.

In my work building AI-native operations platforms, the approach that consistently delivers follows four steps.

1. Build intelligence on the current state. Mine operational data to see where work originates, how often it repeats and what business outcome, if any, it serves.

2. Diagnose the real constraint. Ask whether a given workload exists because of a process gap or a technology gap. The answer determines the fix.

3. Eliminate what should not exist. Retire redundant approvals, fix the root causes behind recurring requests and remove handoffs that add no judgment.

4. Then decide what is left for AI. Only the work that survives elimination earns an agent, and it should be work where speed, scale or consistency truly matters.

The same logic applies well beyond IT operations. In one software delivery engagement, we connected user stories, epics, test cases and years of historical bug reports. The pattern was clear. Many recurring defects traced back to requirements that were never written down. On a retail e-commerce site, for example, localization and currency rules were missing from the stories, so testers never covered them and the same bugs kept returning. Fixing the requirements gap eliminated whole classes of defects. Only then did we train a model on that history, giving the delivery pipeline context specific to the organization. Release times dropped, and code quality improved.

When teams follow this order, they are often surprised by how much smaller and more valuable the AI scope becomes.

The economic case is asymmetric. Work that is eliminated has no run cost, no model to maintain, no guardrails to govern and no incident surface. Work that is automated keeps all of those costs and adds new ones: inference spend, monitoring, exception handling and the human review agentic systems still require.

On a multi-tenant shared managed services platform I built over five years, with customers in insurance, manufacturing and wealth management, every onboarding started the same way. We ran historical intelligence across the customer’s in-scope ticket and request volume, often well over 200,000 records, and sorted each workload into one of three outcomes: eliminate, automate with agents or assist a human expert. Measured against that baseline, eliminating first removed 60% to 80% of the workload and cut operating costs by more than 35%. Most of that value came from the elimination step, not the automation step. It also let us onboard more customers each year while holding people and technology costs flat.

This matters for 2027 budgets because AI costs scale with usage. Automating a bloated process locks in a larger, recurring bill. Eliminating first shrinks the base that every future AI dollar is spent on.

Leaders do not need a new platform to start. They need a few deliberate commitments in this planning cycle.

• Fund a current-state diagnostic before any agent pilot. Scope it to one high-volume domain, such as IT service management or finance operations, and set a firm deadline.

• Set an elimination target alongside the automation target. Measure how much work was removed, not only how much was automated.

• Require a “why does this exist” review for every agent use case. If no one can name the business outcome the workflow serves, it is a candidate for elimination.

• Tie AI spend to the post-elimination baseline. Forecast inference and oversight costs on the work that remains, not on today’s volume.

The organizations that get the most from agentic AI in 2027 will be the ones that first had the discipline to stop doing work that does not serve the business.

The first question in any AI investment review should not be how fast an agent can perform a workload. It should be why that workload exists. Leaders who make that question the gate for every 2027 AI initiative will spend less, govern less and get more from the AI they deploy. Eliminate first. Then automate what is left.
