#2993. Docusign vs. Fastly: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

Docusign has moved far beyond e-signatures, but Fastly is growing revenue faster, and the valuation gap may tip the scales.

By Brendan Coffey – Updated Nov 18, 2026 at 8:50AM EST

Deciding between established software leaders and high-growth infrastructure providers involves weighing profitability against potential. Investors today are comparing Docusign (DOCU -0.90%) and Fastly (FSLY +5.09%) to see which fits better in a long-term portfolio.

Docusign dominates the digital agreement space, while Fastly powers the speed and security of the modern internet. While both operate within the software-as-a-service model, they serve very different niches. This comparison examines their financial health, growth trajectories, and valuation to help you determine which stock aligns with your investment strategy for 2027.

Docusign is a prominent name among tech stocks, providing an intelligent agreement management platform. The company has moved beyond basic e-signatures to help organizations automate the entire lifecycle of a contract. With over 1.8 million customers, its software integrates deeply with major enterprise systems from Salesforce.com Inc. (CRM -3.16%), Microsoft Corp. (MSFT -0.12%), SAP (SAP -3.78%), Alphabet Inc. (GOOG +1.23%), ServiceNow (NOW -1.10%), and Workday (WDAY -1.94%).

In the 12 months ended July 31, 2026, revenue reached about $3.4 billion, representing growth of approximately 8.6%. The company also reported a healthy net income of roughly $329.9 million during this period. This steady expansion highlights how Docusign is managing to maintain growth even as its core electronic signature market becomes more saturated.

As of its January 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio, which compares total debt to shareholder equity, is nearly 0.1x. Its current ratio of approximately 0.7x suggests that short-term liabilities currently exceed its cash and other liquid assets. In the fiscal year ended Jan. 31, 2026, free cash flow was close to $1.1 billion. Note that stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 53.4% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation because it is a non-cash expense added back.

Fastly provides an edge cloud platform designed to help developers build, deliver, and secure digital experiences at high speeds. The company serves global enterprises, particularly in the media and entertainment sectors, including major accounts like TikTok. Partnerships with Comcast Corp. (CMCSA -0.41%) and Jio Platforms further extend its reach. However, its top 10 customers generated roughly 32% of revenue in the 12 months ended December 2025, suggesting a degree of customer concentration.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached around $719.1 million, which is growth of roughly 21.5% over the previous period. Despite this double-digit top-line expansion, the company reported a net loss of approximately $62.9 million. This loss reflects the ongoing costs of scaling its global infrastructure and investing in its edge computing capabilities to compete with larger rivals.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the company maintains a current ratio of approximately 2.6x, indicating a strong ability to cover short-term obligations with current assets. Its debt-to-equity ratio is roughly 0.5x, showing a moderate level of debt relative to shareholder equity. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was approximately $65.8 million. However, note that stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 124.2% of operating cash flow, meaning reported cash generation is heavily inflated by this non-cash add-back.

Fastly carries risks related to its high customer concentration, particularly its reliance on major accounts like TikTok for a significant portion of its sales. The company competes against established content delivery networks like Akamai Technologies Inc. (AKAM +2.56%) and Cloudflare Inc. (NET +2.61%), as well as hyperscale providers such as Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN +1.98%), Google, and Microsoft. Furthermore, any major operational outages could damage its reputation, and the company remains dependent on a limited number of hardware suppliers.

Docusign is cheaper by Forward P/E, tracking future earnings estimates, while Fastly leads on P/S ratio measuring sales over the past twelve months.

Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.

For Docusign, sales in its current fiscal year are seen growing by nearly 9% to $3.5 billion, with a slightly better percentage gain in net income to $346 million.

Docusign's launch and global expansion of the IAM platform with the introduction of AI-powered tools should position the company for future growth. However, the not-so-great projected revenue growth rates suggest that Docusign may be entering a phase of more mature growth and a landscape of increasingly competitive digital agreement and contract management software. In particular, news reports OpenAI would launch a ChatGPT product that would compete head-on with Docusign in the document summary field caused some investor fears. Right now, however, the signature and identity verification part of Docusign's business appears unthreatened by ChatGPT.

Fastly, meanwhile, processes over 5 trillion requests a day, a huge number that is actually just a small part of the total addressable market (TAM) for the business. Management sees the TAM as $22 billion, giving it a long runway for growth. The company has posted three straight quarters of more than 20% growth (year-over-year).

One of the company's competitive edges, it says, is that it delivers its resources dynamically, allocating them in real time to whatever the load is on a global basis. So, for example, one Thursday night, its network might be delivering Thursday Night Football. On Black Friday, the exact same network is handling e-commerce. The next week, it might be handling a video game release. Fastly says that makes it a much more efficient network than competitors, who have siloed networks for security, compute, and delivery, et cetera.

For the current fiscal year, look for sales to grow to $741 million, a 19% rise over the prior year, with a much narrower net loss of about $72 million.

Fastly shares come at a premium to Docusign's, at least through the prism of forward P/E, but it brings along faster growth for the price. For 2027, Fastly is the stock that's the better buy here.

Your best shot at award seats on Qantas and Cathay Pacific flights is often through their own programs. That’s because airlines typically release the most award availability to their own loyalty program members.

While some partner airline programs might offer cheaper award pricing, it can be harder to find award availability through them. That’s why having points and miles with the airline you want to fly on can be so valuable.

This is especially helpful for airlines that operate highly sought-after routes or premium cabin products. For example, Cathay Pacific's Aria Suite in business class is a popular choice for flyers. #2990. Investors Love the S&P 500 Index. Here’s Why I Don’t.

The S&P 500 Index isn't what it used to be.

By Ryan Vanzo – Nov 18, 2026 at 8:56AM EST

10 stocks we like better than S&P 500 Index ›

The S&P 500 index (^GSPC +0.06%) is one of the most popular stock market indexes in the world. Roughly $16 trillion is invested globally in index funds and ETFs tracking the S&P 500. The Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO +0.13%) alone has $1.7 trillion in assets.

Charlie Munger, the longtime business partner of Warren Buffett, once claimed that "95% of people have no chance of beating the S&P 500 Index." But I'm not sure that advice is true in today's market. And there's one glaring reason why.

Most investors believe that the S&P 500 is a diversified basket of stocks that captures the valuation of the entire U.S. economy spanning a broad range of industries and sectors. That's true, but only up to a point.

During the dot-com bubble, technology stocks accounted for roughly one-third of the index. When the bubble burst, S&P 500 investors learned they weren't as diversified as they had believed.

The same proved true during the financial crisis, when financial stocks comprised roughly one-quarter of the entire index. When that bubble burst, the S&P 500's supposed diversification benefits proved less reliable than initially thought.

Today, nearly half of the S&P 500's value is tied up in either AI stocks or companies that supply the AI industry. The math isn't perfect, as many AI stocks engage in many other business activities besides AI. But the lofty valuations of these companies are very much tied to their AI efforts. If the AI story stumbles, nearly half of the S&P 500 could see their valuations compress sharply.

"Artificial intelligence concentration is increasing, both across the economy and in investor portfolios," research from Franklin Templeton warns. "[I]nvestors are now considering how to best mitigate concentration risk without sacrificing the gains from AI, which include economywide productivity growth and potentially superior investment returns."

In almost all cases, sticking with an index fund tracking the S&P 500 is prudent, even during market peaks. If you had purchased shares of an S&P 500 index fund at the peak of every bubble in history, you'd still be sitting on a healthy long-term profit. That's the power of long-term thinking.

The issue today is that the S&P 500 no longer functions like it did in the past. In past bubbles, peak industry concentrations ranged from 25% to 35%. Today's AI concentration hovers around 45%. The decline of a single industry, therefore, could drag down your entire portfolio.

Many long-term, risk-tolerant investors may do well sticking with their traditional index fund exposure. Risk-averse investors such as retirees and those on a fixed income, however, should reassess just how "diversified" their portfolios are. The S&P 500 remains a great index to track long term. But it's no longer the no-brainer investment it used to be.

#2987. If Stocks Tumble, History Says Investors Who Own This 1 Type of Stock Lose About Half as Much as Those Who Don’t.

In market drawdowns of 10% or more since 1973, dividend payers fell about half as much as non-payers. Here's the data and how to use it.

By Matt DiLallo – Nov 18, 2026 at 9:03AM EST

10 stocks we like better than S&P 500 Index ›

The S&P 500 (^GSPC +0.06%) fell 4.4% on Nov. 5, its worst day since April 2025. It was another reminder of how quickly stocks can tumble.

However, when stocks fall, not all tumble as much. Research from Hartford Funds, using Ned Davis Research data, shows that since 1973 the stocks that held up better in big declines have been dividend payers. In market drawdowns of 10% or more, dividend-paying stocks fell 14.4%, versus 28.2% for non-dividend-paying stocks. That's about half as much.

Here is what to look for in a dividend stock to help cushion the blow of a future stock market slump.

Hartford Fund's analysis covers every S&P 500 drawdown of 10% or more from 1973 through 2025. In those periods, dividend-paying stocks fell an average of 14.4%. The equal-weighted S&P 500, a good proxy for the average stock, fell 19%. Meanwhile, stocks that didn't pay dividends tumbled 28.2%.

In other words, dividend payers lost about half as much as non-payers during a stock market correction. While they still lost money, they helped preserve more wealth during a market downdraft.

Hartford suggested two reasons why dividend stocks tend to hold up much better than non-payers during a market downturn. Many dividend stocks tend to be concentrated in industries less sensitive to the economic cycle. For example, most consumer staples and utility stocks pay dividends because companies in these industries generate stable cash flow due to resilient demand.

Additionally, a company typically needs to have a track record of profitability and relatively predictable cash flow before it initiates a dividend. That business maturity would also make a company's stock price less volatile.

While dividend payers have historically delivered higher total returns with less volatility than non-payers, one group of dividend stocks stood out from the pack:

Companies that grew their dividends outperformed the average dividend stock and had lower volatility. Companies that cut or eliminated theirs lost money on average, with the most volatility of any group.

Hartford also found that the highest yields haven't been the best bet. Since 1930, stocks with the highest payout ratios (which typically have the highest yields) outperformed the market about half the time, similar to companies with much lower payout ratios. However, the sweet spot was companies with an average dividend payout ratio of 49%. These companies prioritized dividend payments while maintaining plenty of flexibility to continue growing their dividends even during more challenging times.

Those results point to a few simple ways to put the data to work before the next pullback.

While dividend stocks have historically helped cushion the blow during downturns, that doesn't guarantee they will outperform during the next one. For example, S&P 500 Dividend Aristocrats® (the term Dividend Aristocrats® is a registered trademark of Standard & Poor's Financial Services LLC) -- S&P 500 members with 25 or more years of annual dividend increases -- outperformed the market during the dot-com crash and global financial crisis. However, they underperformed during the COVID crash.

Further, weaker companies tend to cut their dividends during periods of market stress. As we saw before, dividend cutters and eliminators have historically delivered negative total returns. That's why it's important to check a company's dividend payout ratio to ensure it has plenty of cushion to weather a market downturn.

When stocks tumble, history shows dividend payers tend to fall about half as far as stocks that don't pay dividends, and dividend growers have done even better over time. It's a cushion, not a guarantee. If you're worried about a potential pullback, lean toward investing in companies with growing, well-covered dividends rather than non-payers and those with the highest yields.

#2985. World of Hyatt Adds Milestone Rewards, New Delta Benefits

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Hyatt is updating its rewards program in 2027, and it means you'll earn Milestone Rewards even sooner than before.

Editor/Content Strategist & Smart Travel Podcast Host

It’s going to be easier to rack up extra benefits if you’re a frequent Hyatt customer in 2027. World of Hyatt announced new Milestone Rewards, the ability to stack awards (such as Free Night Certificates and Suite Upgrade Awards) on a single stay and a simpler 365-day expiration on all awards.

The news expands on the fresh details revealed Nov. 17, 2026, around World of Hyatt’s partnership with Delta SkyMiles, which was first announced in September.

The additions to the Milestone Rewards are designed to give members more choice and personalization, according to Laurie Blair, senior vice president of global marketing and loyalty at Hyatt.

"We’re shaping the future of World of Hyatt around what our members value most. After a year of listening, one thing is clear: members want more distinctive benefits, more freedom to use their awards and the opportunity to choose awards that matter most to them,” Blair said in an email to NerdWallet.

But top-tier Globalist members will soon have to choose between perks that they previously received automatically. Most notably, Globalists will no longer receive free parking on award nights in 2027. Instead, they can choose a Free Parking Award as a Milestone Reward that they can apply to award or paid stays.

The Delta Air Lines and Hyatt partnership will also mainly benefit frequent flyers and hotel guests. With the exception of the limited-time intro promotion, only Delta or Hyatt members with elite status will earn points in both programs. Hyatt elites will have to purchase premium tickets on Delta — not economy — to earn Hyatt points on the flight.

Starting Jan. 1, 2027, World of Hyatt will extend Milestone Rewards to guests who have not yet qualified for the first level of elite status. Southwest Airlines did the same in its recent revamp to give loyal customers a thank you before they’ve reached any level of elite status.

World of Hyatt members will reach the first Milestone Reward at just 10 nights or 20,000 Base Points. Previously, it was 20 nights or 35,000 Base Points.

The reward choices at the first milestone are:

A tier-qualifying night credit, which gets you closer to the next level of elite status.

A $25 FIND Experience credit (Hyatt’s platform for local experiences such as cooking classes).

A $30 spa credit good at Hyatt Inclusive Collection resorts.

The latter two will likely still require you to pay money out of pocket to use them, as the credit will only cover a portion of your bill. For example, the cheapest spa treatment at Secrets Playa Mujeres Golf & Spa Resort in Cancun, Mexico, will still run you $109 (or $79 after the credit).

The Milestone Rewards start to get good at the higher tiers. Starting at 20 nights, you can select from the existing Milestone Rewards, as well as new items. Some of the new options include:

Free parking on award nights is going away as a Globalist tier benefit. In 2027, a Free Parking Award will be an option that Globalists can select at the 60, 70, 80 and 90 nights The parking award can be used on either a qualifying award or paid stay for up to seven nights.

Hyatt said in a call with NerdWallet that roughly 70% of Globalists weren’t using the free parking benefit at all.

Globalists who have earned status in 2026 for 2027 will be grandfathered into the automatic free parking on award stays through their tier expiration date in February 2028.

To use these new awards, the Hyatt booking process is also getting an upgrade. Previously, awards like Suite Upgrade Awards and Free Night Awards couldn’t be redeemed on the same stay. Starting in 2027, members can combine eligible awards on a single reservation, including Suite Upgrade Awards, Guest of Honor Awards and Free Parking Awards.

The new booking system will also make it easier to pay for some nights of a single reservation with awards, points, cash or a combination of points and cash.

Every award earned going forward will also carry a 365-day expiration from the date it’s issued, replacing the patchwork of different validity windows. Previously, Suite Upgrade and Guest of Honor Awards expired at “rest of year plus 14 days,” which was just a tad confusing. Meanwhile, Free Night Awards earned through Milestone Rewards were valid for 180 days from the date of issuance, which was not a lot of time to plan a trip.

The Milestone Rewards kick in next year, but the other big change around the Delta partnership is available now.

Hyatt elite members can earn World of Hyatt Bonus Points on eligible Delta flights (Delta Comfort, Premium Select, First Class and Delta One). Basic Economy or standard Main Cabin fares will earn nothing from this partnership at all.

Discoverist members earn 1 Bonus Point per $2 spent.

Explorist, Globalist and Lifetime Globalist members earn 1 Bonus Point per $1 spent.

Delta Medallion members (Silver through Diamond) can earn 1 Delta mile per $1 spent at participating Hyatt properties, on top of their regular Hyatt points.

Even if you don’t have elite status with either program, it’s still worth linking accounts to take advantage of the upcoming bonus point promotions:

Those who link their accounts and complete a qualifying Hyatt stay from Nov. 17 to Dec. 31, 2026, will earn one bonus Tier-Qualifying Night Credit.

A second bonus point offer runs Jan. 4 through Feb. 15, 2027, for members who take their first Delta flight or Hyatt stay after linking their accounts. Members will earn 1,000 Delta SkyMiles after the Hyatt stay or 1,000 Hyatt points after their first flight in a premium cabin on Delta.

Hyatt and Delta are also holding a sweepstakes through Nov. 23 — no points or miles required to enter — for a free three-night trip for two at Alila Mayakoba in Riviera Maya, Mexico, plus two $1,000 Delta gift cards. Linking your accounts before entering gets you a bonus entry.

If you are interested in dual accrual in 2027, there are some routes to elite status through travel credit cards. Hyatt’s entry-level elite tier comes as a benefit of holding the World of Hyatt Credit Card, but Discoverists earn Hyatt points at half the rate of Explorist and Globalist elites on premium Delta fares.

The launch of "Grand Theft Auto VI" is poised to take shares of Take-Two to the next level.

By Keith Noonan – Nov 18, 2026 at 9:15AM EST

10 stocks we like better than Take-Two Interactive Software ›

After years of anticipation and repeated release delays, Take-Two Interactive's (TTWO +6.19%) Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA VI) is finally hitting the market on Nov. 19. The game's debut is poised to be a watershed moment for the company and the video game industry at large, and it will likely wind up being one of the most successful entertainment products ever.

GTA VI is the most important game that Take-Two has released since it published Grand Theft Auto V all the way back in 2013, and it's poised to supercharge the company's sales and earnings performance. As such, I think Take-Two stock has what it takes to deliver big wins for shareholders through 2030.

Grand Theft Auto VI has been in development for over a decade and is a follow-up to the most successful game of all time -- GTA V. As of the most recent update from Take-Two, GTA V had shipped more than 235 million copies worldwide. The game also generated billions of dollars in sales through its online multiplayer mode.

Thanks to the combination of unit sales and revenue from in-game purchases, GTA V isn't just the most successful video game ever -- it's the single most profitable entertainment product ever released. Thanks to the high quality of the single-player game and the evolving, highly engaging nature of its online multiplayer mode, Grand Theft Auto V had incredible longevity. The game generated $1 billion in sales across its first three days on the market, and subsequent rereleases on new platforms and new content added to the game's online mode helped keep the title a key performance driver for Take-Two for 13 years. Now, Grand Theft Auto VI is poised to take the series and the company's net income performance to the next level.

The period shortly following GTA VI's release will almost certainly be followed by announcements of huge sales for the game, but investors should understand that these might not cause Take-Two stock to rise in the near term. With such a highly anticipated release, it's not unreasonable to expect that there could be a certain amount of "buy the rumor, sell the news" when it comes to the stock's performance shortly following GTA VI's release. Bearish pressures that have been impacting the broader market as of late could also put a damper on the company's stock performance.

On the other hand, I think the long-term outlook for Take-Two stock appears very promising. With this crucial and long-awaited title finally releasing, Take-Two looks like a worthwhile buy-and-hold investment through 2030.

Neeraj Sabharwal is Co-Founder at Trust3 AI, passionate about bridging the gap between business and technology.

​A few years ago, I watched an engineering team connect an autonomous agent to a production database “just to test it.” Nobody scoped the permissions. The agent inherited full developer-level access because that was the fastest path forward. It stayed that way for months until a routine audit flagged a service account nobody could explain.

That agent never did anything malicious. But it could have. And that’s the uncomfortable truth enterprises keep avoiding: We are handing out master keys to systems that act faster than we are building the locks to control them.

The distinction between a chatbot and an agent isn’t academic. A chatbot answers questions. An agent executes transactions, modifies records, moves data and triggers downstream workflows autonomously, at machine speed. When a chatbot gets something wrong, you get a bad answer. When an agent does, you get a bad action taken in production at a scale no human reviewer can intercept in real time.

Traditional identity and access management assumed a human requests access, uses it and is accountable for it. Agents break that assumption entirely. They are nonhuman identities that can be spun up, reconfigured and repurposed without the friction that normally triggers a permissions review. They don’t change roles through HR workflows. They keep running with whatever permissions they were granted on day one until someone remembers to check.

The result is a growing population of privileged digital workers operating with far less oversight than we would extend to any human employee with equivalent access.

Agent risk concentrates around three recurring failure patterns. None require a sophisticated attacker. They emerge from ordinary operational pressure.

Shadow Agents: Agents deployed without formal review, proofs of concept that quietly become production infrastructure. The pattern mirrors shadow IT, but the stakes are higher because agents act, not just store data. OWASP has begun cataloging this risk class in its guidance on nonhuman identities, flagging unmanaged automated agents as one of the fastest-growing attack surfaces in enterprise environments.

Blank-Check Access: Over-provisioning happens because scoping permissions precisely takes more effort than granting a broad standing role. That’s how the database agent I described ended up with developer-level access for a task that needed almost none. Gartner projects that by 2027, a significant share of AI-related security incidents will trace to misuse enabled by overly broad access—not external compromise.

Moving-Target Agents: Agents are constantly reconfigured as teams iterate. An agent built to summarize support tickets gets expanded to draft responses, then send them, then issue refunds—each step reasonable in isolation but none individually triggering a permissions review. By the time anyone looks closely, the agent’s actual capabilities bear little resemblance to what was originally approved. Under the EU AI Act, organizations remain accountable for what their autonomous systems do, regardless of how incrementally those capabilities evolved.

Each failure shares a common root: a lack of enterprise visibility into what agents exist, what they can do and whether their access still reflects their purpose.

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) and similar standards make it dramatically easier for agents to connect to enterprise tools and data sources. That’s genuinely valuable. It also accelerates the risks above.

Lower integration friction means agents can be connected to new systems faster than governance processes can track. A protocol that makes it trivial to grant access also makes it trivial to grant that access without formal evaluation. MCP doesn’t create the governance gap; it widens it by removing the technical friction that used to slow unmanaged access down.

This is also where authentication and authorization blur dangerously. Authenticating an agent, confirming it is who it claims to be, is a solved problem. Authorizing what that agent should be allowed to do, and continuously verifying that authorization still matches its current task, is not. Most enterprises can confirm an agent connected successfully. Far fewer can confirm it should have or that its access today still reflects its purpose today.

​I didn’t arrive at this framework from a whiteboard. It came from watching the same incident repeat across enterprise environments: an agent with too much access, discovered too late, with no auditable history of what it actually did. The controls needed to prevent it are consistent.

Discover every agent. You cannot govern what you cannot see. Enterprises need continuous discovery that captures every active agent, including shadow deployments that never went through formal registration.

Assign unique identities and purposes. Every agent needs a distinct identity tied to a defined purpose. If you can’t answer “What is this agent for?” in one sentence, it shouldn’t have access to anything yet.

Trace the full chain of action. Enterprises need an auditable record of what each agent did, when and why, not just whether it authenticated. That chain of custody is what turns incident response from guesswork into an investigation.

Enforce policy at the point of access. Governance can’t live only in a policy document. It must be enforced in real time, at the moment an agent requests data or attempts an action, checked against its defined purpose before execution, not after.

Replace standing access with just-in-time, purpose-scoped permissions. Grant agents the minimum permissions required for a specific task, for the duration of that task and nothing more. Standing privilege is a liability that accrues risk every day it goes unused.

Accountability for autonomous system behavior is already here and growing. Organizations that get this right will know which agents are running, what they can do and whether that access still makes sense. That starts with an honest audit and governance built on defined roles, scoped permissions and continuous oversight.​

#2977. Datadog vs. Figma: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

Datadog and Figma pull in opposite directions, one with real profits and one with rapid growth, and the valuation gap may be the deciding factor.

By Brendan Coffey – Updated Nov 18, 2026 at 9:20AM EST

As cloud complexity grows and digital design becomes more collaborative, choosing the right software platform is essential. Investors must weigh whether Datadog Inc. (DDOG +0.36%) or Figma Inc. (FIG -0.83%) provides the better long-term opportunity.

Datadog focuses on observability and security, helping companies monitor their cloud infrastructure and applications. Figma provides a collaborative platform for teams to design and build digital products together. Both companies have become staples in the software ecosystem, but they navigate different market dynamics and financial stages as they look toward 2027.

Datadog sells an AI-powered observability and security platform to organizations of all sizes. The company is a key player among tech stocks, offering tools that monitor infrastructure, logs, and data. It serves approximately 32,700 customers across more than 160 countries and maintains over 1,000 integrations to support various IT environments.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached about $4.3 billion, representing growth of approximately 33.2%. The company reported net income of roughly $262.0 million during this time, resulting in a net margin of about 6.1%. This profitability marks a steady progression as the business scales its suite of cloud-native services.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is 0.4x. This measures the company's total debt against its shareholder equity. The current ratio is 3.4x, indicating the company can comfortably cover its short-term obligations. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow reached about $1.0 billion. Note that stock-based compensation (SBC) represented roughly 71.5% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

Figma provides a collaborative design platform used by global product teams to build digital interfaces. Roughly 85% of its monthly active users are outside the U.S., with India serving as its second-largest market. In its latest annual report, the company noted it moved to an administrator-controlled provisioning model to streamline enterprise adoption and manage complex procurement requirements.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached about $1.4 billion, reflecting growth of roughly 44.4%. However, the company reported a net loss of about $562.5 million for the period, with a net margin of approximately -40.2%. These figures show a company prioritizing rapid expansion and AI investment over immediate profitability.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is 0.1x. The current ratio is 2.6x, demonstrating a healthy ability to meet its near-term financial commitments. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was approximately $246.2 million. Note that stock-based compensation represented roughly 544.2% of operating cash flow, meaning reported cash generation is heavily inflated by this non-cash add-back.

Datadog faces intense competition from established technology companies like Microsoft Corp. (MSFT -0.12%), open-source solutions, and native tools from cloud providers. It also competes with specialized rivals such as Dynatrace (DT +2.69%) and Cisco Systems (CSCO +0.32%). The company's reputation depends on protecting against cyber-attacks and data breaches. Rapid expansion into international markets adds risks from complex local regulations, while its reliance on Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN +2.16%) for cloud infrastructure presents ongoing operational challenges.

Figma relies heavily on the successful adoption of its AI-powered features, though these investments currently pressure operating margins. The company faces stiff competition from design suites like Adobe Systems Inc. (ADBE -2.13%) and emerging AI-native tools. Its reliance on Amazon for hosting its platform exposes it to risks of service outages. Additionally, recent shifts in billing models, including the transition to AI credit-based pricing, risk customer dissatisfaction and create challenges in maintaining high retention rates.

Figma appears cheaper than Datadog based on its P/S ratio, measuring value against sales over the past twelve months, and its Forward P/E.

Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.

Datadog is fast-growing, with revenue expected by Wall Street analysts to jump more than 31% to $4.47 billion in fiscal 2026, and net income to nearly double to more than $203 million. Yet there is some customer concentration risk. It is believed OpenAI is Datadog's largest customer, accounting for more than $100 million--perhaps well more--according to various analyst reports. There are also vague concerns that AI could develop tools that can replace Datadog's services, but that is a general concern for just about any software provider these days.

The good news is Datadog usage continues to increase with both new and established customers. Spending by its largest customer group is rising, with the number of customers providing annual recurring revenue of more than $100,000 accelerating, up about 20% in the third quarter compared to the year-ago period. That cohort rose 23% in the second quarter. Demand seems broad-based across both its AI and non-AI customers. Revenue growth from its non-AI customers climbed meaningfully, too, signaling a ramp in its enterprise segment.

Figma, meanwhile, has seen its user experience design solution become the industry standard for digital asset and mobile application development. The company uses this niche dominance to introduce additional modules, helping transform it from a single-point solution into a full design platform.

One differentiator from competitors is that Figma has done an excellent job not only presenting itself to developers, but to marketers and product managers who have to collaborate on designs. That gives the company more champions in an organization for its products.

For the current fiscal year, revenue should grow quickly, at about a 40% rate, to $1.49 billion. Look for a dramatic reduction in its net loss, from nearly $1.3 billion to about $490 million. Wall Street still sees similarly sized losses ahead for the foreseeable future, however.

So which cloud tech stock is the better buy? Datadog registers profit, which can sometimes be an overlooked metric for tech stocks. It comes at a growth stock premium, but rising sales and net income suggest Datadog can keep the momentum going through 2027 and beyond.

#2974. A Personal AI Assistant For Every One Of Us? Good Idea Or Not?

Michal Rahamim is Co-Founder & COO of Liberty Pixel, leading AI innovation, operations and technology strategy across its gaming portfolio.

​As someone born in the 1980s, I have to say that the world never stops messing with my head.

I was born into a world with no mobile phones, no home internet and, in the worst-case scenario, you went downstairs and yelled to your neighbor to come play with you. In the best-case scenario, you called their house, their parents answered and they let you speak to them.

I lived through the BBS revolution, the internet, then the smartphone, and just when I finally got used to having a TikTok account, I now have to start preparing for the fact that, at some point, I’m going to have a personal AI assistant. Whether it’s Grok Bot, Claude Duet or Meta’s Muse, new tools are popping up like mushrooms after the rain—and let me remind you, we’re in 2026.​

The agentic internet is growing fast, and I believe that around 2030 to 2035, your agent will simply talk to the agent of whatever website you’re visiting and take care of everything by itself based on very simple instructions from you.

This is already starting to happen today, but it will become far more common. And then comes the question: Is this even something you would want?

I’m not going to review all the new tools here. I’m more interested in the psychological and philosophical point behind all of this.

The advantages are obvious: less effort filtering emails and doing repetitive things that consume precious time from your life.

The disadvantages are also obvious: giving an agent enormous control over your life and your apps—okay, we aren’t at Skynet yet—and losing some control over the noise and activity in your own life, or more accurately, the weakening of the thinking muscle.

We already got used to asking our favorite chatbot to write letters to the tax authorities or customer support for us. Now it’s going to do those things on its own.

Ray Kurzweil defined the technological singularity as the point at which the pace of technological progress becomes so fast and exponential that we can no longer predict or fully understand the future, and the boundaries of progress can no longer really be mapped. His timeline estimated that human-level artificial intelligence, or AGI, would arrive around 2029, with the singularity itself arriving around 2045. According to him, that doesn’t leave us much time before we reach a stage where the human brain and technology—AI, nanotechnology and other systems—begin to merge, blurring the line between biological and synthetic.

More realistic estimates suggest that somewhere around 2035, the internet as we know it—browsers, manual searches and isolated apps—will disappear. It will be replaced by an economy of autonomous agents.

Every person, company and government system will have deeply capable AI agents that act, negotiate and make independent decisions 24/7 without human involvement. In other words, they’ll think for you.

Today, we think about reading the news, reading opinion columns—like this one, for example—playing games or enjoying a funny Reel. But once we give agents the power to do everything for us, will we feel that we have more time to enjoy those things, or will we become so passive that we’ll no longer even need to search the internet for the games we love and feel excited about when we find them? Instead, the games will be spoon-fed directly into our mouths—or, to be more accurate, directly into our brains—to the point where the experience of enjoyment itself may look completely different.

You probably think I’m exaggerating. But Kurzweil, that same futurist, argued that toward the end of the 2030s, the internet will become biological and nanobots—tiny robots the size of blood cells—will enter our bloodstream and navigate their way to the brain.

They’ll connect our cortex directly to the cloud. In other words, you want to watch a Reel? You just think about it.

The agentic internet becomes an “internet of thoughts.”​ If you want to know a language or understand quantum physics, you won’t need to search for it online. The AI directly inside your brain will provide the answer instantly, to the point where you may no longer know whether a thought came from your biological side or your digital side.

Admit it. It sounds like an episode of Black Mirror.

But it doesn’t stop there. Futurists argue that by around 2045—only about 20 years from now—humanoid robots will be working around us everywhere, and their prices will eventually become something like buying a pink vest on Temu.​

Then, robots will begin assembling other robots themselves.

Molecular robotics will eventually add the ability to change the structure of matter. This would mean that we could “manufacture” physical objects, clothing or even food directly from software, potentially solving global resource scarcity.

And then, as we approach 2045—the year of the singularity—the digital, non-biological part of our intelligence will become far more dominant than the biological part. Humans will be able to change their physical appearance at will, live inside virtual realities that feel completely real and perhaps even perform “mind uploading” to the cloud, effectively becoming digitally immortal.

Well, at this point, it’s a brave new world.​

Personally, I’m thinking twice before letting the new personal AI assistant take over my life just yet. Because what will I have left to enjoy if I no longer get the challenge of replying to—and arguing with—the customer service department of the website where I ordered my latest luxury bag?

#2972. Is Palantir Overvalued, or Is It Still a Buy at This Price?

Palantir trades at a high P/E ratio, but investors need to factor the company's expected growth into the equation before jumping to conclusions.

By Will Healy – Nov 18, 2026 at 9:22AM EST

10 stocks we like better than Palantir Technologies ›

Palantir (PLTR +0.21%) has attracted considerable attention among businesses and investors alike in recent years. Its data analytics tools have driven eye-popping productivity gains for its clients. As such, interest in its products has soared, and annual revenue growth is approaching triple-digit percentages.

Unfortunately, this has also drawn attention to its valuation, as rapid revenue growth typically means a stock will trade at a considerable premium. Despite its impressive revenue growth, I believe Palantir stock is overvalued. Here's why.

Palantir began as a company focused on supporting national defense and intelligence agencies. Its tools employ artificial intelligence to analyze data and deliver insights. In its early days, the help it provided to U.S. intelligence services in finding Osama bin Laden gained the company considerable attention.

However, seeing the limits of growth within that field, it turned its expertise to the commercial sector. While that broadening of its customer base led to increased growth, it was the release of its Artificial Intelligence Platform (AIP) that was the game changer.

Palantir began offering potential customers the opportunity to enroll in “boot camps” where they were able to immediately see how AIP could be applied to their actual business problems, and as a result, many of its clients began to discover ways to use it to noticeably increase productivity.

Among these companies is GE Aerospace, which applied AIP to fleet management and supply chain coordination, thereby increasing engine production. AIP also helped AIG automate insurance underwriting for more complicated commercial lines of business.

Such improvements helped drive Palantir’s revenue to nearly $5.9 billion in the first nine months of 2026, up 92% from the prior-year period, with a blowout Q3 boosting that growth.

Moreover, since its costs and expenses grew more slowly than revenue, its net income was nearly $3.1 billion during the same period. That was a 201% year-over-year increase. Amid this performance, it is not too surprising that Palantir stock is up by more than 2,300% since the beginning of 2023.

For 2026, revenue will grow 91% if the company's forecasts hold. However, analysts predict that growth will slow to 53% in 2027.

Even though a 53% yearly revenue increase is still impressive, investors tend to frown on slowing growth. That could bode poorly for Palantir, particularly given its lofty valuation.

Palantir now trades at 110 times trailing earnings. Moreover, its forward P/E ratio of 92 is similarly pricey. When also considering the forward 1-year P/E ratio of 62, these metrics suggest Palantir's stock price has years of expected growth already baked into it.

However, as high as these numbers sound, they also offer some hope to investors. The current stock price is around $165 per share as of this writing, a level it first reached in August 2025.

At that time, its P/E ratio stood at 575, while its forward P/E and forward 1-year P/E were 239 and 102, respectively. Over the past year or so, its valuation ratios have eased down to somewhat more reasonable levels.

That may not bode well for near-term stock price gains, though, since its valuations remain high and the stock has been essentially trading sideways for 15 months. On the other hand, Palantir's rapid revenue growth and rising profitability dramatically reduce the odds of this SaaS stock suffering a steep correction, suggesting it is more of a hold than a sell.

Based on Palantir's financial metrics, the stock is overvalued, but that does not mean investors should necessarily dismiss it as a potential portfolio holding.

Its stock price growth in recent years stemmed from the company’s ability to deliver palpable productivity gains to its customers. That has led to massive revenue growth that prompted investors to bid the shares up to high valuations.

Fortunately, Palantir's valuation has contracted somewhat in the past year. Since rapid revenue and profit growth have persisted, the stock offers current shareholders good reason to hold while also suggesting that future investors could buy at a lower premium. These factors alone make Palantir a stock that investors should continue to watch.

#2969. If You'd Invested $1,000 in Berkshire Hathaway (BRKB) Stock 20 Years Ago, Here's How Much You'd Have Today

By Selena Maranjian – Nov 18, 2026 at 9:35AM EST

10 stocks we like better than Berkshire Hathaway ›

Just about all of us know that Warren Buffett is one of the greatest investors ever, and many of us are familiar with the company he built into a trillion-dollar enterprise -- Berkshire Hathaway (BRKA -0.76%) (BRKB -0.95%). He grew the company's value by nearly 20% annually over some 60 years!

Let's say you parked a modest $1,000 in Berkshire Hathaway 20 years ago. What would it be worth today? Well, the answer is $8,310. The shares would have been trading for around $71.29 per share in November 2006, and more recently, they've been around $590 apiece. That's a total gain of 732%, and an annualized one of 11.16% (which still tops the S&P 500's average of 9.3% over the same period).

Whenever I report these kinds of numbers, I like to include reinvested dividends. Berkshire is not a dividend-paying stock at this point, as its leaders have preferred to plow excess earnings into furthering its growth -- and they've occasionally repurchased some shares, too. The S&P 500 does feature dividends, though, and with dividends reinvested over 20 years, its average annual gain would come to 10.6% -- still below Berkshire's gain, but not by a lot.

Multiplying your investment's value eightfold is pretty great. Can you expect that kind of growth over the next 20 years with Berkshire? Well, maybe. I certainly wouldn't count on average annual gains of 20% or more, as the company has delivered in the past -- because it can be especially hard for really large companies to grow.

But Berkshire is built to last, and features a lot of diversification. It owns many businesses in the insurance, energy, transportation, and manufacturing sectors, among others, and has a large portfolio of stocks, too. It's reasonable to hope or expect it to surpass the S&P 500's performance over the long run.

#2968. AI Governance Lessons From An Industry That Can't Afford Mistakes

Stephen Snyder is CEO of CareCloud, leading healthcare IT innovation via M&A, AI-powered solutions, and transformative tech strategy.

A single wrong word in a medical chart can follow a patient for years. If an AI-drafted clinical note mentions the wrong medication or a symptom the patient never had, and no one catches it, every provider who reads that chart afterward treats a version of the patient that doesn’t exist. That’s why every AI-drafted note should stay a suggestion until the provider accepts, rejects or corrects it.

Building safeguards like that one changed how I think about AI governance. A lot of CEOs treat it as paperwork that slows down the people building things. I don’t see it that way. Done right, governance is what lets a company use AI at scale without betting its reputation on every output.

I’ve spent most of my career in healthcare technology, where mistakes get expensive fast. A miscoded claim can turn into a denial, a payer audit or a refund demand. A mishandled patient record can become a HIPAA matter. That pressure forced us to build guardrails earlier than most companies do. Much of what we learned carries over to businesses outside healthcare, regulated or not.

Right now, most companies are adopting AI faster than they can figure out how to manage it. Teams sign up for new tools on their own, often before anyone in leadership knows. When I’ve seen companies stall, it’s usually because nobody documented the rules. If no one knows which uses are approved, every new idea turns into a debate, and the cautious approach wins by default.

Written guardrails fix most of that. Once teams know where they can experiment and where they need a second set of eyes, they stop asking permission for low-risk work.

The most useful governance decision we made was also the simplest: We sort every AI use by what a mistake would cost. The question is blunt: If this output is wrong, what happens?

A clumsy draft of an internal email costs someone a few minutes. A wrong number on a financial statement or a bad decision on a client’s account is a different story.

Low-stakes work runs with light oversight. Anything high stakes needs a named person to review it and sign off before it goes anywhere. For us, that means a provider approves every AI-drafted clinical note before it becomes part of a patient’s chart. Because we wrote those categories down in advance, nobody has to figure it out under pressure.

Healthcare makes you show your work. Auditors, payers and clients can ask how a decision was made, and “the system did it” doesn’t satisfy any of them.

Any company can hold itself to that standard. For an AI system that touches customers or money, you should be able to answer three questions: What went in? What came out? Who signed off?

Something will go wrong eventually. When it does, that record is how you find the problem quickly instead of reconstructing it from memory. It has another benefit, too: Employees are more willing to use AI when they know its work can be checked.

I like committees for writing policy. I don’t like them for running systems. Every AI tool in production should have one owner who watches how it performs, fields the complaints and has the authority to shut it off.

A governance council can still set the standards. But when a model starts drifting at 4 p.m. on a Friday, someone specific has to know it’s their problem.

It’s also possible to overdo all of this. If every use case needs committee review, governance turns into red tape, and people slip back to the unapproved tools.

Match the oversight to the risk and revisit the rules as your teams and tools mature. The goal is to catch the mistakes that would reach a customer and live with the fact that some small ones will get through.

You don’t need a regulator to tell you where AI could hurt your business. You can map it yourself.

This quarter, list every AI tool your teams use, approved or not. Next to each one, write down what happens if it’s wrong and who owns it. The blank spaces tell you where to start. For us, filling them in has also been the fastest way to get comfortable using AI more widely.

People in healthcare love the line about an ounce of prevention being worth a pound of cure. It applies to AI, too. Deciding what each tool is allowed to decide, how its work gets recorded and who owns it takes an afternoon. Cleaning up after an output nobody checked can take months. In a patient’s chart, it can take years.

#2964. Coca-Cola vs. Monster Beverage: Which Consumer Goods Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

Coca-Cola's global scale and steady bottler network go head-to-head with Monster's 20% revenue surge, but the valuation gap may settle the debate.

By Jake Lerch – Updated Nov 18, 2026 at 9:45AM EST

10 stocks we like better than Coca-Cola ›

Investors often choose between established dividend stability and high-octane growth. Choosing between Coca-Cola (KO -1.04%)and Monster Beverage (MNST +1.47%)involves weighing a massive global powerhouse against a rapidly expanding energy drink leader.

While both companies operate in the same broader industry, they serve very different market needs. Coca-Cola offers a diversified portfolio of sodas and juices, while Monster Beverage specializes in the high-growth energy category. This comparison examines their financial health and risk profiles to help you decide which is better.

Coca-Cola sells brands like Sprite, Fanta, and its namesake cola through a vast network of independent bottling partners and retailers in over 200 countries. One significant bottler accounts for nearly 10% of net operating revenues. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business. The company also manages the dairy subsidiary, fairlife, LLC, and maintains an equity investment in Monster Beverage to expand its reach.

In the 12 months ended Oct. 2, 2026, revenue reached approximately $51.1 billion, representing growth of nearly 7.1% over the prior year. Net income for the same period was roughly $14.6 billion. This growth reflects a steady recovery and pricing power in global markets despite varying economic conditions across its geographic segments.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 1.5x, which compares total debt to shareholder equity. The current ratio is roughly 1.5x, indicating its ability to cover short-term liabilities with current assets. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was nearly $5.3 billion, reinforcing its position among beverage stocks.

Monster Beverage develops and sells energy drinks, including Reign and NOS, and relies heavily on the Coca-Cola distribution network to reach 158 countries. Its primary customers include Coca-Cola Europacific Partners (CCEP -0.54%)and Coca-Cola Consolidated (COKE -1.26%), which account for roughly 15% and 10% of net sales, respectively. Such concentration adds a layer of risk to the business, as these two partners account for a significant share of distribution.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached approximately $9.6 billion, a significant growth of nearly 20.2% compared to the previous year. Net income for this period was roughly $2.2 billion. This expansion highlights the increasing consumer appetite for energy beverages and the company's ability to successfully scale its brands globally.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the company carries a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.0x, indicating it has no total debt relative to its equity. The current ratio is approximately 3.7x, suggesting a very strong ability to meet short-term financial obligations. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow reached nearly $2.0 billion. This financial flexibility allows for continued reinvestment into new product lines.

Coca-Cola faces pressure from global economic volatility and geopolitical instability that can disrupt its complex supply chain. The company must navigate intense competition from rivals such as PepsiCo (PEP -0.24%)and Keurig Dr Pepper (KDP +0.79%). Additionally, it manages ongoing tax litigation with the IRS and regulatory scrutiny regarding sugar-sweetened beverage taxes and environmental impacts of packaging.

Monster Beverage is vulnerable to category-specific regulations, such as potential age restrictions or limits on caffeine content in energy drinks. The company relies heavily on the Coca-Cola distribution system, meaning any strategic shift by its partner could impact market access. Furthermore, it faces increasing competition from nimble competitors such as Celsius Holdings (CELH +5.52%)and rising costs for raw materials like aluminum.

Monster Beverage carries a higher Forward P/E and P/S ratio, which divides market cap by sales over the past twelve months, than Coca-Cola.

Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.

When comparing Coca-Cola and Monster Beverage, investors should consider a few key factors. Let's have a look at them and see what that tells us about each stock.

Firstly, we should consider revenue growth. In this category, Monster gains a real edge. Over the last three years, it has averaged 11.8% year-over-year revenue growth, while Coca-Cola has averaged about 4.9%. Moreover, in recent quarters, Monster's revenue growth has surged well above its average, clocking in at 16.7% in its most recent quarter. Coca-Cola has also delivered above-average revenue growth, at 7% in its most recent report.

Another factor to consider is each company's profitability. Over the last 10 years, Coca-Cola has had an average operating margin of 27.1%, while Monster's was 31.7%, seemingly giving Monster the edge here. However, in recent years, Monster's profitability has drifted lower, while Coca-Cola's has increased. In fact, Coca-Cola has now overtaken Monster. Coca-Cola's operating margin is now 32.1%, while Monster's has fallen to 28.5%, giving Coca-Cola an advantage in this category.

Finally, there's valuation. Since both companies are profitable, it makes sense to compare their price-to-earnings (P/E) multiples. Coca-Cola has a P/E multiple of 29x, while Monster's is 40x. That gives Coca-Cola another edge, as its stock is more affordable.

To sum up, investors may want to consider both of these consumer stocks. However, given its more reasonable valuation and its higher profitability, Coca-Cola wins the battle between these two beverage giants, in my opinion. Nevertheless, given its impressive revenue growth, solid profitability, and reasonable valuation, Monster also remains a stock worth considering.

#2963. Rethinking Marketing In Prop Trading: When To Build, Buy And Automate

Justin Hertzberg is the CEO of FPFX Tech, PropAccount and BullRush, leading prop firm technology and white-label solutions.

A few months ago, a prop firm operator showed me an invoice—six weeks of work from a respected agency—and he wanted to know whether he was right to be annoyed.

For that money, he got a discovery deck, a competitor audit and a brand questionnaire. No post had gone live, no email had gone out and no new trader had signed up.

A discovery phase is not a waste. Any agency worth hiring needs to understand a business first. Still, six weeks without a published word is rarely one party’s fault. The scope may never have named a date for the first piece, the onboarding may have been built around interviews rather than output or the two sides may have disagreed about when paid work begins.

A fourth factor repeatedly emerges. Nobody on the account had worked in the industry. Before writing a line, they had to learn what an evaluation challenge is, how payouts work and what a firm can and cannot say. Part of that retainer bought their education.

Prop trading has its own vocabulary, its own legal lines and an audience that spots an outsider in the first sentence. An ordinary marketing agency needs weeks to find its bearings, and every piece after that still moves through briefs and revisions.

The market does not wait. Traders pay closest attention around a central bank decision or a sudden move in volatility, and commentary that lands 10 days later might as well not exist. A firm working from a quarterly plan ends up answering last month’s questions.

None of this argues against outside help. It argues for treating onboarding as a real line item and deciding who pays for it.

The firms that closed this gap did not find a better agency. They sorted the work by department requirements.

Build in-house what depends on knowing your traders. Program updates, payout explanations and anything related to claims about earnings need someone who knows those traders and where the legal lines sit.

Automate production when volume is the constraint. Tools loaded with a firm’s brand guidelines, challenge rules and market vocabulary get terminology right in a first draft, which mainly shortens the editing cycle. That is narrower than better marketing. What a firm can measure is time from idea to published piece and corrections per draft.

Buy outside expertise when it really is expertise. An agency that already works in this market and turns a piece around the same day is worth paying for, and some firms will always be better served by one than by hiring a team. The question isn’t in-house versus agency but whether the people you pay already know the market or are about to learn it on your budget.

Cost deserves the same care. Producing work in-house lowers the cost of a piece, not the cost of marketing. Software, staff time, review, legal checks and distribution still have to be covered. Production has become the cheap part, and a budget that still treats it as the expensive part is pointed the wrong way.

None of this means handing marketing to a machine. AI takes the production work: market commentary, program updates, social captions and email drafts—the volume that used to consume a team’s week. Creator partnerships and owned channels still carry the trust because an educator’s endorsement counts for more than reach.

The human job shifts from creating to deciding: picking topics, editing drafts, checking claims against restricted language and managing creator relationships.

A draft is only as good as its reviewer; a team that skips editing will publish generic copy faster than any agency could, and responsibility concentrates in one or two people. The model works when a firm hires for judgment rather than output, and it fails when nobody reads the work first.

These apply to an agency, a freelancer or a hire.

1. How long from signed contract to first published piece, and what in the scope guarantees it? If nothing holds that date in place, someone is funding an education.

2. Can the work respond to a market event the same day, and who approves it? Same-day response is a workflow question before it is a talent question.

3. How much of the budget goes to producing work versus putting it in front of people? Production is the cheap part now, and the split should show it.

The firms that gain a competitive advantage will be those that allocate resources effectively. By using AI to streamline content production while retaining human oversight of strategy, industry expertise and compliance, firms can build more responsive and efficient marketing operations. ​

In a fast-moving market like prop trading, the real value of AI lies in how effectively it supports business objectives, not simply in how much work it can produce.​

#2960. IonQ Stock Plunged 48% in Six Months. Is It a Bargain Buy?

A sharp share price decline doesn't always equal a bargain.

By Chris Neiger – Nov 18, 2026 at 9:47AM EST

Shares of IonQ (IONQ +0.04%) are down about 48% over the past six months as investors have headed for the exits amid worries the company is spending too much on acquisitions and raising too much capital at the expense of existing shareholder value.

IonQ has always been a speculative bet on an unproven market — quantum computing — but some investors may wonder whether the recent share price pullback makes IonQ stock a bargain right now.

Unfortunately, even with the recent drop, its shares still aren't in the bargain bin. Here's why investors are betting on IonQ, what the company has going for it, and why IonQ stock still isn't a good deal.

The biggest reason for IonQ's recent share price drop was the October announcement that the company would acquire Elisity, a zero-trust cybersecurity company. IonQ said it would make the $1.2 billion acquisition in an all-stock deal, diluting existing shareholders.

IonQ announced just a few days later that it was holding a $2 billion equity offering, cementing investors' concerns about share dilution. By the end of the month, IonQ's stock was down 31%.

This decline came months after IonQ's shares tumbled over the summer as investors fled riskier tech stocks. The AI trade came under pressure during that time as investors questioned the hundreds of billions of dollars tech companies are investing in data centers, and some of the negative sentiment spilled over into quantum computing stocks.

The result was a near-meltdown of IonQ's stock, pushing it down 48% since June.

It's not all bad news for IonQ. The company has a unique edge in the quantum computing space with its trapped-ion technology helping to reduce error rates (a major problem for quantum computers), and its revenue is climbing.

Sales jumped 336% to nearly $174 million in Q3 2026, and management recently raised its full-year guidance to $510 million, at the midpoint. The company also said it has an impressive backlog of $1.2 billion.

IonQ also has $3.7 billion in cash and cash equivalents, so there's no real concern about the company's ability to keep the lights on for the next few years.

There are two simple reasons the stock isn't a bargain: The company remains highly unprofitable, and its shares still look expensive despite the recent drop.

IonQ's operating losses were $433 million in Q3, and its trailing free cash flow was a negative $689 million. It's worth noting that while the company reported a GAAP (generally accepted accounting principles) net profit of $564 million in Q3 2026, management said this was due to an $896 million non-cash accounting gain from warrant revaluations rather than operational profitability.

IonQ CFO Inder Singh said on the latest earnings call that the company is thinking about profitability, but it hasn't publicly estimated when that will occur. "Now that we are moving forward toward potentially being the first quantum company to deliver $1 billion of revenue in the future, it is also time to begin to think about charting out our path to both revenue growth and profitability," Singh said.

What's more, IonQ stock is still expensive. Even after its sell-off, IonQ's shares have a price-to-sales (P/S) ratio of 29.6, which is far higher than the technology sector's average P/S ratio of 6.5.

That's nowhere near bargain territory for a stock, and given that IonQ won't be profitable anytime soon -- not to mention that it's betting on a very speculative quantum computing market -- investors should proceed with caution before buying this one. If you do pick up some shares right now, it's probably a good idea to add a little to your portfolio over time instead of going headfirst into a large position.

This rapid top-line expansion highlights the scaling nature of its integrated digital services across major markets like Brazil and Mexico.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 1.7x, while the current ratio is roughly 1.2x. The current ratio measures the ability of a company to cover its short-term debts with its short-term assets, providing a view of its immediate financial health. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow reached nearly $10.8 billion, reflecting the strong cash generation of its marketplace and fintech platforms.

Booking faces intense global competition from other online travel agencies like Airbnb Inc. (ABNB -0.04%) and technology giants like Alphabet Inc. (GOOG +1.23%). The company depends heavily on third-party traffic sources such as search engines and faces the risk of disintermediation by artificial intelligence assistants. Furthermore, it must navigate complex legal and regulatory landscapes, particularly in the European Union where its status as a gatekeeper imposes restrictive obligations.

MercadoLibre operates in highly competitive markets where it faces pressure from global retailers like Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN +2.16%) and low-price regional entrants. The business is exposed to significant macroeconomic volatility, including high inflation and currency devaluation in core markets such as Argentina and Brazil. Additionally, the company manages credit risk associated with its lending operations and faces potential cybersecurity threats across its integrated fintech and commerce services.

Booking carries a lower Forward P/E based on future earnings estimates, while MercadoLibre has a lower P/S ratio which compares stock price to sales over the past twelve months.

Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.

MercadoLibre has evolved from the so-called eBay of Latin America to something more akin to a combination of Amazon and PayPal Holdings Inc. (PYPL -1.03%). In 2025, the company made large investments in its Brazilian logistics network, cut down the free-shipping threshold in Brazil in June, and nearly doubled its consumer loan book. This drove impressive growth for the company and investors, with an increasing focus on financial services over delivering goods.

Yet the immediate concern with left-of-center Luis Lula winning the Brazilian presidential election last month is that the new administration will start addressing Brazil's high government and consumer debt levels, which will keep interest rates there around their current very high levels. That's bad for a consumer-loan-focused business like MercadoLibre, and shares have been hammered this week as a result.

Long-term, however, such fears are probably overblown. In fact, in the current fiscal year, revenue is expected to jump 45% to $41.9 billion, with slightly higher free cash flow and slightly lower net income. Overall, it's a good picture for MercadoLibre.

Booking Holdings is successfully shifting from an agency model to a primarily merchant model. That means it used to make its money as an agent--connecting travelers to a hotel and collecting a commission while the hotel manages collecting payment from the traveler. In the merchant model, Booking buys capacity from hotels and other providers on its platform and collects payment directly from the traveler. This tends to lead to fatter margins.

The company is also in excellent financial shape. It has $16 billion in cash, which makes its balance sheet investment grade. Another plus for shareholders is that the company has a $20 billion share buyback program. The brand is increasingly a destination for travelers, which means it is paying less to companies like Google for search engine visibility. Today, two-thirds of Booking.com's visitors are organic, meaning they are direct visitors rather than from paid ad traffic.

Revenue will grow about 9% this year to $29.3 billion. And net income takes a healthier 50% leap to about $8.1 billion.

Booking's shares are priced at a discount to the average S&P 500 stock and well below travel rival Airbnb. Yet the company provides more total sales and has good growth, expanding margins, and a pile of cash. It's too good a bargain to pass up at these prices. For 027, go with Booking Holdings
