#2953. 5E Advanced (FEAM) Q1 2027 Earnings Call Transcript

Early V-BOR ramp and grid-independence plans take center stage.

By Motley Fool Transcribing – Nov 18, 2026 at 9:53AM EST

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

5E Advanced (FEAM +8.12%) transitioned from a development-stage entity into an operating producer of borates and industrial minerals following the acquisition of Searles Valley Minerals on Oct. 1, 2026. Management reported that the acquisition includes three processing sites, 54 megawatts of cogeneration capacity, and established infrastructure acquired free and clear of legacy liabilities. The company is currently executing a strategy focused on commercial resets, cost optimization through grid independence, and volume recovery across its California assets. Management stated that boron's status as a critical mineral strengthens the company's strategic position as a domestic supplier to energy and defense markets.

Operator: Good afternoon, and thank you for joining us today for 5E Advanced Materials Fiscal First Quarter 2027 Conference Call and Shareholder Update. During today's call, management will reference the company's quarterly report on Form 10-Q for the quarterly period ended September 30, 2026, which is available in the Investor Relations section of the company's website and on the SEC's website. For a copy of the Form 10-Q, you may also contact PRA Communications at [email protected].

As a reminder, remarks made on today's conference call will contain forward-looking statements within the meaning of the safe harbor provisions of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995, including statements regarding the acquisition of the Searles Valley Minerals assets and the integration of the acquired operations, the bridge facility and promissory note entered in connection with the acquisition, the transition of customers to take-or-pay and fixed price offtake agreements, the ramp of V-BOR sales volumes and the recovery of V-BOR production towards approximately 100,000 short tons annually; the restart of the SAC plant, the restart of idle boric acid production, the well field development program, reducing reliance on purchase power and the expected cost savings, expected future results, cost, production capacity, market dynamics, capital expenditures, liquidity, cash spending, finance objectives and options, customer demand, purchase order commitments, offtake arrangements, customer qualification activities, commercialization strategy, development plans, engineering and project financing activities, including FEED-related work and the timing and scope of future engineering phases, advancement of supply chain initiatives and products, the potential benefits of our ASX delisting, the potential application of our products across energy, defense and industrial markets, government-based financing opportunities, including EXIM-related diligence, the company's ability to continue operating the small-scale facility and developing the project and the potential development of advanced boron derivative projects, including meta boric acid and ferroboron.

These statements are based on management's current expectations and involve risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially and adversely from those projected or discussed. Additionally, information concerning factors that could cause actual results to differ materially and adversely from these forward-looking statements is contained in our disclosures and public filings with the SEC, including our Form 10-Q for the quarter ended September 30, 2026. The company undertakes no obligation to update forward-looking statements, except as required by law.

Today's call may also include a discussion of non-GAAP financial measures as that term is defined in Regulation G, non-GAAP financial measures should not be considered in isolation from or as a substitute for financial information presented in compliance with GAAP. This afternoon's conference call is hosted by 5E Chief Executive Officer, Paul Weibel. Management will first lead off the call by making prepared comments, after which we will open the call for your questions. I will now turn the call over to Paul. Paul?

Paul Weibel: Good afternoon, and thank you for joining us today. The first quarter of fiscal year 2027 marks a defining moment for 5E Advanced Materials. On October 1, one day after quarter end, we closed our asset acquisition of Searles Valley Minerals, acquiring them free and clear of the prior owner's legacy liabilities and historical claims. With that closing, 5E transitioned from a development stage company into an operating revenue-generating producer of borates and industrial minerals. It is worth pausing on what we now own.

Searles Valley includes 3 processing sites, 54 megawatts of on-site cogeneration capacity, the Trona Railway short-line railroad, water utility, approximately 25,000 acres across 3 California counties and mineral tenure across more than 9,000 acres at Searles Lake, operated by an experienced workforce of approximately 250 people. The operation produces V-BOR, which is borax pentahydrate, sodium sulfate and salt, and it includes boric acid production capacity that is currently idled. Together with our Fort Cady project, 5E now holds 2 boron assets in Southern California at a time when boron has been added to the U.S. Department of the Interior's Critical Minerals list. We believe that positions 5E as a strategically important domestic supplier of critical minerals.

Because the acquisition closed just after quarter end, today, I want to focus on our first 5 weeks of ownership and our plan to grow the value of this platform moving forward. That plan is built on the 3 levers we laid out on our acquisition call, price, cost and volume. The focus is now on operational excellence and execution. Each one is already underway, and I will walk you through our progress. First, I'll look at our first month of operations. In October, we produced 6,200 tons of V-BOR, adding to approximately 3,000 tons of V-BOR inventory we carried into the month, and we sold approximately 2,500 tons.

We prioritized our domestic customers in October, while we build out export logistics through the Port of Long Beach. That network is now established, opening container shipments into Asia and the inventory we built in October is positioned to ship into that channel in November. With logistics in place and product on hand, we expect V-BOR sales volumes to ramp as we move through November and into December. Now to the levers starting with price. Through the bankruptcy process, the legacy below-market sales contracts were rejected. That gives us a clean slate on commercial terms, and we have transitioned customers onto new take-or-pay and fixed-price V-BOR offtake agreements.

In our first month, we achieved a V-BOR netback of approximately $767 per ton. Importantly, many of our November V-BOR orders have been prepaid, which speaks to the demand we are seeing for our product. Turning to cost. Power is one of our largest opportunities, and the solution is already on site. We plan to reduce the Westend plant's reliance on purchased power through greater use of our existing 54 megawatts of on-site cogeneration capacity. To enable that, we have engaged a third-party engineering firm to finalize the specifications for a capacitor. We are targeting having that capacitor on order by January with the objective of reducing our reliance on the grid by next summer.

We expect this initiative to require approximately $0.5 million of capital, and it would save approximately $38,000 per day on grid electricity purchases or roughly $14 million gross on an annualized basis, which we expect to reduce operating expenditures by approximately $8 million to $9 million. Beyond power, we are resetting the cost structure through organizational and procurement efficiencies and the elimination of duplicative corporate costs. On to volume. Current V-BOR production is approximately 82,000 short tons on an annualized basis.

Our objective is to recover production towards approximately 100,000 short tons annually through 2 initiatives: the restart of the SAC plant and an engineering-led well field development program, together with incremental byproduct production, including sodium bicarbonate and additional boric acid. We also plan to restart the idle boric acid production at our Trona facility, adding another product line from assets already in place. Reliability underpins that growth. On November 1, we commenced our first planned 5-day maintenance turnaround at the Westend plant. The team completed the work and restarted production on Friday, November 6. This planned downtime allowed us to address equipment reliability and maintenance items that are important to sustaining higher operating rates.

And it is one part of a broader effort to reduce unplanned downtime and strengthen operating performance. During our last update call, we emphasized the restart of the SAC plant, and it remains our most immediate volume catalyst. For those new to the story, SAC stands for Soda Ash Consolidation. It is a small existing facility that was idled as part of the soda ash exit last February, and it can operate independently of the legacy soda ash operation. The SAC plant is designed to capture natural gas emissions into the brine and reduce brine pH, improving brine chemistry and V-BOR output. Bringing it back online is a capital-light way to add volume.

I'm pleased to report that our team has begun the necessary prep work, including maintenance, readiness activities and the steps required for a safe startup. Our target is to have the SAC plant operational in January. Sustained volume growth starts with the resource. So we are also focused on the brine and well field system that underpins production. October brine grade was in line with our modeled expectations, consistent with the assumptions behind our production plan. Today, we kicked off a drilling and workover program addressing 205 wells with new and reworked wells targeting fresh tincal ore with the goal of recovering brine grade towards historical levels.

We also improved heat delivery on the lake by bypassing an underperforming heat exchanger, resulting in more consistent heat. Together with the SAC restart, these initiatives are intended to support stronger brine grades and higher V-BOR production. Beyond borates, our industrial salt and sodium sulfate businesses give us a diversified revenue base serving established industrial customers. Industrial salt operations transitioned seamlessly, averaging approximately 28 trucks per day, delivering industrial salt to key oil and gas customers in Bakersfield, California. In sodium sulfate, we used October to establish the rail and export logistics serving our customers in Mexico.

That work is done, and we are now moving product by rail to the Union Pacific line and onward into Mexico, setting up volumes to build from here. Searles Valley platform also gives us opportunities beyond our current operating plan. We have commenced 2 independent work streams focused on lithium and tungsten, both of which have the potential to become important byproducts that enhance our economics. Reputable third parties have received brine samples and will work to perform initial testing, analytical procedures and process recovery work. These opportunities are at an early stage, but we see them as meaningful optionality on top of our core borates business. We also see longer-term potential in borates expansion and sulfate of potash.

At Fort Cady, we continue to advance our advanced boron material strategy. In August, independent x-ray diffraction analysis confirmed the formation of iron boride in our ferroboron samples. We have since initiated testing at 1,400 degrees Celsius and are planning an approximately 500-gram batch with a third-party metallurgical processing partner as next steps towards producing samples for prospective customers. All of this is being done alongside the integration of the Searles Valley organization into 5E. We held our first employee town hall, and we are working closely with our employees as they transition on to 5E systems, and we have identified critical positions that we intend to fill. I want to personally recognize the Searles Valley team.

Their experience operating this asset is a real advantage for 5E, and I'm grateful for the work they have done during this initial transition. On financing, we ended the quarter with $15.6 million in cash and cash equivalents. And we received $7 million under our bridge facility at closing and are diligently working on the remaining CPs to draw on the remaining $3 million. Customer prepayments on November orders are supporting our working capital and our go-forward plan includes a working capital debt facility supported by our contracted offtake structure, which we are working now to finalize. We remain focused on solutions that optimize 5E's cost of capital.

To sum up, our first 5 weeks have been about establishing a reliable operating platform and a foundation for increasing production, and we have made strong progress. We completed a successful first month, streamlined logistics to drive sales, began resetting our commercial terms, completed a planned maintenance turnaround and advanced the SAC restart that can unlock additional production and sales volumes.

Looking ahead, our milestones are clear: ramping V-BOR sales through November and December, transitioning customers onto new take-or-pay and fixed-price offtake agreements, restarting the SAC plant in January, restarting idle boric acid production in Trona, placing the capacitor order by January, reducing our reliance on the grid by next summer and recovering V-BOR production towards approximately 100,000 short tons annually. Our focus remains on safely increasing volumes, improving reliability and cost and strengthening commercial execution. We believe the combination of Searles Valley's operating platform today and Fort Cady's long-term resource opportunity positions 5E for its next phase of growth, and we are excited about the road ahead. With that, we're ready to open up the call for questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Your first question is coming from Dmitry Silversteyn from Water Tower Research.

Dmitry Silversteyn: I just wanted to clarify your numbers on the sale of V-BOR -- production of V-BOR. You talked about 6,200 tons that you produced in November, and you had, I think you said 1,300 tons in inventory. So that's about 7,500 tons and you sold 2,500. So when you talk about ramp-up in November versus October, are you looking at kind of selling the rest of that? I'm just trying to understand what the run rate in November and December is going to be given the 2,500 ton sale in October.

Paul Weibel: Yes. Inventory was a little over 3,000 tons when we...

Paul Weibel: Yes, 3,000 tons. No, targeted production is about 8,200 tons. So I think we got in, met with the team and I think kind of came out of the gates and then planned for the kind of first downtime. We had a power outage that knocked us down for a day in that month, and then we kind of build back up the rates. So I think the goal and the target right now for November is approximately 8,300 tons. And I think you did 6,200 on month 1. I didn't quite know what it would look like once we came in, Pleasantly surprised to see about 3,000 tons in inventory.

And I think targeting on kind of hitting those rates.

Dmitry Silversteyn: Got it. Okay. And then just to clarify on the cost savings from the switching off the power grid and going to your cogeneration plant. You talked about $40 million in gross savings and then you talked about $8 million to $9 million in savings. Is that -- are both of those annual numbers?

Paul Weibel: Yes. No. So what will happen here is -- and it's good to get into those details. So approximately what we're buying from the grid at Westend is about $38,000 a day, right? So $38,000 times 365 gives you kind of your gross number that we're paying to SoCal Edison. The lines and the infrastructure are set up to fully decouple from the grid, but we get a voltage sag. And so we require a capacitor to ultimately stand that up. And so once we do that, we'll -- there's going to be an incremental MMBtu of natural gas we'll procure.

But all day long at $6 to $6.20 all-in MMBtu, that makes sense to buy that every day of the week. So the net savings, like the OpEx kind of reduction on a net basis is targeted to be $8 million to $9 million.

Dmitry Silversteyn: Understood. So that's -- okay. So that's the cost savings minus the purchase of gas and the cost of operating the plant.

Dmitry Silversteyn: Got it. Okay. And then in your 5-day outage -- maintenance outage, you talked about everything kind of going according to plan. Any -- maybe not surprises, but anything you've learned as you've worked through the maintenance of that equipment that affected you one way or the other about your plans?

Paul Weibel: No. Like it's a good question. I think there was a handful of safety fixes and get-rights that needed to occur right away. There was a tank that hadn't been cleaned out and emptied in about 10 years, hadn't seen the bottom of the tank. That was effectively drained and then cleaned out and the agitators were -- rigs were kind of maintained or working in good order. And there's a lot of leaks -- and we can quantify based on our concentrations, where we are in the process and the solution. A leak of 10 gallons a minute, if it's got 2% to 5%, whatever borax in it, that's dollars that are going on the ground.

So a lot of the focus was on that and just fixing a lot of the leaks and starting to build in redundancies that really focus on uptime reliability. So I think it's -- I think the punchline and takeaway was, listen, it needs TLC. That was a big focus out of the gate and kind of did that. And I think we -- it was very planned. So that's why I think we started November 1st or 2nd and came right out of it on the 5th.

Dmitry Silversteyn: Excellent. So it sounds like you're getting your hands around in at least the first 5 weeks around this asset and really starting to understand what levers you need to pull. So that's good to see.

Operator: Your next question is coming from Adam Kelsey from Titan Partners.

Adam Kelsey: Paul, just one point of clarity. How much of the current V-BOR output falls under the new take-or-pay contracts? And how quickly do you expect to address any remaining legacy contracts?

Paul Weibel: We have -- you're probably about 90% all in. The take-or-pays have -- when I look at them, there's minimum 62,000 tons under contract, but then they also have maximums. And I think not required to sell the maximum, but they're really great customers, and we want to service them. And I think there's a small percentage that are kind of spot or kind of smaller 1,000 tons a year to 1,500 tons that they're kind of contracts via a simple 1-page doc, but there's 5 customers right now, and that accounts for the majority of our volumes.

Adam Kelsey: And with respect to the customer prepayments in November, is that going to be a regular standard course of business? Or is this just kind of a onetime exception?

Paul Weibel: No. I think it's funny. The demand is very real. So I think some of the customers have figured out that, okay, happy to prepay if I can go higher in line and get my allocation. But all these offtakes come with about 60 days of documentary letters of credit. And so the goal here is to actually transition them from prepays. We're working with a financial institution that will basically stand up a working capital facility at basically SOFR plus 4%. And so all of these customers have been vetted. And once we're in the process of transitioning them over to the documentary LCs, which give us the working capital, that's for probably 3 out of the 5.

One of the other offtakes, actually, the customer negotiated, they're prepaying for the first 6 months. So you kind of -- you have a bit of a mix, and it is quite helpful on the working capital draw.

Adam Kelsey: Got it. And obviously, it's still early days with about 6 weeks since you acquired the asset. I would appreciate, though, to see any early learnings or anything that surprised you from the last 6 weeks?

Paul Weibel: No, great question. Listen, I think I don't -- I want to give the team a lot of credit for opening up those supply chains for all the exports. All the -- the majority of the sodium sulfate is going down into Mexico and 4 out of our 5 contracted by customers are all based out of Asia. And so you're dealing with -- they've been navigating. -- there's a new union contract getting negotiated in Long Beach that have kind of caused -- it's been moving, but like everyone is paying attention to that.

And I think there's inspections that have been required and just bills of lading needs to match and we stood up a new entity, the actual contracting entity was stood up probably maybe September 15th, 5E SVM was the buyer, but below 5E SVM are 3 stand-alone entities. And so all that -- there's a lot that goes into the basic execution of taking product up in Trona, packaging it, getting that onto a truck with a container, making sure that gets them into the right loading dock in Long Beach that gets on the right container destined for Malaysia, getting to then Malaysia and then to customers.

So that was probably -- we knew it would be not so straightforward. And maybe a little bit of turbulence there, but I think a lot of lessons learned, and we now are -- we're stood up and we're going. I think we're 15 trucks a day picking up all that product that's staged in the warehouse and it's moving.

Adam Kelsey: Great. Final question for me, and I'll jump back in the queue. You mentioned that there are some positions that you need to fill. I just want to clarify, are these existing legacy positions? Or are these newly created positions? And is there a theme amongst what you need to address?

Paul Weibel: Yes. I think there was -- when we came in, there was still employees that were kind of working through the wind down of some of the soda ash contracts. And so then there was some employees based at Overland Park that didn't get offers. And I think we didn't want to mess too much with org charts. And there was some kind of -- there was definitely a population of open roles that were on the org chart, but we sort of just said, let's get in, let's assess, and then go from there. And so I think HR has a role that we've posted, there's a mechanic. Utilities has 3 operators that they need to fill.

So we're gearing up to start posting those roles. And for the utilities team, they're critical roles because the stack plant literally sits right next to our utilities control room, and they have capacity to kind of manage the SAC plant as well. So we want to get those roles kind of filled to get people trained up. And it's -- we're not talking about a bunch of roles, but there's probably 5, 6, 7 roles that are going to get filled here in the next kind of 4 to 6 weeks.

And to the extent that SAC comes online here in January, as we expect, we have a 30-day drill program going into fresh tincal ore, if that can drive a higher brine grade, that drives more primary borax production, and that brings on Trona and restarting boric acid and maximizing Westend sooner than later. So I think we kind of -- my model is pretty conservative, but like we'll kind of see how it goes.

Operator: Your next question is coming from Heiko Ihle from H.C. Wainwright.

Heiko Ihle: Paul, I somehow got into the queue a little later than I thought, so bear with me here. But just building on the last question a little bit. Can you walk us through the mood at site as you're seeing it right now? How are customers -- or rather employees taking the transition? I assume everyone is getting along fine. It sounds like you're hiring additional staff, at least to a certain extent. Maybe just walk us through what you're seeing in the tranches and maybe give a bit of color beyond what we saw in the press release.

Paul Weibel: Yes. Heiko, glad you're here. Appreciate the question, too. Listen, the culture and that integration is probably one of the more taller orders in this acquisition. I think in the first kind of -- it took about 1.5 weeks or so, and then I've been up there twice a week with the team and just really getting to know our people. We had a town hall. We'll actually -- we're scheduling our next town hall. We'll do it after every quarter. A lot of questions. It was definitely a bumpy -- for a lot of the employees, we went from 25 people to 250 people as of October 1, approximately. And we had 5E benefits. Now we're a smaller company.

So our benefits weren't as good as what they previously had. But we were able to at least offer benefits and bolt everyone on. Now we'll go back to market here in the new year. And so I think out of the gate, there was definitely received skepticism as I think would be kind of normal, but I think there's a rational reason on why we've done something or made a decision. And similar to how I need to answer to shareholders, the leadership team here at 5E needs to answer to our employees. And there's not just an arbitrary decision.

And I think what we've seen is a positive inflection over culture as we just talk to people and get to know them. And so it's really that boots on the ground implementation and letting people know and explaining to them why we've done what we've done. And so candidly, out of the gate, probably saw some resistance. But I think once we've started to talk to people and really explain them and I've met with -- I've been able to make turnover shifts at 6:00 a.m. or 6:00 p.m. and I've gotten to talk to Westend teams and utilities, but not every team within the organization, there's 4 shifts.

So I'm trying to catch people at turnovers and just talk through them. And there's -- we're having leadership meetings on a weekly basis that basically can ensure that everyone is over the details of the organization because it really is an integrated facility and platform where power drives heat to the lake, lake drives brine and borates to Westend, Westend puts out tons, and they need power and good brine to run. So it's very much an integrated organization and just making sure people are informed and there's a rhyme and a reason for decision has been critical.

Heiko Ihle: Fair enough. Walk me through -- just as a follow-up, I guess, walk me through your conversations with clients. I mean, obviously, the economy and the world geopolitically has changed quite a bit in the last, call it, 9 months, 6 months, whatever. Capital markets are much more volatile than they were. I assume getting product from geopolitically safe jurisdictions is what they want. I assume a bit of a conversation in regards to paying a premium for that is actually going over reasonably well. Same thing, what are you seeing in your actual conversations that maybe you could comment here on a public call?

Paul Weibel: Yes, great question. I think the buying from a U.S. entity domestic is important. We have one of the best jurisdictions in the world. I think customers appreciate that third supplier in an oligopoly market, which is what we really are able to offer. And I'll be honest, like we've -- our commercial team has -- I've seen it through the website inbound as well as our commercial team. Mark's been in the borate business for 25-plus years. And, man, if we could produce 200,000 tons of V-BOR, we could sell the V-BOR. It is a very tight market.

I think USGS got it right in November last year by adding boron as a critical mineral, and it is truly a supply and demand story. And I think the belief is -- I think customers see it. A lot of these customers, Mark was able to be in Asia like the first week out of the acquisition. That definitely helped lay the groundwork for the prepays. And I think customers are quite uncomfortable being that this is an oligopoly structure, and they do like that it's an American-owned company that they're able to buy from.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Thank you. That concludes our Q&A session. I will now hand the conference back to Chief Executive Officer, Paul Weibel, for closing remarks. Please go ahead.

Paul Weibel: Thank you to everyone for joining the call today. We look forward to keeping you updated as we work hard to achieve the next phase of milestones. Have a great day.

Operator: Thank you. Everyone, this concludes today's event. You may disconnect at this time, and have a wonderful day. Thank you for your participation.

#2949. Under CEO Satya Nadella, Microsoft Stock Has Soared at a 23% Annualized Rate for 12 Years. Can the Tech Titan Keep Up the Pace?

Microsoft's AI spending is generating solid results, but sustaining rapid growth gets progressively harder for multitrillion-dollar companies.

By Marc Guberti – Nov 18, 2026 at 9:57AM EST

10 stocks we like better than Microsoft ›

Microsoft (MSFT -0.12%) has enjoyed a roughly 14-fold share price increase since CEO Satya Nadella took over in 2014. That amounts to an annualized growth rate of 23%, but some investors worry that the company’s heavy spending on AI could disrupt future gains.

Such worries are justified, since experienced investors may remember that the tech stock went through a “lost decade” of long-term negative returns before Nadella took over. No Microsoft shareholder wants a repeat of that, and while those concerns appear overblown, they shouldn’t be ignored.

In its fiscal 2027 Q1, Microsoft's results featured 19% year-over-year revenue growth. That was a little lower than prior quarters, but was still a respectable growth rate. One thing that stood out is the relative lack of growth in non-AI segments.

Microsoft groups all of its revenue under two categories: "agents and infrastructure" and "devices and consumer." The latter segment made up $15.5 billion of Microsoft's $92.3 billion in quarterly revenue. That part of the business was down by 3% year over year, with Xbox sales growth remaining sluggish for multiple years.

Unsurprisingly, the agents and infrastructure segment performed well, posting 25% year-over-year growth. Microsoft's AI spending goes toward this category, and its 73% year-over-year increase in commercial remaining performance obligations is a meaningful result.

Azure has been the company's bread and butter from a growth perspective, and it certainly didn't disappoint at the start of the tech giant's fiscal 2027. This part of the business was up 48% year over year, and Microsoft Cloud revenue was up 30% year over year.

It's important to keep this context in mind when assessing its rising AI infrastructure costs. Microsoft is the second-largest cloud infrastructure provider in the world, and is investing hundreds of millions of dollars a year into expanding and enhancing its cloud platform. If it reduces its capital expenditure, then No. 1 Amazon Web Services and Alphabet-owned No. 3 Google Cloud will be more than happy to take big bites out of Microsoft's market share.

Maintaining high growth rates for Azure will be critical to the stock's performance. If Microsoft’s cloud computing growth decelerates, it could trigger a prolonged correction for the stock. The company is sitting on enough cash to support higher AI spending, and each additional investment in infrastructure makes it that much harder for competitors to take any of Microsoft's AI data center market share.

Right now, its AI investments are bearing positive results. Elevated revenue growth rates and net operating income are some of the highlights. It's powering the remaining part of Microsoft's business that is still gaining market share, at a meaningful price that justifies the current price.

Although AI spending is necessary for Microsoft to keep up with the competition, that doesn't mean it will be able to maintain its long-term 23% annualized growth rate.

The company produced only a 16.1% annualized revenue growth rate over the past five years. It's hard for a company to deliver annualized stock returns that exceed its annualized revenue growth rate. That partially explains why Microsoft stock has only an annualized return of 9.9% over the past five years.

Microsoft is also approaching a $4 trillion market cap. It's harder for trillion-dollar tech giants to deliver the type of growth required to justify significant share price gains compared to smaller tech companies.

Microsoft's net income has been trending higher as its margins expand, but the company would likely have to deliver at least 23% year-over-year revenue growth over an extended period to achieve a steady 23% CAGR in its stock price again. That prior period of rapid stock price growth also included a time when Microsoft's cloud segment was much smaller, and a smaller amount of revenue and earnings gains were required to move the needle for the hyperscaler.

#2944. Should You Buy the Worst-Performing Magnificent Seven Stock of 2026 Before 2027?

Tesla’s EV business is beating expectations again. Its stock is still the worst performer among the Magnificent Seven this year.

By Prosper Junior Bakiny – Nov 18, 2026 at 10:05AM EST

The Magnificent Seven refers to a group of prominent market leaders. It includes Alphabet (GOOG +1.23%) (GOOGL +1.17%), Amazon (AMZN +1.98%), Apple (AAPL +0.85%), Meta Platforms (META -0.04%), Microsoft (MSFT -0.12%), Nvidia (NVDA -0.46%), and Tesla (TSLA +1.52%). They have been called "magnificent" because they are among the top players in their respective industries and have crushed broader equities over the long run. However, some of them haven't been so magnificent this year -- several have lagged the S&P 500 to date. And the worst-performing, as of writing, has been Tesla (though Nvidia is a very close second). Is the electric vehicle (EV) company a buy on the dip before 2027?

One puzzling fact about Tesla's performance this year is that despite lagging the market, its core EV business has beaten expectations. In the second and third quarters, Tesla's deliveries exceeded analysts' projections. There were several reasons for that. Here are two of the most important. First, Tesla benefited from macroeconomic factors. Conflicts in the Middle East led to soaring oil prices and, as a result, many consumers decided to buy EVs instead of gas-powered cars.

This led to a boost in sales across much of the industry. Second, Tesla's management has argued that the company's Full Self-Driving (FSD) software is increasingly attracting buyers. In the third quarter, the company's FSD attach rate (the percentage of new car buyers who opt in for the monthly FSD service) grew almost 20 percentage points quarter-over-quarter in North America, reaching over 75%.

Total FSD subscriptions for the period came in at 1.74 million, up 67% year-over-year (including lifetime subscriptions purchased upfront, though Tesla no longer offers those). On the earnings call, management confirmed FSD subscriptions are now generating revenue at an annual run rate approaching $1 billion.

That's a small fraction of the company's trailing 12-month revenue of $103.57 billion, but at the rate they are growing, FSD subscriptions could become a meaningful growth driver over the medium term. That could matter for the bottom line, since subscription revenue arguably comes with juicier margins than car sales. Over time, it could give Tesla's profits a lift.

So why has Tesla's stock dropped so much this year despite EV deliveries beating expectations and FSD subscriptions growing fast, which is driving demand for the company's vehicles? One reason is that its actual financial results have been mixed. In the third quarter, Tesla's revenue of about $28 billion remained pretty much flat year over year.

But the company's GAAP earnings per share of $0.22 dropped 44% compared to the year-ago period. Tesla R&D spending has increased significantly as the company continues to invest in future opportunities. The question is whether these projects can pay off. Consider Tesla's robotaxi ambitions.

It has also made some headway in that market this year. In September, Tesla launched the Cybercab, a two-seat autonomous vehicle built without a steering wheel, pedals, or mirrors. Tesla hopes it becomes the cornerstone of its robotaxi fleet. If it can scale its fleet over the next few years and attract significant business, robotaxi sales -- and profits -- might soar.

Tesla also recently announced it would start selling the Cybercab to select customers. It will cost about $30,000 upfront, pretax, plus a mandatory $299-per-month Autonomy Subscription (without it, the car can't go anywhere). It can be operated only in certain geographic locations.

At that price and with those subscription fees, Tesla could collect more than $35,000 in subscription fees alone over 10 years on each Cybercab -- so customers would essentially be spending a little more than the initial purchase price every decade they own it, assuming no price changes. If Tesla can attract enough customers, this business could become highly lucrative for the company.

With all that said, Tesla faces considerable uncertainty. First, the Cybercab may not attract the kind of business the company hopes for, whether as a robotaxi or for personal use. Second, Tesla could face significant pushback from regulators. In fact, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) opened an audit into how Tesla certified the Cybercab's compliance with federal safety standards as soon as it hit the roads back in September.

Third, Tesla's shares trade at a steep premium, which may be one of the most important reasons the stock has gone nowhere this year, despite progress in its robotaxi and core EV businesses. Shares are currently trading at 159.3x forward earnings. At current levels, I'd rather stay away. If Tesla stock falls much further before 2027, perhaps it'll be worth investing in the company.

#2942. Reactive Customer Success Was A Math Problem, Not A Discipline Problem

Abhishek Yadav is the founder and CEO of Meza AI, an AI customer success platform for B2B SaaS companies.

​For roughly a decade, the customer success profession has been given the same advice, and it’s been close to useless. Be proactive. Get ahead of risk. Don’t wait for the escalation. Every keynote says it, every onboarding deck repeats it, and almost every CSM I’ve met already agreed before anyone said it aloud.

Yet the function stayed stubbornly reactive, and the reason has nothing to do with willingness. We were handing out moral advice for a problem that was fundamentally arithmetic.

Consider the actual conditions of the job as it’s been staffed for most of its history. A CSM carries 40 to 100 accounts. The health dashboard refreshes weekly at best, and the signals that matter most, such as a champion going quiet or an integration failing silently, often don’t surface in it at all.

Under those conditions, proactive attention is a scarce resource you ration. The top handful of accounts get genuine foresight, and everyone else gets whatever you notice in the 30 minutes before their call.

That’s triage, and it’s the rational response to having less attention than you have accounts. The industry mistook a capacity constraint for a character flaw and then spent years telling practitioners to try harder.

This conversation is different now because the constraint itself is moving. Salesforce’s November 2025 State of Service research, a double-anonymous survey of 6,500 service professionals and decision makers across 40 countries, found that AI already handles around 30% of cases and that teams expect that to reach half by 2027.

The more useful figure is the quieter one in the same research: Reps working with AI spend about 20% less time on routine cases, roughly four hours a week returned to them.

Four hours a week is a proactive budget. It’s the difference between reviewing the accounts on your calendar and reviewing the accounts that need you, and it exists only because something else absorbed the mechanical work that used to consume it. The same research found that service professionals expect agentic AI to lift upsell revenue by around 15%, which tells you where that recovered attention goes once it exists.

The uncomfortable half of the story is that once detection becomes continuous and covers the entire book rather than a sampled top tier, the limiting factor becomes whether anyone’s willing to act on a signal before the evidence feels conclusive.

This is harder than it sounds, and the data suggests the profession hasn’t solved it. Gainsight’s 2023 Customer Success Index, produced with Benchmarkit across more than 400 North American SaaS companies, found that 48% had a formal digital customer success program. However, only 27% of those running one had well-established KPIs, while 60% described theirs as under construction. The tooling arrived considerably faster than the discipline did.

That gap is where reactive behavior survives even inside teams that have bought every platform. A signal with no owner, no threshold and no agreed response is a more expensive way to be surprised. Acting early means acting on incomplete information and occasionally being wrong in front of a customer, whereas acting late is emotionally safer because by then, the problem is undeniable and no one can question your judgment. Reactive has always been the defensible choice. That’s precisely why it persists.

The practical version is specific to each stage and to each role that owns it.

In onboarding, proactive means treating time to first value as the leading indicator of a renewal 11 months away rather than a setup milestone to close out. The CSM and the customer engineer own this jointly because most failures here are technical rather than relational, and a warmer relationship later won’t rescue a deployment that never cleared the customer’s data or security reality.

In adoption, the shift is from watching levels to watching direction. Most health scores tell you who’s red today, which is usually too late to act on. What matters is who’s drifting, the account still showing green but whose usage, breadth of active users or support sentiment has been bending the wrong way for six weeks.

In expansion, proactive means the account manager arrives with the consumption evidence before the customer hits a ceiling, not after procurement raises it. For the customer engineer, the most under-watched churn signal in B2B software remains the integration that fails quietly for a month while everyone assumes the quarter is fine.

If the mechanical work of noticing is being absorbed, then the value a practitioner adds moves decisively toward judgment. It’s no longer narrating what happened to an account. It’s deciding what happens next, early, with imperfect information and a willingness to be held to that call.

That’s a harder—and more valuable—job than the one most of us were hired into. The teams that make this transition will be the ones that defined, in advance, who owns which signal and what they’re empowered to do the moment it fires.

Patrick Mercer: Thank you, Trip. Good afternoon, everyone, and thanks for being with us today. The recently completed quarter included some of the most important structural progress we have made recently as a company. Key among the many recent developments was the completion of our manufacturing relocation to our new headquarters in San Jose. Also noteworthy during the quarter was the significant improvement in gross margins, increasing 10 percentage points year-over-year and 8 percentage points sequentially. During the third quarter of 2025, we recorded a one-time write-off of approximately $0.8 million to cost of goods sold. Excluding this impact, pro forma gross margin was 38.7%, representing a solid 370 basis point improvement.

Together, these examples underscore the meaningful progress underway as we continue to retool and reposition our business, executing on our commitment to achieving sustainable profitability. While we continue to make meaningful progress on our longer-term strategic initiatives and operational improvements, we did encounter some headwinds in the third quarter, with revenue coming in below expectation. This was primarily driven by the timing of international retina orders, international distributors working through program inventory accumulated in anticipation of our manufacturing relocation, and ongoing regulatory delays. The third quarter results were disappointing, particularly given that they diverged from the positive trends we had observed earlier in the quarter.

Regardless of the contributing factors, our results fell short of expectations, and we have already begun taking decisive steps to address these headwinds. Our focus is clear. Every significant decision we make during the remainder of 2026 will be guided by a single objective: positioning IRIDEX to achieve greater profitability in 2027. I'll spend part of today outlining the actions we are taking and what the path forward looks like. In reviewing our forward-looking plans, let's start with operations. On October 5th, we finished moving our manufacturing operations from Mountain View to newer, more efficient, and significantly less expensive space in nearby San Jose.

The relocation was a complex project, and our team executed it while keeping our quality systems intact. Since completing the move, we have successfully completed both our TUV and BSI audits, and we are now waiting on the final audit reports and certificates to initiate manufacturing for international markets at our new location. We anticipate this relocation to deliver approximately $600,000 in annualized rent savings, with additional opportunities for manufacturing benefits expected as the new site is fully integrated into day-to-day operations. The new location gives us a facility that is rightsized for the business we intend to run.

As we outlined on our last call, a change in our manufacturing address requires re-registration in a number of international markets, and this creates short windows where we cannot ship under the new registration. To protect our distributors and their customers during those windows, we built safety stock utilizing the old address. That increased inventory is now starting to convert to revenue as international regulatory clearances are completed, and we continue to receive orders tied to upcoming blackout periods. This will become a tailwind for cash flows as working capital and inventory is steadily converted back into cash.

The combination of our inventory investment and the lower-than-expected third quarter revenue resulted in a cash use of roughly $1 million in the quarter. As safety stock converts to revenue and we collect the related receivables, we are driving towards a return to cash flow break-even. Glaucoma developments continue to be very encouraging, and the U.S. G6 product family revenue grew, supported by higher average selling prices and an increase in system placements. Internationally, probe orders were lower in the quarter as distributors worked through inventory they purchased in the first half, a pattern we flagged last quarter. In retina, U.S. PASCAL sales were the highlight of this segment, with year-over-year sales increasing by approximately 50%.

The rest of the retina business was challenged as a mix of deferred orders, regulatory constraints, and competitive pricing in specific international markets impacted results. I will now discuss each segment in further detail, starting with glaucoma. We saw several bright spots in U.S. glaucoma performance throughout the quarter, driven by the same 3 factors we highlighted last quarter: Medicare LCD tailwinds, targeted outreach through MedScout, and higher average selling prices. First, the Medicare LCD changes continue to improve the reimbursement environment and are encouraging physicians to consider MicroPulse TLT with G6 earlier in the treatment pathway. Our 2-year clinical follow-up data on MicroPulse TLT reinforces that shift.

Longer-term outcome data gives us a strong foundation for physician education and supports earlier use of the therapy, including in selected patients with mild to moderate disease. Second, our utilization platform continues to sharpen our commercial focus. MedScout helps our team target mid-utilization accounts and high-volume MIGS surgeons, where we see the clearest path to greater adoption. We also left the American Academy of Ophthalmology Conference with strong physician interest and active commercial conversations, which we expect to support adoption and utilization in the months ahead. Third, pricing remains a meaningful contributor. U.S. G6 probe ASP increased in 2025, and we have held that higher price level consistently throughout 2026.

We believe this reflects the value physicians place on MicroPulse therapy. G6 probe volume in the U.S. was 6,900 units, roughly in line with the prior year period, and we placed 8 G6 systems in the U.S. compared to 7 in the prior year quarter. Global G6 probe volume was approximately 11,900 units versus 14,900 in the prior year, with the declines coming primarily from international distributor ordering patterns. On systems, we placed 28 G6 systems in the quarter compared to 30 in the third quarter of 2025. Going deeper into details impacting our international glaucoma business, in Europe, Middle East, and Africa, results were shaped mainly by order timing.

Distributors accelerated G6 console and probe orders in the first and second quarters, which reduced third-quarter demand, and tighter inventory and purchasing controls at one of our larger distribution partners added to the effect. Supply constraints also delayed fulfillment of some G6 Probe Illuminate orders. In Germany and Austria, they continue to perform above plan as we recover business previously handled by our former distributor. New G6 console placements remain competitive, particularly against the A.R.C. FOX platform. In Asia, continued economic challenges in China contributed to relatively stagnant order activity in the third quarter.

In Japan, customers had placed significant orders in the second quarter ahead of our headquarters relocation and the associated business transition, resulting in lighter third-quarter purchasing as anticipated. Stocking orders in Korea and Malaysia ahead of the address change helped partially offset softer demand elsewhere in the region. Importantly, all outstanding EndoProbe backorders carried over from the second quarter for customers in China and Japan have now been fulfilled. In Latin America and Canada, G6 probe sales were stable. Orders from Peru and Chile offset lower purchasing in Brazil, where our distributor built inventory in the second quarter. Canada continues to deliver steady results following the commercial changes we made earlier this year.

Overall, the drivers of our glaucoma business remain intact: favorable reimbursement, a growing body of clinical evidence, more focused selling, and disciplined pricing. We remain focused on turning those advantages into steady probe volume growth and additional system placements. Now turning to retina. Our retina strategy continues to rest on 3 priorities: advancing the PASCAL upgrade cycle in the U.S., expanding PASCAL's international reach, and securing regulatory clearances for our next-generation platforms. We saw several bright spots domestically this quarter: U.S. PASCAL revenue increased approximately 50% year-over-year. Internationally, retina faced challenges concentrated in Asia and Europe. Turning first to Asia, in Japan, our partner deferred PASCAL shipments into the fourth quarter after building inventory ahead of our manufacturing relocation.

This deferral included 1 particular order of approximately $300,000 that we expect to ship in the fourth quarter. In China, economic weakness, regulatory challenges, and slow tender cycles continue to limit activity. In India, registration delays continue to limit our business to PASCAL sales only. In Europe, Middle East, and Africa, medical retina faced aggressive pricing pressure from larger competitors across Europe. Delays in PASCAL MDR certification also continued to restrict sales in key markets, including Germany and Austria. We continue to expect PASCAL MDR approval in the first half of 2027 and anticipate solid demand once completed. In Latin America and Canada, PASCAL sales have resumed after early market disruption, and we expect further improvement through year-end.

We anticipate some of the third-quarter retina impact, especially the Japan shipments, could be realized in the fourth quarter. Competitive pricing and regulatory timelines likely could take longer to work through, and we are planning accordingly. I will also want to acknowledge the Middle East. We removed the region from our guidance earlier in the year, and recent developments in Saudi Arabia will continue to weigh on the activity in the region. We will continue to serve customers in the region where we can, but we are not including recovery in our near-term outlook.

Looking at the remainder of the year, particularly to the fourth quarter, we expect financial results to benefit from the release of remaining safety stock, open international orders, and the deferred Japan PASCAL shipments, along with the typical year-end seasonal lift. At the same time, we expect these benefits to be offset by a continuation of headwinds discussed today, namely regulatory delays and competitive pricing pressure in retina, along with continued volatility in international ordering. Accordingly, we are updating our full-year 2026 revenue guidance to $46 million to $48 million, which continues to exclude revenue from the Middle East.

While this lowers our outlook for 2026, these same decisions are why we believe 2027 to be a more profitable year for IRIDEX. Romeo will provide more detail in a moment. Looking ahead to 2027, we expect to see, for the first time, the combined benefit of our cost-saving and margin initiatives. This includes the San Jose facility savings, the administrative function transfer, and the operating expense reductions we have made over the past 2 years. Beyond these activities, we are evaluating and planning additional meaningful operating expense reductions, which we expect to further lower our cost base in 2027. Second, we expect meaningful gross margin improvement as our major products move to third-party contract manufacturers.

We remain on track to complete that transition in 2027, and once our major products are contract manufactured, we expect gross margins to increase. Third, we are undertaking a comprehensive strategic review of our product portfolio and distribution model with the objective of sharpening our focus on higher-margin, more profitable revenue streams. As part of this effort, we are evaluating opportunities to streamline our product lines and reduce the overall size and complexity of our portfolio. A more focused product offering will not only improve operational efficiency, but also help reduce the ongoing costs and complexities associated with product obsolescence, inventory management and maintaining regulatory clearances across multiple markets.

In parallel, we are assessing distribution alternatives in select international markets to better align our commercial structure with our profitability objectives. In some regions, this may mean accepting lower revenue in exchange for stronger margins, a lower cost to serve, and more predictable ordering patterns. Ultimately, we expect these efforts to result in higher margins, a lower cost structure, and a more consistent cash flow-generating business model. With that, I'll turn the call over to Romeo to review the financials.

Patrick Mercer: Thanks, Romeo. The foundation for next year is strong. #2939. Dolby (DLB) Q4 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Video patent program partners jumped from six to 47 as licensing momentum builds.

By Motley Fool Transcribing – Nov 18, 2026 at 10:08AM EST

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Management reported that Dolby (DLB -3.01%) is transitioning toward a high-performance culture with a focus on simplifying internal operations to accelerate product development. The company indicated that it intends to lead the industry in the AI era by integrating machine learning technologies into its research labs and expanding core capabilities beyond traditional entertainment use cases. Management stated that the long-term strategy involves diversifying business models toward recurring services and usage-based revenue to complement the durable licensing franchise. The company noted that the current macroeconomic environment impacts unit volumes across consumer electronics. Management reported that the company remains focused on disciplined capital allocation and operational efficiency.

Operator: Ladies and gentlemen, thank you for standing by. Welcome to the Dolby Laboratories Conference Call discussing Q4 fiscal year 2026 financial results. Marc Whitten: Thank you, Peter, and thanks to everyone tuning in. I'm excited to be here with you today on my first earnings call. For those of you who I've not had the chance to meet, allow me to provide a little background. I've spent my 30-plus-year career building, scaling and transforming media businesses through leadership roles at Microsoft with Xbox, Amazon with Fire TV, Meta, Sonos and Unity.

In those roles, I've helped connect creators, partners and consumers into some of the largest and most innovative content ecosystems in the world. I've led businesses through rapid change and significant and profitable growth. And I've been a Dolby customer many times over, licensing its technology in support of creating a more powerful and differentiated user experience. As someone who has spent his career following and using Dolby's industry-leading products, I'm here because I believe we have a unique opportunity to grow and scale this great brand. This is enabled by our mission-driven people, our technology expertise and IP, and our deep long-standing partnerships. In my first 2.5 months at Dolby, I've met countless valued partners and employees.

I've spent time understanding what we are doing well, where we have the right to win and what we must do to adapt in order to capture the opportunities in front of us. My conclusion is clear. Dolby has a highly durable and valuable licensing franchise. It has differentiated technology, exceptional partner relationships and the financial capacity to invest in growth. Our opportunity now is to operate with greater focus, to extend our leadership into the AI era and to identify and capture additional scalable sources of profitable growth.
